subtopic: Constant acceleration from integration: velocity, displacement and greatest displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration $-4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. At $t=0$ seconds its velocity is $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $3$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$. [2] (b) Show that the displacement $s$ meters at time $t$ is $s=3+10t-2t^2$. [2] (c) Find the greatest displacement of the particle from $O$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\int -4\,dt=-4t+c$ [M1] $v(0)=10$ gives $v=10-4t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=\int(10-4t)\,dt=10t-2t^2+k$ [M1] $s(0)=3$ so $k=3$ [A1] $s=3+10t-2t^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Greatest displacement occurs when $v=0$ [M1] $10-4t=0$ so $t=2.5$ [A1] $s=3+25-12.5=15.5$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The constant-acceleration formulas are just the result of integrating a constant twice, so use integration and the initial conditions. A turning point of the displacement occurs where the velocity is zero.

subtopic: Acceleration from velocity as a function of displacement using v dv/ds
statement: The velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ of a particle moving along a straight line, when its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $s$ meters, is given by $v=4-s^2$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that the acceleration is $a=2s^3-8s$. [3] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle when $s=1$. [1] (c) Find all values of $s$ for which the acceleration is zero. [2]
tips: When velocity is given in terms of displacement, the chain rule gives $a=v\frac{dv}{ds}$ directly, with no need to introduce time. Factorize fully when asked for zeros.

subtopic: Acceleration proportional to velocity: v dv/ds and dv/dt, never reaching the limit
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration $a=-0.5v\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is its velocity. At $t=0$ seconds the particle is at the origin $O$ with $v=8$. Let $s$ meters be the displacement from $O$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v=8-0.5s$. [4] (b) Hence find the value of $s$ at which $v=0$. [1] (c) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, find $v$ in terms of $t$. [3] (d) Find $s$ in terms of $t$, and hence explain why the particle never actually reaches the position found in part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-0.5v$ [M1] Since $v\ne0$, $\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-0.5$ [A1] $v=-0.5s+c$ [M1] $s=0,\ v=8$ gives $c=8$, so $v=8-0.5s$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $8-0.5s=0$ gives $s=16$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-0.5v$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{v}\,dv=\int -0.5\,dt$ [M1] $\ln v=-0.5t+c$ [A1] $v=8e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int 8e^{-0.5t}\,dt=-16e^{-0.5t}+k$ [M1] $s(0)=0$ gives $s=16-16e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] Since $e^{-0.5t}>0$ for all $t$, $s<16$ always, so $s=16$ is approached but never reached [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (a) you may divide by $v$ because the particle is moving. A particle can approach a limiting position as $t\to\infty$ without ever getting there, so check the time-based formula when a question asks whether a position is reached.

subtopic: Trigonometric displacement with exact total distance over a full period
statement: The displacement of a particle from a fixed point $O$ on a line is $s=t-2\sin t$ meters at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le2\pi$. (a) Find the exact values of $t$ for which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [4] (b) Find the exact displacement of the particle at each of these times. [2] (c) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle during the first $2\pi$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=1-2\cos t$ [M1][A1] $1-2\cos t=0$ gives $\cos t=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $s\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt3$ [A1] $s\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}+\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s(0)=0$ and $s(2\pi)=2\pi$. Sum the absolute changes between the turning points: [M1] $\left(\sqrt3-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\sqrt3\right)+\left(\sqrt3-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] $=4\sqrt3+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split the journey at every time when $v=0$ and add the absolute values of the changes in displacement. Check the sign of each change: here the first and last legs are in the negative direction relative to the previous point, so a sketch of $s$ values on a number line helps.

subtopic: Maximum speed on a closed interval with endpoint check and total distance
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity is $v=t^2-6t+5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le6$, where $t$ is in seconds. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin. (a) Find the time at which the velocity is least, and state the least value of $v$. [3] (b) Find the greatest speed of the particle during the six seconds, justifying your answer. [3] (c) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle in the six seconds. [4]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=2t-6=0$ [M1] $t=3$ [A1] $v(3)=9-18+5=-4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Speed is $|v|$. The least velocity is $-4$, which has speed $4$ [M1] At the endpoints $v(0)=5$ and $v(6)=5$ [A1] Since $v$ is a quadratic with least value $-4$ at $t=3$, on $0\le t\le6$ we have $-4\le v\le5$, so the greatest speed is $5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $v=(t-1)(t-5)=0$ at $t=1,\ 5$ [A1] $s=\displaystyle\int(t^2-6t+5)\,dt=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-3t^2+5t$ [M1] $s(1)=\dfrac73,\ s(5)=-\dfrac{25}{3},\ s(6)=-6$ [A1] Distance $=\dfrac73+\dfrac{32}{3}+\dfrac73=\dfrac{46}{3}$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Maximum speed on a closed interval can occur at an endpoint rather than at the stationary point of the velocity. Compare $|v|$ at the turning point of $v$ and at both ends.

subtopic: Acceleration given as an exponential: terminal velocity and displacement from rest
statement: A particle starts from rest at the origin $O$ and moves along a straight line with acceleration $a=12e^{-2t}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the value that $v$ approaches as $t\to\infty$, giving a reason. [1] (c) Show that the displacement from $O$ is $s=6t+3e^{-2t}-3$. [3] (d) Find the exact time at which the velocity is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and the exact displacement of the particle at that time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int12e^{-2t}\,dt=-6e^{-2t}+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=0$ gives $c=6$, so $v=6-6e^{-2t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to0$, so $v\to6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int(6-6e^{-2t})\,dt=6t+3e^{-2t}+k$ [M1][A1] $s(0)=0$ gives $3+k=0$, so $k=-3$ [A1] $s=6t+3e^{-2t}-3$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $6-6e^{-2t}=3$ gives $e^{-2t}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=\dfrac12\ln2$ [A1] $s=3\ln2+\dfrac32-3=3\ln2-\dfrac32$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the initial conditions after each integration to find the constants. A velocity that approaches a finite limit is a terminal velocity, found by letting $t\to\infty$.

subtopic: Simple harmonic style displacement: acceleration relation and maximum speed via amplitude
statement: Consider a particle on a straight line whose displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds is $s=3\sin2t+4\cos2t$ meters. (a) Find an expression for the velocity of the particle. [2] (b) Show that the acceleration $a$ satisfies $a=-4s$. [2] (c) Find the maximum speed of the particle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=6\cos2t-8\sin2t$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-12\sin2t-16\cos2t$ [M1][A1] $=-4(3\sin2t+4\cos2t)=-4s$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Write $6\cos2t-8\sin2t=R\cos(2t+\alpha)$ with $R=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $R=10$ [A1] The maximum speed is $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Combining a sine and a cosine of the same angle into a single cosine gives the amplitude immediately, which is the maximum value of $|v|$. Differentiate twice and compare with $s$ for the acceleration relation.

subtopic: Two particles with exponential and quadratic displacements: rest, meeting and greatest separation
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move along the same straight line. Their displacements from a fixed point $O$, in meters, at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, are $s_A=5te^{-0.2t}$ and $s_B=\dfrac{t^2}{4}$. (a) Show that $A$ is instantaneously at rest when $t=5$, and find the displacement of $A$ at this time. [4] (b) Find the time $t>0$ at which the particles meet. [2] (c) Find the greatest distance between the particles for $0\le t\le t_m$, where $t_m$ is the time found in part (b). [3] (d) Find the velocity of each particle at time $t_m$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v_A=5e^{-0.2t}-te^{-0.2t}$ [M1][A1] $=(5-t)e^{-0.2t}$, which is zero when $t=5$ since $e^{-0.2t}>0$ [A1] $s_A(5)=25e^{-1}=9.20$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) Solve $5te^{-0.2t}=\dfrac{t^2}{4}$ for $t>0$ using the GDC [M1] $t=6.01$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance apart $d=s_A-s_B$ (since $s_A\ge s_B$ on this interval) [M1] Maximum of $d$ on the GDC occurs at $t=2.69$ [A1] Greatest distance $=6.04$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v_A(6.01)=-0.304\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] $v_B=\dfrac t2=3.01\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to solve equations that cannot be rearranged, and report answers to 3 significant figures. When maximizing the gap between two particles, define the distance as one function and find its maximum on the correct interval.

subtopic: Vector position with Pythagorean speed: speed, distance and velocity parallel to a given direction
statement: A particle moves in a plane. Its position vector relative to the origin $O$ at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac13t^3-t \\ t^2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters. (a) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$, and hence the velocity and the speed of the particle when $t=2$. [3] (b) Show that the speed of the particle at time $t$ is $t^2+1$. [2] (c) Find the distance traveled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the exact value of $t$ at which the particle is moving in the direction of the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} t^2-1 \\ 2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf v(2)=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Speed $=\sqrt{9+16}=5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $|\mathbf v|^2=(t^2-1)^2+(2t)^2=t^4+2t^2+1$ [M1] $=(t^2+1)^2$, so speed $=t^2+1$ since $t^2+1>0$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^3(t^2+1)\,dt$ [M1] $=\left[\dfrac{t^3}{3}+t\right]_0^3=12$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) The components must be equal and positive: $t^2-1=2t$ [M1] $t^2-2t-1=0$ [A1] $t=1+\sqrt2$ (the root $1-\sqrt2$ is negative and rejected) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, and the distance traveled along a path is the integral of speed. For motion in a given direction, set the components of velocity in proportion and make sure both point the correct way.

subtopic: Projectile with parametric position: maximum height, range and clearing a fence
statement: A ball is hit from a point above horizontal ground. Its position at time $t$ seconds after being hit, in meters relative to the point on the ground directly below the hitting point, is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 18t \\ 1.2+14t-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$, for $t\ge0$ until the ball lands. The first component is horizontal distance and the second is height above the ground. (a) Find the maximum height of the ball above the ground. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball lands and the horizontal distance it has then traveled. [3] (c) A vertical fence of height $6$ m stands at a horizontal distance of $45$ m from the hitting point, in the path of the ball. Determine whether the ball passes over the fence. [3]
markscheme: (a) Vertical velocity $14-9.8t=0$ [M1] $t=1.43$ [A1] Maximum height $=1.2+14(1.4286)-4.9(1.4286)^2=11.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $1.2+14t-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=2.94$ s [A1] Horizontal distance $=18(2.9404)=52.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $18t=45$ gives $t=2.5$ [A1] Height $=1.2+35-30.625=5.575$ m [A1] Since $5.575<6$ the ball hits the fence and does not pass over it [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the time at which the ball reaches the fence from the horizontal component, then substitute into the vertical component. Use the GDC to solve the quadratic for landing time and keep full accuracy until the end.

subtopic: Projectile from a cliff: time of flight, impact speed and angle, minimum speed
statement: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff that is $10$ m above the sea. Its position, in meters, $t$ seconds after it is thrown, relative to the point at sea level directly below the throwing point, is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 25t\cos40^\circ \\ 10+25t\sin40^\circ-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$, where the first component is horizontal. (a) Find the time at which the stone hits the sea and its horizontal distance from the base of the cliff at that time. [4] (b) Find the speed of the stone when it hits the sea, and the angle below the horizontal at which it is moving. [4] (c) Find the minimum speed of the stone during its flight, and the time at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solve $10+25t\sin40^\circ-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=3.81$ s [A1] Horizontal distance $=25(3.8145)\cos40^\circ$ [M1] $=73.1$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 25\cos40^\circ \\ 25\sin40^\circ-9.8t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] At $t=3.8145$: $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 19.15 \\ -21.31 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Speed $=\sqrt{19.15^2+21.31^2}=28.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] Angle $=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{21.31}{19.15}\right)=48.1^\circ$ below the horizontal [A1] [4 marks] (c) The horizontal component is constant, so the speed is least when the vertical component is zero, at $t=\dfrac{25\sin40^\circ}{9.8}=1.64$ s [M1] Minimum speed $=25\cos40^\circ=19.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Horizontal velocity is constant in projectile motion, and the vertical velocity is the derivative of the vertical position. The speed is smallest when the vertical velocity component is zero, at the highest point.

subtopic: Elliptical path: velocity, speed function, extreme speeds and acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a plane so that its position vector at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t \end{pmatrix}$ meters relative to the origin, for $0\le t\le\pi$. (a) Find the velocity vector of the particle. [2] (b) Show that the speed of the particle is $\sqrt{9+7\sin^2t}$. [3] (c) Find the minimum and maximum speeds of the particle, and the values of $t$ at which they occur. [3] (d) Show that the acceleration vector satisfies $\mathbf a=-\mathbf r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} -4\sin t \\ 3\cos t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf v|^2=16\sin^2t+9\cos^2t$ [M1] $=9\sin^2t+9\cos^2t+7\sin^2t$ [A1] $=9+7\sin^2t$ using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ [A1] so speed $=\sqrt{9+7\sin^2t}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $0\le\sin^2t\le1$ [M1] Minimum speed $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=0$ and $t=\pi$ [A1] Maximum speed $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} -4\cos t \\ -3\sin t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=-\begin{pmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t \end{pmatrix}=-\mathbf r$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks]
tips: To find extreme speeds, rewrite the squared speed so that a single trigonometric term remains, then use its range. Remember that acceleration is the derivative of velocity, so differentiate componentwise twice.

subtopic: Vector position with quadratic components: parallel to an axis and exact minimum speed
statement: A drone moves in a horizontal plane. Its position vector relative to the origin at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 2t^2-3t \\ 8t-t^2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters. (a) Find the velocity vector and the acceleration vector at time $t$. [2] (b) The drone is moving parallel to the $y$-axis at time $t=T$. Find $T$ and the position vector of the drone at this time. [3] (c) Show that the square of the speed of the drone is $20t^2-56t+73$. [2] (d) Find the exact minimum speed of the drone. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 4t-3 \\ 8-2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x$-component of velocity is zero: $4t-3=0$ [M1] $T=\dfrac34$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac98 \\ \dfrac{87}{16} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|\mathbf v|^2=(4t-3)^2+(8-2t)^2$ [M1] $=16t^2-24t+9+64-32t+4t^2=20t^2-56t+73$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Minimum of $20t^2-56t+73$ at $t=\dfrac{56}{40}=\dfrac75$ [M1][A1] Minimum $|\mathbf v|^2=\dfrac{169}{5}$, so minimum speed $=\dfrac{13}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{13\sqrt5}{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Moving parallel to an axis means the other velocity component is zero. For a minimum speed, minimize the squared speed, which is a quadratic here, rather than differentiating a square root.

subtopic: Trigonometric acceleration: velocity never changes sign, distance equals displacement
statement: A particle starts at the origin $O$ and moves along a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=8\sin2t\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, and its initial velocity is $0$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$. [3] (b) Hence show that the particle never moves in the negative direction. [2] (c) Find the distance traveled by the particle during the first $\pi$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int8\sin2t\,dt=-4\cos2t+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=0$ gives $c=4$, so $v=4-4\cos2t$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $v=4(1-\cos2t)$ [M1] Since $\cos2t\le1$, $v\ge0$ for all $t$, so the particle never moves in the negative direction [R1] [2 marks] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int(4-4\cos2t)\,dt=4t-2\sin2t$ with $s(0)=0$ [M1][A1] Since $v\ge0$, distance equals displacement: $s(\pi)=4\pi$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If the velocity never changes sign, the distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement, so no splitting of the interval is needed. Use the initial condition immediately after each integration.

subtopic: Velocity with a reciprocal term: times at rest, total distance and final displacement on the GDC
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v=t-6+\dfrac{8}{t+1}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0\le t\le6$. (a) Show that the particle is at rest when $t^2-5t+2=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the times at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the six seconds. [2] (d) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position at $t=6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $t-6+\dfrac{8}{t+1}=0$ gives $(t-6)(t+1)+8=0$ [M1] $t^2-5t-6+8=t^2-5t+2=0$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}$, so $t=0.438$ and $t=4.56$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^6|v|\,dt$ [M1] $=4.79$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) Displacement $=\displaystyle\int_0^6v\,dt$ [M1] $=-2.43$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: On a calculator paper, enter $|v|$ into the integral for total distance rather than splitting by hand, but know the difference between $\int|v|\,dt$ and $\int v\,dt$. A negative displacement means the final position is on the negative side of the start.

subtopic: Inverse-square acceleration: v dv/ds with initial condition, greatest displacement and return speed
statement: A particle moves along a straight line away from the origin $O$. When its displacement from $O$ is $s$ meters, $s>0$, its acceleration is $a=-\dfrac{16}{s^2}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. When $s=2$, the velocity of the particle is $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v^2=\dfrac{32}{s}-12$. [4] (b) Find the greatest value of $s$ reached by the particle. [2] (c) Find the speed of the particle when $s=1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac{16}{s^2}$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int v\,dv=\int-16s^{-2}\,ds$ [M1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=\dfrac{16}{s}+c$ [A1] $s=2,\ v=2$: $2=8+c$, so $c=-6$ [A1] $v^2=\dfrac{32}{s}-12$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$: $\dfrac{32}{s}=12$ [M1] $s=\dfrac83$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v^2=32-12=20$, speed $=2\sqrt5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When acceleration is given in terms of position, separate variables using $a=v\frac{dv}{ds}$ and integrate both sides with respect to their own variable. The velocity is zero at the greatest displacement.

subtopic: Velocity requiring a substitution to integrate, then acceleration by the chain rule
statement: On a straight track, at time $t\ge0$ seconds, a particle has velocity $v=3t\sqrt{t^2+16}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. When $t=0$ the displacement of the particle from a fixed point $O$ is $0$. (a) Use the substitution $u=t^2+16$ to show that the displacement is $s=(t^2+16)^{\frac32}-64$. [4] (b) Hence find the displacement when $t=3$. [1] (c) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=3$. [3]
tips: A product of $t$ and a function of $t^2+16$ signals the substitution $u=t^2+16$. For the acceleration, differentiate with the product rule and the chain rule, then substitute the value of $t$.

subtopic: Displacement with a product of polynomial and exponential: rest, zero acceleration and exact maximum speed
statement: A bead slides along a straight wire. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $s=t^2e^{-t}$ meters. (a) Show that the velocity is $v=t(2-t)e^{-t}$. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle at the time $t>0$ when it is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Show that the acceleration is $a=(t^2-4t+2)e^{-t}$, and hence find the exact times at which the acceleration is zero. [4] (d) Find the exact maximum speed of the particle for $t\ge0$, justifying that it is the maximum. [4]
markscheme: (a) $v=2te^{-t}-t^2e^{-t}$ [M1] $=t(2-t)e^{-t}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $v=0$ with $t>0$ gives $t=2$ [A1] $s=4e^{-2}$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $a=(2-2t)e^{-t}-(2t-t^2)e^{-t}$ [M1] $=(t^2-4t+2)e^{-t}$ [AG] [A1] $t^2-4t+2=0$ [M1] $t=2\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) The speed is greatest where $a=0$, so evaluate $v$ at $t=2\pm\sqrt2$ [M1] $v(2-\sqrt2)=2(\sqrt2-1)e^{\sqrt2-2}\approx0.461$ [A1] $v(2+\sqrt2)=-2(\sqrt2+1)e^{-2-\sqrt2}\approx-0.159$, so the speed there is about $0.159$ [A1] Also $v=0$ at $t=0$ and $v\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, so the maximum speed is $2(\sqrt2-1)e^{\sqrt2-2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Candidates for maximum speed are the zeros of acceleration, but compare $|v|$ at each one and check the behavior at $t=0$ and as $t\to\infty$. Factorize the velocity before differentiating again to keep the algebra manageable.

subtopic: Vertical throw from a height: maximum height, time to hit the ground and impact speed
statement: A ball is thrown vertically upward from a point $1.5$ m above horizontal ground. Its height above the ground at time $t$ seconds is $s=1.5+12t-4.9t^2$ meters, until it hits the ground. (a) Find an expression for the velocity of the ball at time $t$. [1] (b) Find the maximum height of the ball above the ground. [3] (c) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (d) Find the speed of the ball when it hits the ground. [2]
tips: The maximum height occurs when the velocity is zero. Discard the negative root of the quadratic and remember that speed is the magnitude of the velocity, so give a positive value.

subtopic: Sinusoidal velocity with a constant offset: times at rest, total distance, displacement and greatest speed
statement: A particle moves along a straight line, starting at the origin $O$ at $t=0$. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v=3\sin(0.9t)-1.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (b) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the ten seconds. [3] (c) Find the displacement of the particle from $O$ when $t=10$. [2] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle during the ten seconds, and the time at which it first occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) Solve $3\sin(0.9t)-1.2=0$ on the GDC [M1] $t=0.457$ and $t=3.03$ [A1] and $t=7.44$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^{10}|v|\,dt$ [M1] using the turning times from part (a) as breakpoints (or the GDC absolute value) [A1] $=17.7$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s(10)=\displaystyle\int_0^{10}v\,dt$ [M1] $=-5.63$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) The velocity is least when $\sin(0.9t)=-1$, giving $v=-4.2$; the greatest positive velocity is only $1.8$, so the greatest speed is $4.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [M1][A1] This occurs when $0.9t=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so $t=5.24$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the GDC graph of $v$ to see how many times it crosses the axis before choosing breakpoints. For greatest speed compare the most negative and the most positive velocities, since speed is $|v|$.

subtopic: Plane motion with trigonometric component: velocity direction, distance along path and acceleration magnitude
statement: In a plane, a particle has position vector $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} t^2-4t \\ 3\sin2t \end{pmatrix}$ meters relative to the origin at time $t\ge0$ seconds, where $2t$ is in radians. (a) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$. The particle first moves parallel to the $y$-axis at time $t=T$; find $T$ and the velocity of the particle at this time. [4] (b) Find the distance traveled by the particle along its path from $t=0$ to $t=3$. [3] (c) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle when $t=1.5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 2t-4 \\ 6\cos2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Moving parallel to the $y$-axis requires $2t-4=0$ [M1] $T=2$ [A1] $\mathbf v(2)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -3.92 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^3|\mathbf v|\,dt$ [M1] $=\displaystyle\int_0^3\sqrt{(2t-4)^2+36\cos^22t}\,dt$ [A1] $=12.8$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -12\sin2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] At $t=1.5$: $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1.69 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $|\mathbf a|=2.62\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the calculator to radians for trigonometric functions of time. Path length is the integral of speed, not the magnitude of the displacement between the endpoints.

subtopic: Intervals where speed is increasing from the signs of velocity and acceleration
statement: The velocity of a particle on a straight path at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $v=t^2-5t+4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at time $t$. [1] (c) Find all values of $t\ge0$ for which the speed of the particle is increasing. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(t-1)(t-4)=0$ [M1] $t=1,\ t=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=2t-5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The speed is increasing when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign [R1] $v>0$ for $0\le t<1$ and $t>4$; $v<0$ for $1<t<4$; $a<0$ for $t<2.5$ and $a>0$ for $t>2.5$ [M1] Both negative: $1<t<\dfrac52$ [A1] Both positive: $t>4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and decreases when their signs differ. Build a sign table using the zeros of $v$ and $a$ to avoid missing an interval.

subtopic: Acceleration proportional to displacement: v dv/ds, amplitude, verification and time to reach a position
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its acceleration is $a=-9s\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $s$ meters is its displacement from a fixed point $O$. At $t=0$ seconds the particle is at $O$ with velocity $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the positive direction. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v^2=144-9s^2$. [4] (b) Find the greatest displacement of the particle from $O$. [2] (c) Verify that $s=4\sin3t$ satisfies the acceleration relation and both initial conditions. [3] (d) Find the first time at which the particle is at $s=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-9s$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int v\,dv=\int-9s\,ds$ [A1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=-\dfrac{9s^2}{2}+c$ [A1] $s=0,\ v=12$ gives $c=72$, so $v^2=144-9s^2$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$: $9s^2=144$ [M1] $s=4$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v=12\cos3t$ and $a=-36\sin3t=-9(4\sin3t)=-9s$ [A1][A1] $s(0)=0$ and $v(0)=12$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4\sin3t=2$ gives $\sin3t=\dfrac12$ [M1] First positive solution $3t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{18}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Acceleration proportional to negative displacement produces oscillation, and the greatest displacement is where the velocity is zero. To verify a proposed solution, differentiate it twice and check the initial values too.

subtopic: Acceleration depending on velocity squared: separation of variables with arctan, stopping time and distance
statement: A particle travels on a straight track with acceleration $a=-(1+v^2)\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is its velocity at time $t$ seconds. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$ with $v=1$. Let $s$ meters be its displacement from $O$. (a) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, show that $v=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)$ for as long as $v>0$. [4] (b) Find the exact time at which the particle first comes to rest. [1] (c) By using $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$, find an expression for $s$ in terms of $v$, and hence find the exact distance the particle travels before coming to rest. [4] (d) Verify your answer to part (c) by integrating the velocity found in part (a). [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-(1+v^2)$ so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int-1\,dt$ [M1] $\arctan v=-t+c$ [A1] $v(0)=1$ gives $c=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] $v=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t=0$, so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-(1+v^2)$ so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{v}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int-1\,ds$ [M1] $\dfrac12\ln(1+v^2)=-s+c$ [A1] $s=0,\ v=1$ gives $c=\dfrac12\ln2$, so $s=\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{2}{1+v^2}$ [A1] At rest, $v=0$: $s=\dfrac12\ln2$ m [A1] [4 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)dt$ [M1] $=\left[\ln\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)\right]_0^{\pi/4}$ [A1] $=\ln1-\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac12\ln2$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose the form of acceleration that matches the variables in the equation: $\frac{dv}{dt}$ gives velocity against time, while $v\frac{dv}{ds}$ gives velocity against position. Recognize $\frac{1}{1+v^2}$ as the derivative of arctan, and $\frac{v}{1+v^2}$ as a logarithmic derivative.

subtopic: Two particles in the plane: velocities, no collision and minimum distance between them
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move in a plane. Relative to the origin, their position vectors at time $t\ge0$ seconds are $\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix} 1+2t \\ 4-t \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix} 8-t \\ 1+t \end{pmatrix}$, in meters. (a) Find the speed of each particle. [2] (b) Show that the particles never collide. [2] (c) Show that the square of the distance between the particles at time $t$ is $13t^2-54t+58$. [2] (d) Find the minimum distance between the particles and the time at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v_A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, speed $\sqrt5=2.24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] $\mathbf v_B=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, speed $\sqrt2=1.41\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Equal $x$: $1+2t=8-t$ gives $t=\dfrac73$; equal $y$: $4-t=1+t$ gives $t=\dfrac32$ [M1] The times differ, so the particles are never at the same point at the same time [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix} 7-3t \\ 2t-3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $d^2=(7-3t)^2+(2t-3)^2=13t^2-54t+58$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Minimum of $\sqrt{13t^2-54t+58}$ found on the GDC (or at $t=\dfrac{54}{26}$) [M1] $t=2.08$ s [A1] Minimum distance $=1.39$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To show two moving points never collide, find the times that match each coordinate separately and show they disagree. Minimizing the squared distance gives the same time as minimizing the distance.

subtopic: Quartic with a complex root and real coefficients
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=x^4-6x^3+ax^2-30x+25$ has real coefficients, and $1+2i$ is a root of $p(x)=0$. (a) Write down a second complex root of $p(x)=0$. [1] (b) Hence show that $x^2-2x+5$ is a factor of $p(x)$. [2] (c) Find the value of $a$. [3] (d) Solve $p(x)=0$ completely. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-2i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sum of the two roots $=2$ and product $=1+4=5$ [M1] so $(x-(1+2i))(x-(1-2i))=x^2-2x+5$ is a factor [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) $p(x)=(x^2-2x+5)(x^2+qx+5)$ [M1] Coefficient of $x^3$: $q-2=-6$, so $q=-4$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^2$: $5-2q+5=a$, so $a=18$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Other factor $x^2-4x+5=0$ [M1] $x=2\pm i$ so the roots are $1\pm2i$ and $2\pm i$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, and a conjugate pair always gives a real quadratic factor. Equate coefficients after writing the second quadratic factor with a constant term chosen so the constant terms match.

subtopic: Cubic with roots in arithmetic progression
statement: The equation $x^3-12x^2+kx-28=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, has three real roots in arithmetic progression. (a) Show that one of the roots is $4$. [2] (b) Find the three roots and the value of $k$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Let the roots be $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$. Sum of roots $=3a=12$ [M1] so $a=4$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Product of roots: $4(16-d^2)=28$ [M1] $d^2=9$, so $d=\pm3$ [A1] The roots are $1$, $4$, $7$ [A1] Sum of products in pairs: $k=1\times4+4\times7+1\times7$ [M1] $=39$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Writing three terms of an arithmetic progression as $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$ makes the sum of roots collapse to $3a$ immediately. Then use the product (or pair sums) of the roots to find $d$ and the unknown coefficient.

subtopic: Cubic with roots in geometric progression
statement: The equation $x^3-7x^2+kx-8=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, has three real roots that form a geometric progression. (a) Show that one of the roots is $2$. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the other two roots. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let the roots be $\dfrac{a}{r}$, $a$, $ar$. Product of roots $=a^3=8$ [M1] so $a=2$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $x=2$ is a root: $8-28+2k-8=0$ [M1] $k=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Divide by $(x-2)$: $x^3-7x^2+14x-8=(x-2)(x^2-5x+4)$ [M1] [A1] $=(x-2)(x-1)(x-4)$ so the other roots are $1$ and $4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Writing the roots as $a/r$, $a$, $ar$ means the product of the roots is $a^3$ regardless of $r$. Once one root is known, use the factor theorem for the unknown and polynomial division for the rest.

subtopic: Sums of powers of roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of the equation $x^3-4x^2+x+6=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. [2] (c) Without solving the equation, show that $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=34$. [3] (d) Find a cubic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ and $\gamma^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=4$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=1$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=-6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$ [M1] $=16-2=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Each root satisfies $x^3=4x^2-x-6$ [M1] Summing over the three roots: $\sum\alpha^3=4\sum\alpha^2-\sum\alpha-18$ [M1] $=4(14)-4-18=34$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (d) Sum of the new roots $=14$ and product $=(\alpha\beta\gamma)^2=36$ [A1] Sum of pair products $=(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)^2-2\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ [M1] $=1+48=49$, so the equation is $x^3-14x^2+49x-36=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For sums of squares use $(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$. For higher powers, use the fact that each root satisfies the original equation and add the three copies. Note that the roots are rational here, so you can check your answers by solving.

subtopic: Remainder in terms of a parameter and a unique real value
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-kx+2$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find, in terms of $k$, the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-k)$. [2] (b) Show that $(x-k)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ for exactly one real value of $k$, and state this value. [4] (c) For this value of $k$, solve $f(x)=0$, giving all roots, real and complex, in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Remainder $=f(k)$ [M1] $=k^3-k^2+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Require $k^3-k^2+2=0$ [M1] $(k+1)(k^2-2k+2)=0$ [A1] Discriminant of $k^2-2k+2$ is $4-8=-4<0$ so no real roots [R1] Hence the only real value is $k=-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f(x)=x^3+x+2=(x+1)(x^2-x+2)$ [M1] $x=-1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt7}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The remainder theorem still applies when the divisor contains a parameter: substitute $x=k$. To show a cubic in $k$ has exactly one real root, factorize and check the discriminant of the remaining quadratic.

subtopic: Equating coefficients to write a cubic in powers of (x-2)
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3+2x^2-5x+1$. The polynomial can be written in the form $f(x)\equiv(x-2)^3+A(x-2)^2+B(x-2)+C$, where $A$, $B$ and $C$ are constants. (a) Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$. [4] (b) Hence write down the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-2)^2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Expand the right-hand side [M1] Coefficient of $x^2$: $-6+A=2$ so $A=8$ [A1] Coefficient of $x$: $12-4A+B=-5$ so $B=15$ [A1] Constant: $-8+4A-2B+C=1$ so $C=7$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f(x)=(x-2)^2[(x-2)+8]+15(x-2)+7$ [M1] Remainder $=15(x-2)+7=15x-23$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Alternatively, put $u=x-2$ and substitute $x=u+2$. Once the polynomial is written in powers of $(x-2)$, every term except the last two is a multiple of $(x-2)^2$, so the remainder can be read off.

subtopic: Cubic with a repeated root and an unknown constant
statement: The equation $2x^3-9x^2+12x+k=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, has roots $\alpha$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, where $\alpha\neq\beta$. (a) By considering the sum of the roots and the sum of the products of the roots in pairs, show that $\alpha^2-3\alpha+2=0$. [4] (b) Hence find the two possible values of $k$ and, in each case, the roots of the equation. [5]
markscheme: (a) $2\alpha+\beta=\dfrac92$ so $\beta=\dfrac92-2\alpha$ [M1] [A1] $\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta=6$ [M1] $\alpha^2+9\alpha-4\alpha^2=6$ so $-3\alpha^2+9\alpha-6=0$, giving $\alpha^2-3\alpha+2=0$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) $\alpha=1$ or $\alpha=2$ [A1] Then $\beta=\dfrac52$ or $\beta=\dfrac12$ respectively [A1] Product of roots $\alpha^2\beta=-\dfrac k2$ [M1] $\alpha=1$: $k=-5$, roots $1,1,\dfrac52$ [A1] $\alpha=2$: $k=-4$, roots $2,2,\dfrac12$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: A repeated root means two of the three Vieta roots are equal, so write the roots as $\alpha,\alpha,\beta$ and eliminate $\beta$. Check each case by confirming that $\alpha\neq\beta$.

subtopic: Odd-degree polynomials and locating a real root
statement: Let $f(x)=x^5+x^3+x-1$. (a) Explain why every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real root. [2] (b) Show that $f(x)=0$ has exactly one real root. [3] (c) Show that this root lies between $0.6$ and $0.7$. [2] (d) Find the root, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) As $x\to\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$ an odd degree polynomial tends to values of opposite sign [R1] A polynomial is continuous, so its graph crosses the $x$-axis at least once [R1] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=5x^4+3x^2+1$ [M1] $f'(x)>0$ for all real $x$ [A1] so $f$ is strictly increasing and crosses the $x$-axis exactly once [R1] [3 marks] (c) $f(0.6)=-0.106<0$ [M1] $f(0.7)=0.211>0$ so there is a sign change and the root lies in $(0.6,0.7)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=0.637$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For an exactly-one-root argument, combine existence (continuity and sign change) with uniqueness (strictly monotonic). Use your GDC to find the root of $f(x)=0$ once you have bracketed it.

subtopic: Cubic polynomial model fitted to data
statement: The number of daily users of a new app, in thousands, is modeled by $U(t)=at^3+bt^2+ct+d$ (the model allows for a small dip as the initial novelty fades, followed by growth through word of mouth), where $t$ is the number of weeks after launch and $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$. The recorded values are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline U & 2 & 6 & 6 & 8 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [5] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum of $U$ for $0\leq t\leq4$. [3] (c) Find the first time at which the model predicts that the app has $15$ thousand daily users. [2] (d) Use the model to estimate the number of daily users at $t=10$, and comment on the validity of this estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $U(0)=2$ gives $d=2$ [A1] $a+b+c=4$, $8a+4b+2c=4$, $27a+9b+3c=6$ [M1] Solving with GDC: $a=1$, $b=-5$, $c=8$ [A1] [A1] [A1] [5 marks] (b) $U'(t)=3t^2-10t+8=0$ [M1] $t=\dfrac43$ [A1] (or $t=2$, the local minimum) Local maximum at $(1.33,6.15)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $t^3-5t^2+8t+2=15$ [M1] $t=3.79$ weeks [A1] [2 marks] (d) $U(10)=582$ thousand users [A1] This is unlikely to be valid since a cubic model has been extrapolated far outside the data range $0\leq t\leq3$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: With four data points and four unknown coefficients you can solve a system of linear equations, or use cubic regression on the GDC. When commenting on validity, mention extrapolation outside the data range.

subtopic: Quartic with complex roots: building the polynomial
statement: The quartic polynomial $p(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has real coefficients, and two of its roots are $1-i$ and $i$. (a) Write down the other two roots. [2] (b) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [4] (c) Hence show that $p(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. [2]
tips: Pair each root with its conjugate, so each pair multiplies to a real quadratic. For positivity, complete the square on the quadratic factors.

subtopic: Quartic: sums of roots and reciprocals
statement: The roots of the equation $x^4-x^3+2x^2+3x-5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta$ and $\sum\alpha\beta$, the sum of the products of the roots taken two at a time. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2$. [2] (c) Hence explain why the equation does not have four real roots. [2] (d) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta+\dfrac1\gamma+\dfrac1\delta$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum\alpha=1$ [A1] $\sum\alpha\beta=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum\alpha^2=(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=1-4=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) If all roots were real, each square would be non-negative [R1] so the sum of squares could not be negative; since it equals $-3$, at least one root is non-real [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\sum\dfrac1\alpha=\dfrac{\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta\delta+\alpha\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}$ [M1] Sum of triple products $=-3$ [A1] and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=-5$ so the value is $\dfrac35$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a quartic $x^4+px^3+qx^2+rx+s$: $\sum\alpha=-p$, $\sum\alpha\beta=q$, $\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=-r$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=s$. Watch the alternating signs.

subtopic: Power sums of roots of a quadratic by recurrence
statement: The roots of the equation $x^2-4x+1=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Let $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, with $s_0=2$. (a) Show that $s_{n+2}=4s_{n+1}-s_n$ for $n\geq0$. [3] (b) Find $s_0$, $s_1$ and hence find $s_4$. [3] (c) Given that the roots of the equation are $2+\sqrt3$ and $2-\sqrt3$, write down the value of $(2+\sqrt3)^4+(2-\sqrt3)^4$. [1] (d) Show that $(2+\sqrt3)^4$ differs from an integer by less than $0.01$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Since $\alpha^2=4\alpha-1$, multiply by $\alpha^n$: $\alpha^{n+2}=4\alpha^{n+1}-\alpha^n$ [M1] Similarly $\beta^{n+2}=4\beta^{n+1}-\beta^n$ [M1] Adding gives $s_{n+2}=4s_{n+1}-s_n$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $s_0=2$, $s_1=\alpha+\beta=4$ [A1] $s_2=14$, $s_3=52$ using the recurrence [M1] $s_4=4(52)-14=194$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(2+\sqrt3)^4+(2-\sqrt3)^4=s_4=194$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $(2+\sqrt3)^4=194-(2-\sqrt3)^4$ [M1] $\sqrt3>1.7$ so $0<2-\sqrt3<0.3$ [A1] Hence $(2-\sqrt3)^4<0.3^4=0.0081<0.01$, so $(2+\sqrt3)^4$ is within $0.01$ of $194$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The recurrence comes from each root satisfying the quadratic itself. In part (d), you do not need a calculator: bound $2-\sqrt3$ using an inequality for $\sqrt3$.

subtopic: Division by a quadratic and remainders with unknown coefficients
statement: Let $p(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. When $p(x)$ is divided by $x^2+1$ the remainder is $2x-3$, and when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)$ the remainder is $5$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [6] (b) Find the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x^2+1)(x-1)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $p(x)=(x^2+1)(x+a)+(b-1)x+(c-a)$ [M1] Equating the remainder with $2x-3$: $b-1=2$ so $b=3$ [A1] and $c-a=-3$ [A1] $p(1)=5$: $1+a+b+c=5$ so $a+c=1$ [M1] $a=2$ [A1] $c=-1$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $p(x)=x^3+2x^2+3x-1$ and $(x^2+1)(x-1)=x^3-x^2+x-1$, so the quotient is $1$ [M1] Remainder $=p(x)-(x^3-x^2+x-1)$ [A1] $=3x^2+2x$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When dividing by a quadratic, write $p(x)=(x^2+1)q(x)+r(x)$ with $r$ of degree at most 1. A cubic divided by a cubic with the same leading coefficient has quotient 1.

subtopic: Solving |x-a|=bx+c by squaring with rejection of an extraneous root
statement: Solve the equation $|x-4|=3x-2$. [5]
markscheme: Square both sides: $x^2-8x+16=9x^2-12x+4$ [M1] $8x^2-4x-12=0$, so $2x^2-x-3=0$ [A1] $(2x-3)(x+1)=0$, so $x=\dfrac32$ or $x=-1$ [A1] Check: for $x=-1$ the right-hand side is $-5<0$ but $|x-4|\geq0$, so reject [R1] $x=\dfrac32$ (check: $|1.5-4|=2.5=3(1.5)-2$) [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions, so always substitute back into the original equation. A modulus can never equal a negative number.

subtopic: Graph of |f(x)| for a quadratic and number of solutions of |f(x)|=k
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$. (a) For the graph of $y=|f(x)|$, write down the coordinates of the $x$-intercepts and the $y$-intercept, and find the coordinates of the local maximum point. [4] (b) Solve the equation $|f(x)|=2$, giving your answers in exact form. [3] (c) Find the value of $k>0$ for which the equation $|f(x)|=k$ has exactly three solutions. Justify your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x$-intercepts $(-1,0)$ and $(3,0)$ [A1] $y$-intercept $(0,3)$ [A1] The vertex of $y=f(x)$ is $(1,-4)$ [M1] Reflecting in the $x$-axis, the local maximum of $y=|f(x)|$ is $(1,4)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f(x)=2$ or $f(x)=-2$ [M1] $x^2-2x-5=0$ gives $x=1\pm\sqrt6$ [A1] $x^2-2x-1=0$ gives $x=1\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The horizontal line $y=k$ meets the graph three times when it passes through the local maximum, so $k=4$ [R1] [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To sketch $y=|f(x)|$, reflect the parts of the graph below the $x$-axis upward. The new local maximum has the same height as the old minimum depth.

subtopic: Sum of two modulus functions with different slopes: piecewise form, equation and minimum
statement: Let $f(x)=|2x-1|+|x+3|$. (a) Write $f(x)$ as a piecewise-defined function with no modulus signs. [3] (b) Solve the equation $f(x)=6$. [3] (c) Find the minimum value of $f(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) For $x<-3$: $f(x)=-3x-2$ [A1] For $-3\leq x\leq\dfrac12$: $f(x)=-x+4$ [A1] For $x>\dfrac12$: $f(x)=3x+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $f(x)=6$ in each piece [M1] $-3x-2=6$ gives $x=-\dfrac83$, which is not less than $-3$, so reject $-x+4=6$ gives $x=-2$ [A1] $3x+2=6$ gives $x=\dfrac43$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The slopes are $-3$, $-1$, $3$, so the minimum occurs at the change from negative to positive slope, $x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $f\left(\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac72$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Break the real line at the values where each modulus expression equals zero and check each candidate solution lies in its own interval. The minimum of such a function occurs at one of these break points.

subtopic: Rational inequality using a sign diagram
statement: Solve the inequality $\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}<\dfrac{x}{x-1}$. [7]
markscheme: Bring to one side: $\dfrac{(2x-1)(x-1)-x(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-1)}<0$ [M1] $\dfrac{x^2-6x+1}{(x+3)(x-1)}<0$ [A1] Roots of the numerator: $x=3\pm2\sqrt2$ [M1] [A1] Critical values $-3$, $3-2\sqrt2$, $1$, $3+2\sqrt2$ in increasing order; sign diagram (numerator and denominator signs) [M1] Expression is negative for $-3<x<3-2\sqrt2$ [A1] and for $1<x<3+2\sqrt2$ [A1] [7 marks]
tips: Never multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown. Move everything to one side, factorize, and use a sign diagram, remembering that denominator zeros are excluded.

subtopic: Proof of the triangle inequality and applying it to bound expressions
statement: (a) Prove that $|x+y|\leq|x|+|y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. [4] (b) Hence show that $|u|-|v|\leq|u-v|$ for all $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$. [2] Given that $|x-2|<0.5$ and $|y+1|<0.3$: (c) show that $|x+y-1|<0.8$. [2] (d) Show that $|x-y|>2.2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Both sides are non-negative, so it suffices to compare squares [R1] $(x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2$ and $(|x|+|y|)^2=x^2+2|x||y|+y^2$ [M1] Since $xy\leq|xy|=|x||y|$ [A1] $(x+y)^2\leq(|x|+|y|)^2$ and taking non-negative square roots gives the result [R1] [4 marks] (b) $u=(u-v)+v$ [M1] so $|u|\leq|u-v|+|v|$ by (a), giving $|u|-|v|\leq|u-v|$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) $x+y-1=(x-2)+(y+1)$ [M1] $|x+y-1|\leq|x-2|+|y+1|<0.5+0.3=0.8$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (d) $x-y=3+e$ where $e=(x-2)-(y+1)$ [M1] $|e|\leq|x-2|+|y+1|<0.8$ by (a) [M1] Then $|x-y|=|3+e|\geq3-|e|>2.2$ by (b) [A1] [AG] [3 marks]
tips: For absolute value inequalities with both sides non-negative, squaring is a clean strategy. To bound an expression, rewrite it as a sum of terms whose moduli you know.

subtopic: Algebraic proof of AM-GM type inequalities
statement: (a) Show that, for $p,q>0$, $\dfrac{p+q}{2}\geq\sqrt{pq}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $x+\dfrac4x\geq4$ for all $x>0$, and state the value of $x$ for which equality holds. [3] (c) Hence prove that, for $a,b,c>0$, $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\geq8abc$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\geq0$ [M1] $p-2\sqrt{pq}+q\geq0$ [A1] so $\dfrac{p+q}{2}\geq\sqrt{pq}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) Apply (a) with $p=x$, $q=\dfrac4x$ [M1] $\dfrac12\left(x+\dfrac4x\right)\geq\sqrt4=2$ so $x+\dfrac4x\geq4$ [A1] Equality when $x=\dfrac4x$, so $x=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $a+b\geq2\sqrt{ab}$, $b+c\geq2\sqrt{bc}$, $c+a\geq2\sqrt{ca}$ [M1] All sides are positive, so the inequalities can be multiplied [R1] $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\geq8\sqrt{a^2b^2c^2}$ [M1] $=8abc$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The key step is $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\geq0$. Remember to state why inequalities between positive quantities can be multiplied together.

subtopic: Tolerance model with a normal distribution
statement: A machine produces bolts. A bolt is accepted if its diameter $d$ mm satisfies $|d-12.50|\leq0.04$. (a) Write the acceptance condition in the form $a\leq d\leq b$. [2] The diameter of a bolt produced by the machine is modeled by the normal distribution $N(12.51,\,0.03^2)$. (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen bolt is accepted. [2] A random sample of $20$ bolts is taken. (c) Find the probability that at least $18$ of them are accepted. [3] The machine is recalibrated so that the mean diameter is $12.50$ mm. The standard deviation $\sigma$ is now adjustable. (d) Find the greatest value of $\sigma$ so that at least $95\%$ of bolts are accepted. [3]
markscheme: (a) $-0.04\leq d-12.50\leq0.04$ [M1] $12.46\leq d\leq12.54$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(12.46\leq d\leq12.54)$ [M1] $=0.794$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $X\sim B(20,0.7936\ldots)$ [M1] $P(X\geq18)=1-P(X\leq17)$ [M1] $=0.187$ (using the unrounded probability; accept $0.188$ if the rounded value $0.794$ is used) [A1] [3 marks] (d) Require $P(|Z|\leq0.04/\sigma)\geq0.95$ [M1] $\dfrac{0.04}{\sigma}\geq1.96$ [A1] $\sigma\leq0.0204$ so the greatest value is $0.0204$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Interpret $|d-c|\leq t$ as the interval $c-t\leq d\leq c+t$ before using normal probabilities. Keep unrounded values in later parts.

subtopic: Solving |f(x)|<g(x) for a cubic using a GDC
statement: Let $f(x)=|x^3-4x|$ and $g(x)=x+1.5$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of all points of intersection of the graphs of $f$ and $g$. [4] (b) Hence solve the inequality $|x^3-4x|<x+1.5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Plot both graphs on GDC (or solve $|x^3-4x|=x+1.5$) [M1] $x=-0.306$ [A1] $x=0.558$ [A1] $x=1.38$ and $x=2.37$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) The graph of $f$ lies below the line where [M1] $-0.306<x<0.558$ [A1] or $1.38<x<2.37$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Sketch both graphs on the GDC first so you know how many intersections to expect. For an inequality, read off the intervals where one graph lies below the other.

subtopic: Equation and inequality with |x^2-2x| using factorization
statement: (a) Show that $|x^2-2x|=|x|\,|x-2|$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. [2] (b) Hence solve the inequality $|x^2-2x|>3|x-2|$. [4] (c) Let $k>0$. Find the value of $k$ for which the equation $|x^2-2x|=k|x-2|$ has exactly two distinct real solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-2x=x(x-2)$ [M1] and $|ab|=|a||b|$ [R1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $|x-2|\,(|x|-3)>0$ [M1] $|x-2|>0$ for $x\neq2$, and at $x=2$ the inequality fails [R1] so require $|x|>3$ [M1] $x<-3$ or $x>3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $|x-2|\,(|x|-k)=0$ [M1] gives $x=2$, $x=k$, $x=-k$ [A1] These are only two distinct values when $k=2$ (since then $x=k=2$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factorize before squaring or splitting into cases: a common factor $|x-2|$ lets you reduce the problem a lot. Always treat the case where the common factor is zero separately.

subtopic: Finding parameters in |ax+b| from a solution set
statement: The solution set of the inequality $|ax+b|\leq7$, where $a>0$, is $-3\leq x\leq4$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [4] (b) Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation $|ax+b|=|x+5|$. [4]
tips: The endpoints of the solution interval are where $ax+b=\pm7$. For $|A|=|B|$, squaring (or $A=\pm B$) is efficient and creates no extraneous solutions.

subtopic: Modulus in a periodic temperature context
statement: The temperature, $T$ degrees Celsius, in a greenhouse $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $T(t)=21+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi(t-9)}{12}\right)$, for $0\leq t\leq24$. (a) Write down the maximum and minimum temperature predicted by the model. [2] The greenhouse is classed as comfortable when $|T-21|\leq1.2$. (b) Find the times during the day when the greenhouse is comfortable. [3] (c) Find the total time, in hours, that the greenhouse is comfortable. [2] (d) Find the temperature at midnight. [1]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $24$ [A1] minimum $18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $3|\sin\theta|\leq1.2$ where $\theta=\dfrac{\pi(t-9)}{12}$ [M1] $7.43\leq t\leq10.6$ [A1] $19.4\leq t\leq22.6$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\times(10.57-7.43)$ [M1] $=6.29$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (d) $T(0)=21+3\sin\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}4\right)=18.9$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Convert $|T-21|\leq1.2$ into $|\sin\theta|\leq0.4$, then use the GDC to find where the graph of $|T-21|$ lies below the line $y=1.2$. Check both daily intervals.

subtopic: Total distance as a sum of three modulus terms
statement: Three shops are located at positions $2$, $5$ and $11$ km along a straight road. A warehouse is placed at position $x$ km, and $D(x)=|x-2|+|x-5|+|x-11|$ is the total distance to the three shops. (a) Find an expression for $D(x)$ when $2\leq x\leq5$, simplifying your answer. [2] (b) Find the position of the warehouse that minimizes $D(x)$, and the minimum value of $D$. [3] (c) Find all values of $x$ for which $D(x)=12$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $D(x)=(x-2)+(5-x)+(11-x)$ [M1] $=14-x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) For $5\leq x\leq11$: $D(x)=x+4$, so $D$ decreases up to $x=5$ and increases afterwards [M1] Minimum at $x=5$ [A1] $D(5)=9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $D(x)=12$ in each region [M1] $2\leq x\leq5$: $14-x=12$ gives $x=2$ [A1] $5\leq x\leq11$: $x+4=12$ gives $x=8$ [A1] (for $x<2$, $18-3x=12$ gives $x=2$, not less than $2$; for $x>11$, $3x-18=12$ gives $x=10$, rejected) Solutions $x=2$ or $x=8$ [3 marks]
tips: With three absolute values, split at each break point and compute the expression in every region. The minimum total distance occurs at the median.

subtopic: Equation and inequality with two modulus expressions of different coefficients
statement: (a) Solve the equation $|x-1|=2|x+3|$. [4] (b) Hence solve the inequality $|x-1|>2|x+3|$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x-1=2(x+3)$ [M1] $x=-7$ [A1] $x-1=-2(x+3)$ [M1] $x=-\dfrac{5}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $|x-1|>2|x+3|$ holds between the two roots because the inequality holds at $x=-3$ (left side $4$, right side $0$) [M1] $-7<x<-\dfrac{5}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] Alternatively, squaring both sides gives $(x+7)(3x+5)<0$, with the same interval (no additional marks)
tips: Either split into the two sign cases $x-1=\pm2(x+3)$ or square both sides. For the inequality, test a point to decide whether the region between the roots or outside them is correct.

subtopic: Number of solutions of |f(x)|=k for a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the $x$-intercepts and the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $y=f(x)$. [3] (b) Write down the coordinates of the local maximum point of the graph of $y=|f(x)|$. [2] (c) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation $|f(x)|=k$ has exactly four distinct solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-2x-3=(x+1)(x-3)$ [M1] $x=-1$ and $x=3$ [A1] vertex $(1,-4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The part of the curve below the $x$-axis is reflected in the $x$-axis [M1] local maximum at $(1,4)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The graph of $y=|f(x)|$ is W-shaped, so the horizontal line $y=k$ cuts it four times when it lies above the $x$-axis and below the local maximum [R1] $0<k<4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch $y=|f(x)|$ and slide a horizontal line $y=k$ up the page, counting intersections. Check the boundary cases $k=0$ and $k=4$ separately because they give fewer than four solutions.

subtopic: Graph of f(|x|) and number of solutions of f(|x|)=k
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Solve the equation $f(|x|)=0$. [3] (b) Determine the number of real solutions of the equation $f(|x|)=k$ for each possible value of $k$, giving your answer in terms of $k$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $|x|^2-4|x|+3=0$ so $(|x|-1)(|x|-3)=0$ [M1] $|x|=1$ or $|x|=3$ [A1] $x=\pm1,\ \pm3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The graph of $y=f(|x|)$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis [M1] for $x\ge0$ it follows $y=f(x)$, with minimum point $(2,-1)$ and $y$-intercept $(0,3)$ [A1] $k<-1$: no solutions; $k=-1$: 2 solutions [A1] $-1<k<3$: 4 solutions [A1] $k=3$: 3 solutions; $k>3$: 2 solutions [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The graph of $y=f(|x|)$ keeps the right-hand part of $y=f(x)$ and reflects it in the $y$-axis. At $k=3$ the line passes through the $y$-intercept, where the two halves meet, so count that point once.

subtopic: Rational inequality with modulus in the denominator
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $\dfrac{3}{|x|-2}<1$. [6] (b) Hence write down the number of integers $n$ with $|n|\le 8$ that satisfy $\dfrac{3}{|n|-2}<1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) The expression is undefined for $x=\pm2$. Case $|x|>2$: the denominator is positive, so $3<|x|-2$ [M1] $|x|>5$ [A1] $x<-5$ or $x>5$ [A1] Case $|x|<2$: consider the denominator negative [M1] so the left side is negative and the inequality is always true [R1] $-2<x<2$ [A1] Solution: $x<-5$, $-2<x<2$ or $x>5$ [6 marks] (b) Integers: $-8,-7,-6,-1,0,1,6,7,8$, so $9$ integers [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Multiplying by $|x|-2$ would reverse the inequality sign for some $x$, so split into the cases $|x|>2$ and $|x|<2$ instead. Exclude the values that make the denominator zero.

subtopic: Proof of x + 1/x >= 2 and consequences
statement: (a) Prove that $x+\dfrac{1}{x}\ge 2$ for all $x>0$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\dfrac{a}{b}+\dfrac{b}{a}\ge 2$ for all $a,b>0$. [2] (c) Deduce that $(a+b)\left(\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}\right)\ge 4$ for all $a,b>0$. [2] (d) State the condition on $a$ and $b$ for equality in part (c). [1]
markscheme: (a) $x+\dfrac1x-2=\dfrac{x^2-2x+1}{x}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{x}$ [A1] this is non-negative because $(x-1)^2\ge0$ and $x>0$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Let $x=\dfrac{a}{b}$, which is positive [M1] then $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $(a+b)\left(\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b\right)=2+\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba$ [M1] $\ge2+2=4$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Equality when $x=1$, that is $a=b$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: To prove an inequality, move everything to one side and show the result is a square divided by a positive quantity. In (b) and (c), use the earlier result with a clever substitution.

subtopic: Cauchy-style inequality for two pairs of numbers
statement: Let $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)-(ac+bd)^2=(ad-bc)^2$. [3] (b) Hence deduce that $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)\ge(ac+bd)^2$, and state the condition on $a,b,c,d$ for equality. [2] (c) Given that $3x+4y=25$, where $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, find the minimum value of $x^2+y^2$ and the values of $x$ and $y$ for which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=a^2c^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2+b^2d^2$ [M1] subtracting $(ac+bd)^2=a^2c^2+2abcd+b^2d^2$ gives $a^2d^2-2abcd+b^2c^2$ [A1] $=(ad-bc)^2$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $(ad-bc)^2\ge0$, so the difference is non-negative [R1] equality if and only if $ad=bc$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Use part (b) with $a=x$, $b=y$, $c=3$, $d=4$: $(x^2+y^2)(25)\ge(3x+4y)^2=625$ [M1] $x^2+y^2\ge25$ [A1] minimum value is $25$ [A1] equality when $4x=3y$; with $3x+4y=25$ this gives $\dfrac{25x}{3}=25$ so $x=3$, $y=4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: In (c) match the given linear expression $3x+4y$ with $ac+bd$ to see which numbers to choose. Always check that the equality condition can actually be met by values satisfying the constraint.

subtopic: AM-GM inequality for two numbers with an optimization application
statement: (a) Prove that $\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}$ for all $a,b\ge0$. [3] (b) Hence show that $4x+\dfrac{9}{x}\ge12$ for all $x>0$. [3] (c) Find the value of $x$ for which $4x+\dfrac{9}{x}=12$. [2] (d) A rectangle has area $50\text{ m}^2$. Use the result of part (a) to show that its perimeter is at least $20\sqrt2$ m. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^2\ge0$ because it is a real square [R1] $a-2\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0$ [M1] $a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$, so $\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Apply (a) with $a=4x$ and $b=\dfrac9x$, both positive for $x>0$ [M1] $ab=36$ [A1] $\dfrac{4x+\frac9x}{2}\ge\sqrt{36}=6$, so $4x+\dfrac9x\ge12$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) Equality when $4x=\dfrac9x$ [M1] $x^2=\dfrac94$, so $x=\dfrac32$ (since $x>0$) [A1] [2 marks] (d) Sides $x$ and $y$ with $xy=50$: $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}=2\sqrt{50}$ [M1] perimeter $2(x+y)\ge4\sqrt{50}=20\sqrt2$ [A1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: Start (a) from the observation that a square is never negative. In (b), spot that the product of $4x$ and $9/x$ is a constant, which is the signal to use AM-GM.

subtopic: Modulus function written as a piecewise function
statement: Let $h(x)=|2x-4|+x$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Express $h(x)$ as a piecewise function without modulus signs. [3] (b) Find the range of $h$. [2] (c) Solve the inequality $h(x)\le5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|2x-4|=2x-4$ for $x\ge2$ and $4-2x$ for $x<2$ [M1] $h(x)=3x-4$ for $x\ge2$ [A1] $h(x)=4-x$ for $x<2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The minimum value occurs at $x=2$, where $h(2)=2$ [M1] range is $h(x)\ge2$, that is $[2,\infty)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) For $x\ge2$: $3x-4\le5$ gives $x\le3$, so $2\le x\le3$ [M1] [A1] For $x<2$: $4-x\le5$ gives $x\ge-1$, so $-1\le x<2$ [A1] Combined: $-1\le x\le3$ [3 marks]
tips: Find where the expression inside the modulus changes sign and write each branch with its own domain. When solving an inequality on a piecewise function, always intersect each answer with the domain of its branch.

subtopic: Equation and inequality with a modulus inside a modulus
statement: (a) Solve the equation $\big||x|-3\big|=2$. [4] (b) Solve the inequality $\big||x|-3\big|<2$. [3] (c) Solve the equation $\big||x|-3\big|=x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|x|-3=2$ or $|x|-3=-2$ [M1] $|x|=5$ or $|x|=1$ [A1] $x=\pm5$ [A1] $x=\pm1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $-2<|x|-3<2$ [M1] $1<|x|<5$ [A1] $-5<x<-1$ or $1<x<5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The left side is non-negative, so $x\ge0$ [R1] then $|x-3|=x$ [M1] $3-x=x$ gives $x=\dfrac32$ (the case $x-3=x$ has no solution) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Peel the modulus signs off one layer at a time, starting with the outer one. In (c), use the fact that a modulus cannot be negative to restrict $x$ before solving.

subtopic: Modulus of a trigonometric function on a given domain
statement: (a) Solve the equation $|\cos 2x|=\dfrac12$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [4] (b) Hence solve the inequality $|\cos 2x|\le\dfrac12$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos 2x=\dfrac12$ or $\cos2x=-\dfrac12$ [M1] $0\le2x\le2\pi$ [A1] $\cos2x=\dfrac12$: $2x=\dfrac\pi3,\dfrac{5\pi}3$, so $x=\dfrac\pi6,\dfrac{5\pi}6$ [A1] $\cos2x=-\dfrac12$: $2x=\dfrac{2\pi}3,\dfrac{4\pi}3$, so $x=\dfrac\pi3,\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $|\cos2x|\le\dfrac12$ where the graph lies between the lines $y=\pm\dfrac12$, for example at $x=\dfrac\pi4$ where $\cos2x=0$ [M1] $\dfrac\pi6\le x\le\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] $\dfrac{2\pi}3\le x\le\dfrac{5\pi}6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Change the domain of the angle first: for $2x$ it is $0$ to $2\pi$, which gives twice as many solutions. For the inequality, test a point between two consecutive roots rather than trusting a guess.

subtopic: Quadratic inside a modulus with integer solutions
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $|x^2-20|<10$, giving your answers in exact form. [4] (b) Hence write down all integers $n$ satisfying $|n^2-20|<10$. [2] (c) Find all integers $n$ that satisfy both $|n^2-20|<10$ and $|n-1|\le4$. [2]
tips: Convert $|u|<a$ into $-a<u<a$ and solve the resulting double inequality for $x^2$ before taking square roots. Use approximate square roots only to decide which integers fall inside an exact interval.

subtopic: Solving |f(x)|=k for a cubic and counting solutions by parameter
statement: Let $g(x)=x^3-3x$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Use your graphic display calculator to solve $|g(x)|=1$, giving all solutions to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) For $k>0$, determine the number of solutions of the equation $|g(x)|=k$ for each possible value of $k$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Solve $g(x)=1$ and $g(x)=-1$, or plot $y=|g(x)|$ and $y=1$ [M1] three correct values from $x=-1.88,\ -1.53,\ -0.347,\ 0.347,\ 1.53,\ 1.88$ [A1] all six correct [A1] [3 marks] (b) $g'(x)=3x^2-3=0$ [M1] $x=\pm1$ [A1] local maximum $(-1,2)$ and local minimum $(1,-2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Reflect the part below the $x$-axis to obtain $y=|g(x)|$, whose local maxima both have height $2$ [M1] $0<k<2$: 6 solutions [A1] $k=2$: 4 solutions [A1] $k>2$: 2 solutions [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the turning points from part (b) to decide where the line $y=k$ changes the number of intersections. At $k=2$ the line touches two turning points, so some solutions are repeated and the count drops.

subtopic: Graphical solution of a modulus-exponential equation and inequality
statement: Let $f(x)=|e^{x}-4|$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Solve the equation $f(x)=3$, giving exact answers. [3] (b) Use your graphic display calculator to solve $f(x)=5-x^2$, giving your answers to three significant figures. [3] (c) Hence solve the inequality $f(x)\le5-x^2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $e^x-4=3$ or $e^x-4=-3$ [M1] $x=\ln7$ [A1] $x=\ln1=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Plot $y=|e^x-4|$ and $y=5-x^2$ and find the intersections [M1] $x=-1.15$ [A1] $x=1.77$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The curve $y=f(x)$ lies on or below the parabola between the two intersection points [M1] $-1.15\le x\le1.77$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a graphical solution, state which two functions you plot and read the intersections to the accuracy requested. For the inequality, compare the graphs: decide which one is higher in between the intersections by testing a point such as $x=0$.

subtopic: Proof of the reverse triangle inequality
statement: You may use the triangle inequality $|p+q|\le|p|+|q|$ for all $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) By choosing $p=a-b$ and $q=b$, show that $|a|-|b|\le|a-b|$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\big||a|-|b|\big|\le|a-b|$. [3] (c) Given that $|x-5|<1$, use the result of part (b) to show that $|x|>4$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Substitute $p=a-b$, $q=b$ so that $p+q=a$ [M1] $|a|\le|a-b|+|b|$ [A1] rearranging, $|a|-|b|\le|a-b|$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Interchanging $a$ and $b$ in (a): $|b|-|a|\le|b-a|=|a-b|$ [M1] [A1] so both $|a|-|b|$ and $-(|a|-|b|)$ are at most $|a-b|$, hence $\big||a|-|b|\big|\le|a-b|$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $\big||x|-5\big|\le|x-5|<1$ [M1] $-1<|x|-5<1$ so $|x|>4$ [A1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: Writing $a=(a-b)+b$ is the key trick in (a). For (b), remember that $|u|\le c$ means both $u\le c$ and $-u\le c$.

subtopic: Inequality in terms of u=|x+1| with a reciprocal modulus
statement: Consider the inequality $\dfrac{2}{|x+1|}\ge|x+1|+1$, for $x\ne-1$. (a) Let $u=|x+1|$. Show that the inequality is equivalent to $u^2+u-2\le0$. [3] (b) Hence solve the inequality. [4]
markscheme: (a) $u>0$ because $x\ne-1$, so multiplying both sides by $u$ keeps the inequality direction [R1] $2\ge u(u+1)$ [M1] $u^2+u-2\le0$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $(u+2)(u-1)\le0$ [M1] $-2\le u\le1$ and $u>0$ gives $0<u\le1$ [A1] $|x+1|\le1$ gives $-2\le x\le0$ [A1] excluding $x=-1$: $-2\le x<-1$ or $-1<x\le0$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A substitution turns the modulus problem into a quadratic inequality. Keep track of the restriction on $u$ (and the excluded value of $x$) as you go back to $x$.

subtopic: Equations with a modulus of a logarithm
statement: (a) Solve the equation $|\log_2x|=2$. [3] (b) Solve the inequality $|\log_2x|<2$. [2] (c) Solve the equation $|\log_2x|=\log_23-\log_2x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\log_2x=2$ or $\log_2x=-2$ [M1] $x=4$ [A1] $x=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $-2<\log_2x<2$ [M1] $\dfrac14<x<4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The domain is $x>0$. Case $x\ge1$: $\log_2x=\log_23-\log_2x$, so $\log_2x=\tfrac12\log_23$ [M1] $x=\sqrt3$, which satisfies $x\ge1$ [A1] Case $0<x<1$: $-\log_2x=\log_23-\log_2x$ gives $\log_23=0$, which is impossible [R1] so the only solution is $x=\sqrt3$ [3 marks]
tips: Because $2^t$ is increasing, $-2<\log_2x<2$ translates directly into $2^{-2}<x<2^2$. In (c), split at $x=1$, where $\log_2x$ changes sign.

subtopic: Pearson correlation, regression line and interpolation versus extrapolation
statement: A kiosk owner records the maximum daily temperature, $x$ degrees Celsius, and the number of cold drinks sold, $y$, on eight days. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 14 & 17 & 19 & 22 & 24 & 27 & 29 & 31 \\ \hline y & 41 & 52 & 55 & 68 & 72 & 86 & 90 & 99 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient $r$. [1] (b) Describe the correlation. [1] (c) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (d) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in this context. [1] (e) Use the regression line to estimate the number of drinks sold on a day when the maximum temperature is $25^\circ$C, and state whether this is interpolation or extrapolation. [2] (f) The owner uses the line to estimate sales for a day with maximum temperature $40^\circ$C. Give one reason why this estimate may be unreliable. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.997$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Strong positive linear correlation [A1] [1 mark] (c) $y=3.39x-7.07$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (d) For each increase of $1^\circ$C in maximum temperature, about 3.39 more drinks are sold [A1] [1 mark] (e) $y=3.39(25)-7.07\approx77.6$, so about 78 drinks [A1] $25$ lies within the range of the data ($14$ to $31$), so this is interpolation [R1] [2 marks] (f) $40$ is outside the range of observed temperatures, so this is extrapolation [R1] the linear relationship may not continue (for example, sales may level off or the kiosk may run out of stock) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Enter the data into the statistics menu of your GDC and read off $r$, $a$ and $b$ directly. Whenever you predict, check whether the value of $x$ lies inside the range of the data before commenting on reliability.

subtopic: Using a given regression line: prediction, residual and mean point
statement: A teacher studies the relationship between the number of hours, $x$, that students practice per week and their score, $y$ (out of $100$), on a skills test. The data cover students who practice between $2$ and $12$ hours per week, with mean practice time $\bar{x}=7.5$ hours. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $$y=3.2x+41.5.$$ (a) Interpret the gradient of the line in this context. [1] (b) Estimate the score of a student who practices for $5$ hours per week. [2] (c) A student who practices for $6$ hours scored $64$. Find the residual for this student, and state whether the line over- or underestimates the score. [2] (d) Explain why the line should not be used to estimate the score of a student who practices for $20$ hours per week. [2] (e) Find the mean score $\bar{y}$ of the students. [2]
markscheme: (a) Each extra hour of weekly practice is associated with an increase of $3.2$ points in the score [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y=3.2(5)+41.5$ [M1] $=57.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Predicted score $3.2(6)+41.5=60.7$ [M1] residual $=64-60.7=3.3$, so the line underestimates this score [A1] [2 marks] (d) $20$ hours is outside the range of the data (extrapolation) [R1] the line would predict $3.2(20)+41.5=105.5$, which exceeds the maximum possible score of $100$ [R1] [2 marks] (e) The regression line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ [M1] $\bar{y}=3.2(7.5)+41.5=65.5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value, so a positive residual means the line underestimates. The regression line always passes through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$, which gives a quick way to find a missing mean.

subtopic: Effect of an outlier on the correlation coefficient and regression line
statement: A gardener measures the height, $y$ cm, of seven seedlings of the same species at $x$ weeks after planting. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x \text{ (weeks)} & 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 9 & 11 \\ \hline y \text{ (cm)} & 14 & 15 & 21 & 22 & 28 & 31 & 35 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the value of $r$ and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for these seven seedlings. [3] An eighth seedling, which was damaged by frost, is measured at $x=12$ weeks and has height $5$ cm. (b) Find the value of $r$ and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for all eight seedlings. [3] (c) Describe the effect of the eighth seedling on the correlation coefficient and on the gradient of the regression line. [2] (d) Use an appropriate regression line to estimate the height of an undamaged seedling at $10$ weeks, justifying your choice of line. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.996$ [A1] $y=2.44x+8.4$ [M1] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=0.243$ [A1] $y=0.663x+16.7$ [M1] [A1] [3 marks] (c) $r$ decreases sharply from $0.996$ to $0.243$ (a much weaker correlation) [A1] the gradient decreases from $2.44$ to $0.663$, so the outlier pulls the line toward itself [A1] [2 marks] (d) Use the line from (a), since the frost-damaged seedling is not representative of an undamaged seedling [R1] $y=2.44(10)+8.4\approx32.8$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A single point far from the pattern can change both $r$ and the line dramatically. If there is a sound reason to exclude an outlier, base predictions on the line calculated without it.

subtopic: Regression line from summary statistics and effect of linear changes of variable
statement: For a set of bivariate data $(x,y)$, the following summary statistics are known: $\bar{x}=40$, $\bar{y}=25$, standard deviation of $x$ is $8$, standard deviation of $y$ is $6$, and $r=-0.8$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Use the regression line to estimate $y$ when $x=35$. [1] New variables are defined by $u=2x-10$ and $w=3-4y$. (c) Write down the value of the correlation coefficient between $u$ and $w$, giving a reason for your answer. [2] (d) Find the equation of the regression line of $w$ on $u$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=-0.8\times\dfrac68$ [M1] $=-0.6$ [A1] $y-25=-0.6(x-40)$, so $y=-0.6x+49$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=-0.6(35)+49=28$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $u$ is an increasing linear function of $x$ and $w$ is a decreasing linear function of $y$, so the sign of the correlation reverses [R1] $r_{uw}=0.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\bar u=70$, $\bar w=-97$, $s_u=16$, $s_w=24$ [A1] gradient $=0.8\times\dfrac{24}{16}=1.2$ [M1] $w+97=1.2(u-70)$, so $w=1.2u-181$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The gradient of $y$ on $x$ is $r\,s_y/s_x$, and the line passes through the mean point. Adding a constant to a variable changes its mean but not its spread, while multiplying by $k$ multiplies the spread by $|k|$; a negative multiplier flips the sign of $r$.

subtopic: Fitting a power model y = a x^b using logarithms
statement: A researcher believes that the area $y$ square centimeters of a spreading stain is related to the time $x$ minutes since it appeared by a model of the form $y=ax^b$, where $a,b>0$. The following measurements are taken. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 10 & 12 \\ \hline y & 3.1 & 8.4 & 15.6 & 24 & 34.5 & 45.2 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Show that $\ln y=b\ln x+\ln a$. [2] (b) Find the correlation coefficient between $\ln x$ and $\ln y$, correct to four decimal places. [1] (c) Find the equation of the regression line of $\ln y$ on $\ln x$. [2] (d) Hence find the values of $a$ and $b$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) Use the model, with your values of $a$ and $b$ from the unrounded regression line, to estimate the area of the stain after $7$ minutes. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\ln\left(ax^b\right)$ [M1] $=\ln a+\ln\left(x^b\right)=b\ln x+\ln a$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $r=0.9998$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\ln y=1.50\ln x+0.0718$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (d) $b=1.50$ [A1] $a=e^{0.0718}=1.07$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $y=1.0744\times7^{1.4999}$ [M1] $\approx19.9\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A power model $y=ax^b$ becomes linear when you plot $\ln y$ against $\ln x$: the gradient is $b$ and the intercept is $\ln a$. Keep unrounded values in the GDC for the final prediction to avoid rounding error.

subtopic: Fitting an exponential model y = ab^x using logarithms
statement: The number of bacteria, $y$, in a culture is recorded at $t$ hours after the start of an experiment. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline y & 120 & 165 & 258 & 340 & 520 & 690 & 1080 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ It is proposed that $y=ab^t$, where $a>0$ and $b>1$. (a) Show that the model implies that $\ln y$ is a linear function of $t$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $\ln y$ on $t$. [2] (c) Find the correlation coefficient between $t$ and $\ln y$. [1] (d) Hence find the values of $a$ and $b$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) Use the unrounded regression line to estimate the time at which the number of bacteria first exceeds $2000$. Give your answer in hours, correct to three significant figures. [2] (f) Interpret the value of $b$ in this context. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\ln a+t\ln b$ [M1] this has the form $\ln y=mt+c$ with $m=\ln b$ and $c=\ln a$, which is linear in $t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\ln y=0.363t+4.78$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $r=0.9987$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $a=e^{4.7764}=119$ [A1] $b=e^{0.36264}=1.44$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Solve $4.7764+0.36264t=\ln2000$ [M1] $t=7.79$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (f) The number of bacteria is multiplied by about 1.44 each hour, an increase of about 44% per hour [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For $y=ab^t$ take logs to get $\ln y=\ln a+t\ln b$, then undo the logarithm to recover $a$ and $b$ from the intercept and gradient. Remember that $b$ is a growth factor per unit of $t$.

subtopic: Regression lines of y on x and x on y from summary sums
statement: Ten students record the number of hours per week, $x$, that they spend on revision and their percentage score, $y$, on a test. The results are summarized as $$\sum x=85,\quad\sum y=462,\quad\sum x^2=815,\quad\sum y^2=22300,\quad\sum xy=4130.$$ (a) Write down the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, giving the coefficients to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the value of the correlation coefficient $r$. [2] (d) A student wants to know how many hours of revision would be associated with a score of $60\%$.
