Find the equation of the appropriate regression line and use it to estimate this number of hours. [3] (e) Explain why rearranging the equation in part (b) would not give the best estimate in part (d). [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=8.5$ and $\bar y=46.2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $S_{xx}=815-\dfrac{85^2}{10}=92.5$ and $S_{xy}=4130-\dfrac{85\times462}{10}=203$ [M1] gradient $=\dfrac{203}{92.5}=2.19$ [A1] $y=2.19x+27.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S_{yy}=22300-\dfrac{462^2}{10}=955.6$ [M1] $r=\dfrac{203}{\sqrt{92.5\times955.6}}=0.683$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The appropriate line is the regression line of $x$ on $y$, since $x$ is being estimated [R1] $x=0.212y-1.31$ [A1] at $y=60$: $x\approx11.4$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (e) The line of $y$ on $x$ minimizes the vertical distances (errors in $y$), not the horizontal distances, so rearranging it would give $14.8$ hours, a less appropriate estimate [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $S_{xx}=\sum x^2-\frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}$ and $S_{xy}=\sum xy-\frac{\sum x\sum y}{n}$. The line of $y$ on $x$ is for predicting $y$; to predict $x$ you need the separate line of $x$ on $y$, with gradient $S_{xy}/S_{yy}$.

subtopic: Negative correlation with prediction and an impossible extrapolated value
statement: A homeowner records the average outside temperature, $x$ degrees Celsius, and the heating energy used, $y$ kWh per day, on eight winter days. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 3 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 9 & 12 & 13 & 15 \\ \hline y & 34 & 30 & 31 & 24 & 25 & 17 & 16 & 12 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the correlation coefficient $r$ and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in this context. [2] (d) Estimate the energy used on a day when the average outside temperature is $10^\circ$C. [2] (e) Explain why the regression line cannot be used to estimate the energy used when the average outside temperature is $25^\circ$C. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=-0.989$ [A1] strong negative linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=-1.87x+40.3$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) The gradient is $-1.87$: for each $1^\circ$C increase in outside temperature, the energy used decreases by about $1.87$ kWh per day [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=-1.87(10)+40.3$ [M1] $\approx21.5$ kWh [A1] [2 marks] (e) $25^\circ$C is far outside the range of the data ($3$ to $15$), so this is extrapolation [R1] the line gives $y\approx-6.61$, which is negative and therefore impossible [R1] [2 marks]
tips: When describing correlation, comment on both strength (from $|r|$) and direction (from the sign). A negative predicted value for a quantity that cannot be negative is a clear sign of unreliable extrapolation.

subtopic: Finding means, correlation and standard deviation from two regression lines
statement: For a bivariate data set $(x,y)$, the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=0.5x+3$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x=1.28y+0.48$. (a) Find the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$. [3] (b) Find the value of the correlation coefficient $r$, justifying its sign. [3] (c) Given that the standard deviation of $y$ is $3$, find the standard deviation of $x$. [2] (d) Use an appropriate line to estimate $y$ when $x=15$, and justify your choice. [2]
markscheme: (a) Both lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ [M1] substitute: $\bar x=1.28(0.5\bar x+3)+0.48$, so $0.36\bar x=4.32$ [A1] $\bar x=12$ and $\bar y=0.5(12)+3=9$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r^2=0.5\times1.28=0.64$ [M1] $|r|=0.8$ [A1] both gradients are positive, so $r=0.8$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) The gradient of $y$ on $x$ is $r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}$, so $0.5=0.8\times\dfrac{3}{s_x}$ [M1] $s_x=4.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Use the line of $y$ on $x$, because $y$ is the quantity being estimated [R1] $y=0.5(15)+3=10.5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The two gradients multiply to give $r^2$, and the sign of $r$ matches the sign of both gradients. The point where the two regression lines intersect is the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

subtopic: Negative correlation and limits of a linear model
statement: A cafe owner records the maximum daily temperature, $x$ degrees Celsius, and the number of cups of hot chocolate sold, $y$, on eight days. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 5 & 8 & 11 & 14 & 17 & 20 & 23 \\ \hline y & 148 & 131 & 118 & 96 & 85 & 63 & 52 & 34 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Use your graphic display calculator to find the value of $r$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Estimate the number of cups sold on a day when the maximum temperature is 10 degrees Celsius. [1] (d) Interpret the gradient of the regression line. [1] (e) Find the temperature above which the model predicts negative sales, and explain what this shows about the model. [2]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $r=-0.998$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=-5.43x + 159.$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=-5.43254\times 10 + 158.782=104.$, so approximately 104 cups [A1] [1 mark] (d) For each 1 degree rise in temperature, sales fall by about 5.43 cups on average [A1] [1 mark] (e) Predicted sales are negative when $x>\dfrac{158.782}{5.43254}=29.2$ degrees [A1] Negative sales are impossible, so the linear model is not valid for high temperatures (outside the data range) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For a negative gradient say that the quantity decreases. Always check whether a model gives impossible values (negative counts, probabilities above 1) outside the data range.

subtopic: Sleep and reaction time: prediction and reliability
statement: A researcher records the number of hours of sleep, $x$, a volunteer had the night before and the volunteer's mean reaction time, $y$ milliseconds, in a computer test. Eight volunteers took part. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 4 & 5 & 5.5 & 6 & 7 & 7.5 & 8 & 9 \\ \hline y & 412 & 380 & 365 & 350 & 322 & 318 & 290 & 275 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$, and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Estimate the mean reaction time of a volunteer who slept for 6.8 hours. [1] (d) Interpret the gradient of the regression line. [1] (e) Another volunteer slept for 12 hours. Use the regression line to estimate this volunteer's reaction time, and comment on the validity of your answer. [2] (f) Comment on the reliability of the estimate in part (c). [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $r=-0.995$, a strong negative linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=-27.6x + 518.$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=-27.6154\times 6.8 + 518.500=331.$ ms [A1] [1 mark] (d) Each extra hour of sleep is associated with a decrease in mean reaction time of about 27.6 ms [A1] [1 mark] (e) $y=187.$ ms [A1] This is extrapolation (12 is outside $4\le x\le 9$) and the model is not valid there [R1] [2 marks] (f) $x=6.8$ lies within the range of the data and $|r|$ is close to 1, so the estimate is reliable [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Reliability depends on two things: whether the $x$ value lies inside the data range (interpolation) and how strong the correlation is. Mention both when asked to comment.

subtopic: Finding the mean point and r from two regression lines
statement: Two regression lines are found for a dataset of pairs $(x,y)$: the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=0.4x+5$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x=1.6y-4.4$. (a) Find the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$. [3] (b) Find the value of the product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$, justifying its sign. [3] (c) Use an appropriate regression line to estimate the value of $x$ when $y=12$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Both lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ [R1] Substituting: $y=0.4(1.6y-4.4)+5$ [M1] $0.36y=3.24$, so $\bar y=9$ and $\bar x=10$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r^2=0.4\times 1.6=0.64$ [M1] $r=0.8$ [A1] Positive since both gradients are positive [R1] [3 marks] (c) Use the line of $x$ on $y$ [M1] $x=1.6(12)-4.4=14.8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The two regression lines always meet at the mean point, so solve them simultaneously. The product of the two gradients equals $r^2$, and the sign of $r$ matches the sign of the gradients.

subtopic: Combining two groups and the mean point
statement: Twenty students take part in a study of the number of hours of practice per week, $x$, and the test score, $y$. Twelve of the students attend school A and have mean values $\bar x=5$ and $\bar y=62$. The other eight students attend school B and have mean values $\bar x=8$ and $\bar y=80$. (a) Find the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$ for all twenty students. [3] (b) The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for all twenty students has gradient 4.5. Find its equation in the form $y=4.5x+c$. [2] (c) The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for school B alone has gradient 3.5. Find its equation. [2] (d) The gradients of the regression lines for school A and for school B are both less than 4.5. Give a reason why the gradient for the combined data is larger. [1]
markscheme: (a) Total of $x$: $12\times 5+8\times 8=124$ [M1] $\bar x=\dfrac{124}{20}=6.2$ [A1] $\bar y=\dfrac{12\times 62+8\times 80}{20}=69.2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The line passes through $(6.2,\,69.2)$ [M1] $c=69.2-4.5\times 6.2=41.3$, so $y=4.5x+41.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The line passes through $(8,80)$ [M1] $y-80=3.5(x-8)$, so $y=3.5x+52$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) School B has both higher practice hours and higher scores than school A, so combining the groups adds an extra positive trend between the groups, which steepens the line [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A regression line of a combined dataset passes through the combined mean, which is a weighted average of the group means (weights are the group sizes). Do not average the group gradients.

subtopic: Linear changes of both variables in a regression line
statement: A kiosk records the daily maximum temperature, $x$ degrees Celsius, and the daily sales, $y$ thousand dollars. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=3.6x-8$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=0.92$. The temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is $u=1.8x+32$ and the sales in dollars is $w=1000y$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $w$ on $u$, in the form $w=pu+q$. [3] (b) Write down the correlation coefficient between $u$ and $w$. [1] A third variable is defined by $v=10-2x$. (c) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $v$, and write down the correlation coefficient between $v$ and $y$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=\dfrac{u-32}{1.8}$ and $y=\dfrac{w}{1000}$ [M1] $\dfrac{w}{1000}=3.6\times\dfrac{u-32}{1.8}-8=2u-72$ [M1] $w=2000u-72000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=0.92$ (both transformations have positive multipliers) [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x=\dfrac{10-v}{2}$ [M1] $y=3.6\times\dfrac{10-v}{2}-8=10-1.8v$ [A1] $r=-0.92$ (the multiplier of $x$ is negative, so the sign of $r$ changes) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a linear change of variable, substitute it into the regression equation. $r$ keeps its magnitude, and its sign changes only if exactly one multiplier is negative.

subtopic: Coded data and the regression line
statement: The height, $x$ cm, and mass, $y$ kg, of seven athletes are recorded. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 150 & 155 & 160 & 165 & 170 & 175 & 180 \\ \hline y & 52 & 57 & 59 & 66 & 68 & 75 & 79 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find $r$ and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] The heights are coded using $u=\dfrac{x-165}{5}$. (b) Use your graphic display calculator to find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $u$, giving the coefficients to three significant figures. [2] (c) Use $u=\dfrac{x-165}{5}$ to show that your answer to part (b) is consistent with your answer to part (a). [3] (d) Write down the correlation coefficient between $u$ and $y$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $r=0.993$ [A1] $y=0.900x - 83.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Calculate $u$ values: $-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$ [M1] $y=4.50u + 65.1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Substitute $u=\dfrac{x-165}{5}$: $y=4.50000\times\dfrac{x-165}{5}+ 65.1429$ [M1] $=0.9x-148.5+ 65.1429$ [A1] $=0.9x - 83.4$, the same as part (a) [R1] [3 marks] (d) $r=0.993$, unchanged by the linear change of variable [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Coding $x$ by $u=(x-a)/b$ with $b>0$ does not change $r$. To convert back, substitute $u$ in terms of $x$ into the regression line.

subtopic: Interpreting gradient and intercept in a delivery model
statement: A delivery service records the distance, $x$ km, of each of six deliveries and the total time, $y$ minutes, from order to delivery. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1.2 & 2.5 & 3.1 & 4.8 & 6.0 & 7.4 \\ \hline y & 14 & 19 & 22 & 28 & 36 & 41 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Use your graphic display calculator to find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (b) Interpret the gradient of the line in this context. [1] (c) Interpret the $y$-intercept of the line in this context. [1] (d) Estimate the delivery time for a distance of 5.5 km. [1] (e) Explain why the line should not be used to estimate the delivery time for a distance of 30 km. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $y=4.44x + 8.16$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Each extra kilometer adds about 4.44 minutes to the delivery time [A1] [1 mark] (c) A delivery over a distance close to zero would take about 8.16 minutes, which represents the fixed time for preparing and dispatching the order [A1] [1 mark] (d) $y=4.44183\times 5.5 + 8.15903=32.6$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (e) $30$ km lies far outside the range of the data ($1.2\le x\le 7.4$), so this is extrapolation and the linear model may not hold (for example, speeds may change on long routes) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The intercept is the predicted value when $x=0$; interpret it in context rather than just stating it. Estimates outside the data range are extrapolations and are not reliable.

subtopic: Correlation does not imply causation
statement: Over many fires, a city records the number of fire engines sent to each fire and the cost of the damage caused. The product-moment correlation coefficient between the two variables is $r=0.82$. (a) Describe the correlation between the number of fire engines and the cost of the damage. [1] A city councillor concludes: "Sending more fire engines causes more damage, so we should send fewer." (b) Explain why the councillor's conclusion is not justified by the value of $r$. [2] (c) Suggest a third variable that could explain the correlation. [1]
markscheme: (a) Strong positive (linear) correlation [A1] [1 mark] (b) Correlation shows only an association between the variables [R1] It does not show that one variable causes the other; a third (confounding) variable may affect both [R1] [2 marks] (c) The size (severity) of the fire: larger fires need more engines and also cause more damage [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Never write that a high $r$ proves cause and effect. Give a specific confounding variable and say how it affects both quantities.

subtopic: Validity and reliability of predictions from a regression line
statement: A park manager records the maximum temperature, $x$ degrees Celsius, and the number of visitors, $y$, on seven days. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 12 & 15 & 18 & 21 & 24 & 27 & 30 \\ \hline y & 210 & 260 & 235 & 330 & 345 & 420 & 400 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the value of $r$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Describe the strength and direction of the linear correlation. [1] (d) Use the regression line to estimate the number of visitors when the maximum temperature is (i) 20 degrees Celsius, (ii) 45 degrees Celsius. [2] (e) For each estimate in part (d), comment on its validity and reliability. [3]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.947$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=11.9x + 64.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Strong positive linear correlation [A1] [1 mark] (d) (i) $y=11.9048\times 20 + 64.2857=302.$, about 302 visitors [A1] (ii) $y=600.$, about 600 visitors [A1] [2 marks] (e) $x=20$ is within the data range (interpolation) and the correlation is strong, so the estimate is reasonably reliable [R1] $x=45$ is far outside the data range (extrapolation), so it is not reliable [R1] The model may break down at extreme temperatures (for example, very hot days may reduce attendance), so the estimate may not be valid [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Distinguish the two ideas: an estimate is reliable when it is an interpolation and $|r|$ is high; a model is valid only over the range where the linear relationship was observed.

subtopic: Regression of x on y for age and reaction time
statement: Eight adults of different ages took a reaction test. The age, $x$ years, and the mean reaction time, $y$ milliseconds, of each adult are shown. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 21 & 28 & 35 & 42 & 50 & 58 & 66 & 74 \\ \hline y & 310 & 330 & 355 & 350 & 395 & 415 & 440 & 455 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (b) A ninth adult has a mean reaction time of 400 milliseconds. (i) Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$. [2] (ii) Use it to estimate the age of this adult. [1] (c) Comment on the reliability of your estimate in part (b)(ii). [1] (d) Find the coordinates of the point where the two regression lines intersect, and state what this point represents. [2] (e) Let $b$ be the gradient of the line in part (a) and $d$ the gradient of the line in part (b)(i). Show that $r=\sqrt{bd}$, and use this to verify that $r=0.989$ to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $y=2.81x + 250.$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) (i) Use of GDC for $x$ on $y$ [M1] $x=0.348y - 85.9$ [A1] (ii) $x=0.348054\times 400 - 85.9454=53.3$ years [A1] [3 marks] (c) The estimate is an interpolation ($310\le y\le 455$) and $r$ is close to 1, so it is reliable [R1] [1 mark] (d) The lines intersect at the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)=(46.8,\,381.)$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (e) $b=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}$ and $d=r\dfrac{s_x}{s_y}$, so $bd=r^2$ [M1] $r=\sqrt{2.81076\times 0.348054}=0.989$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks]
tips: The regression line of $x$ on $y$ is the right choice when estimating $x$ from $y$. The two lines meet at $(\bar x,\bar y)$ and the product of their gradients is $r^2$.

subtopic: Both regression lines from summary statistics
statement: For a set of paired data $(x,y)$ the summary statistics are $\bar x=50$, $\bar y=30$, $s_x=10$, $s_y=6$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=-0.6$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$. [3] (c) Use an appropriate regression line to estimate the value of $x$ when $y=24$. [2] (d) A student rearranges the equation in part (a) to estimate $x$ when $y=24$. Find this estimate, and explain why it differs from your answer to part (c). [2]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=-0.6\times\dfrac{6}{10}$ [M1] $=-0.36$ [A1] $y-30=-0.36(x-50)$, so $y=-0.36x+48$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Gradient $=r\dfrac{s_x}{s_y}=-0.6\times\dfrac{10}{6}$ [M1] $=-1$ [A1] $x-50=-(y-30)$, so $x=-y+80$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Use the line of $x$ on $y$ [M1] $x=-24+80=56$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=\dfrac{24-48}{-0.36}=\dfrac{200}{3}\approx 66.7$ [A1] The line of $y$ on $x$ minimizes vertical distances and is meant for estimating $y$; the two lines coincide only if $|r|=1$, so the estimates differ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The gradients are $r s_y/s_x$ for $y$ on $x$ and $r s_x/s_y$ for $x$ on $y$; both lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$. Use $x$ on $y$ whenever $x$ is the quantity being estimated.

subtopic: Combining two datasets and the effect on r
statement: Two bakeries record the amount spent on advertising in a week, $x$ hundred dollars, and the weekly sales, $y$ hundred dollars, over six weeks. Bakery A: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline y & 12 & 15 & 19 & 21 & 26 & 28 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ Bakery B: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline y & 40 & 47 & 49 & 58 & 61 & 70 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the correlation coefficient for each bakery separately. [2] The twelve data pairs are now combined into one dataset. (b) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the combined data. [3] (c) Explain why the correlation coefficient for the combined data is smaller than for each separate bakery. [2] (d) Find the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$ for the combined data, and verify that the regression line from part (b) passes through this mean point. [2]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] Bakery A: $r=0.995$, Bakery B: $r=0.988$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC on all 12 pairs [M1] $r=0.81$ [A1] $y=7.70x + 2.51$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The two bakeries follow different linear patterns: for the same $x$, bakery B has much higher sales [R1] Combining them mixes the two relationships, so the points lie further from a single line [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\bar x=\dfrac{54}{12}=4.50$, $\bar y=\dfrac{446}{12}=37.2$ [A1] $y=7.70213\times 4.50+ 2.50709=37.2$, so the line passes through the mean point [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A correlation can weaken sharply when two groups with different relationships are merged. Use the unrounded regression values when checking that the line passes through the mean point.

subtopic: Regression after coding both variables from summary statistics
statement: For a set of paired data $(x,y)$, the summary statistics are $\bar x=14$, $\bar y=40$, $s_x=4$, $s_y=9$ and the covariance is $s_{xy}=-27$. New variables are defined by $u=\dfrac{x-10}{2}$ and $w=\dfrac{y-4}{3}$. (a) Find $\bar u$, $\bar w$, $s_u$ and $s_w$. [3] (b) Find the covariance $s_{uw}$ and the correlation coefficient between $u$ and $w$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the regression line of $w$ on $u$. [2] (d) Hence find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, in the form $y=ax+b$. [3]
tips: A linear change of variable scales the covariance by the product of the multipliers and the variance by the square of the multiplier. Check your final gradient against $r s_y/s_x=-0.75\times 9/4$.

subtopic: Regression and correlation from sums and sums of squares
statement: A cafe records the number of flyers handed out, $x$ hundred, and the weekly sales, $y$ hundred dollars, for $n=10$ weeks. The data give $\sum x=100$, $\sum y=411$, $\sum x^2=1190$, $\sum xy=4667$ and $\sum y^2=18545$. (a) Write down the values of $\bar x$ and $\bar y$. [1] (b) Calculate $S_{xx}=\sum x^2-n\bar x^2$, $S_{xy}=\sum xy-n\bar x\bar y$ and $S_{yy}=\sum y^2-n\bar y^2$. [3] (c) Hence find the product-moment correlation coefficient $r=\dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}$. [2] (d) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, given that its gradient is $\dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$. [2] (e) Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$, given that its gradient is $\dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}$. [2]
tips: Compute $S_{xx}$, $S_{xy}$ and $S_{yy}$ once and reuse them in every part. Both regression lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so you only need each gradient.

subtopic: Separable equation needing integration by parts
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=xe^{x-y}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [7] (b) Find the value of $y$ when $x=1$. [1] (c) Show that the solution in part (a) is defined for all real $x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=xe^{x}e^{-y}$, so $\int e^{y}\,\mathrm{d}y=\int xe^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $e^{y}=\ldots$ on the left [A1] Integration by parts: $\int xe^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ [M1] [A1] $e^{y}=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ Using $y=0$, $x=0$: $1=-1+C$ [M1] $C=2$ [A1] $y=\ln\left((x-1)e^{x}+2\right)$ [A1] [7 marks] (b) $y=\ln 2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Let $f(x)=(x-1)e^{x}+2$, so $f'(x)=xe^{x}$ [M1] $f'(x)<0$ for $x<0$ and $f'(x)>0$ for $x>0$, so the minimum value is $f(0)=1>0$, hence $f(x)>0$ for all $x$ and $\ln f(x)$ is defined [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate so that every $y$ is on one side with $\mathrm{d}y$ and every $x$ is on the other with $\mathrm{d}x$. Remember to include the constant of integration before applying the initial condition.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with a trigonometric integrating factor
statement: The function $y$ satisfies $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+y\tan x=\cos x$, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this equation is $\sec x$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (c) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. [1] (d) Show that at any stationary point of the curve, $(x+2)\tan x=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int \tan x\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{-\ln(\cos x)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}=\sec x$ [AG] (valid since $\cos x>0$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(y\sec x\right)=\cos x\sec x=1$ [M1] $y\sec x=x+C$ [A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $2=C$ [M1] $y=(x+2)\cos x$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}+2\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+1$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\cos x-(x+2)\sin x$ [M1] Setting to zero and dividing by $\cos x\neq 0$: $1=(x+2)\tan x$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the equation in the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$, multiply by $e^{\int P\,\mathrm{d}x}$ and recognize the left side as a product derivative. For part (d) you can differentiate the solution or use the original equation with $y'=0$.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation involving tan(y/x)
statement: Let $y$ be the solution of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{y}{x}+\tan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$, for $0<x\le 1$, where $y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan v$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (c) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$. [1] (d) Show that the solution curve has a vertical tangent at the point $\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ gives $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+\tan v$, so $x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan v$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\cot v\,\mathrm{d}v=\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $\ln(\sin v)=\ln x+C$ [A1] [A1] Using $x=1$, $v=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\ln 1=\ln 1+C$, so $C=0$ [M1] $\sin v=x$, so $y=x\arcsin x$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $y=\dfrac{1}{2}\arcsin\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+\tan v$ where $v=\arcsin x$ [M1] As $x\to 1$, $v\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan v\to\infty$, so the gradient is unbounded: vertical tangent [R1] [2 marks]
tips: After substituting $y=vx$ the equation must separate in $v$ and $x$; do not forget the product rule when finding $\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x$. Replace $v$ by $y/x$ at the end.

subtopic: Euler's method with a convexity argument
statement: A curve satisfies the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\ln(x+y)$, where $y=1$ when $x=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step length of $h=0.25$ to find an approximation for the value of $y$ when $x=2$. Give each intermediate value of $y$ to four significant figures. [4] (b) Show that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{1+\ln(x+y)}{x+y}$. [2] (c) Given that $x+y>1$ for $x\ge 1$ on the solution curve, explain why your answer to part (a) is an underestimate of the true value of $y$ at $x=2$. [2] (d) State how the accuracy of the approximation could be improved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.25\ln(x_n+y_n)$ [M1] $y(1.25)\approx 1+0.25\ln 2=1.173$ [A1] $y(1.5)\approx 1.173+0.25\ln(2.423)=1.395$ [A1] $y(1.75)\approx 1.660$, $y(2)\approx 1.967$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{1}{x+y}\left(1+\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1+\ln(x+y)}{x+y}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) If $x+y>1$ then $\ln(x+y)>0$ and $x+y>0$, so $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}>0$ [R1] The solution curve is concave up, so each tangent line segment used by Euler's method lies below the curve and the estimate is too small [R1] [2 marks] (d) Use a smaller step length $h$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method follows tangent lines, so it underestimates on a concave-up curve and overestimates on a concave-down curve. Carry full calculator precision between steps.

subtopic: Logistic model of a fish population
statement: The number of fish, $P$, in a lake $t$ years after stocking is modeled by $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{1200}\right)$. (a) Find the rate of growth of the population when $P=300$. [2] (b) Show that the rate of growth is greatest when $P=600$, and find this greatest rate. [3] The solution of the differential equation can be written as $P=\dfrac{1200}{1+Ae^{-0.15t}}$, where $A$ is a constant. The initial population is 200 fish. (c) Find the value of $A$. [2] (d) Find the time taken for the population to reach 900 fish. [3] (e) Describe what happens to the population in the long term. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15\times 300\times\left(1-\dfrac{300}{1200}\right)$ [M1] $=33.75$ fish per year [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15P-\dfrac{0.15}{1200}P^2$, a quadratic in $P$ with negative leading coefficient [R1] Maximum at $P=\dfrac{0.15}{2\times 0.15/1200}=600$ [AG] [M1] Greatest rate $=0.15\times 600\times 0.5=45$ fish per year [A1] [3 marks] (c) $200=\dfrac{1200}{1+A}$ [M1] $A=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $900=\dfrac{1200}{1+5e^{-0.15t}}$ [M1] $e^{-0.15t}=\dfrac{1}{15}$ [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln 15}{0.15}=18.1$ years [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P\to 1200$ as $t\to\infty$: the population approaches the carrying capacity of 1200 fish [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In a logistic model the growth rate is largest at half the carrying capacity. Treat $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}t$ as a quadratic in $P$ when maximizing it.

subtopic: Exponential decay of a radioactive isotope
statement: The mass, $m$ mg, of a radioactive isotope at time $t$ days satisfies $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}=-km$, where $k>0$. Initially the mass is 120 mg and the half-life of the isotope is 8 days. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $m=120e^{-kt}$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the mass to fall to 15 percent of its initial value. [2] (d) Find the rate at which the mass is decreasing when $t=10$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{m}\,\mathrm{d}m=\int -k\,\mathrm{d}t$ [M1] $\ln m=-kt+C$ [A1] Using $m=120$ when $t=0$: $m=120e^{-kt}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $60=120e^{-8k}$ [M1] $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{8}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $18=120e^{-kt}$, so $e^{-kt}=0.15$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{8\ln(1/0.15)}{\ln 2}=21.9$ days [A1] [2 marks] (d) $m(10)=120e^{-10k}=50.45\ldots$ [M1] $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}=-km=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{8}\times 50.45\ldots=-4.37$, so the mass decreases at $4.37$ mg per day [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Half-life gives $k$ directly through $\tfrac12=e^{-kT}$. Keep $k$ exact until the final calculation to avoid rounding errors.

subtopic: Isoclines of a slope field and a solution curve
statement: The differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=y-x^2$ defines a slope field: at each point $(x,y)$ the short line segment has gradient $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. (a) Show that the points where the segments have gradient $m$ lie on the curve $y=x^2+m$, and write down the equation of the curve along which all segments are horizontal. [2] (b) The solution curve passes through the point $(1,1)$. Show that this point is a local maximum of the solution curve. [3] (c) Show that $y=x^2+2x+2$ is a solution of the differential equation. [2] (d) By considering the gradient of the slope field at points on the curve $y=x^2+2x+2$, explain why this solution curve is increasing for $x>-1$ and decreasing for $x<-1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y-x^2=m$ gives $y=x^2+m$ [A1] Horizontal segments: $m=0$, so $y=x^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) At $(1,1)$: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=1-1=0$, so the point is stationary [A1] $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-2x$ [M1] $=0-2=-2<0$, so it is a local maximum [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x+2$ [M1] $y-x^2=2x+2$, which equals $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (d) On this curve the gradient of the slope field is $y-x^2=2x+2$ [M1] This is positive for $x>-1$ and negative for $x<-1$, so the curve increases then decreases (minimum at $x=-1$) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The isocline for gradient $m$ is found by setting $\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x=m$. To classify a stationary point on a solution curve, differentiate the equation implicitly to get $\mathrm{d}^2y/\mathrm{d}x^2$.

subtopic: Separable equation with an exponential in y
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\,e^{-y}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Separating variables: $\int e^{y}\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $e^{y}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=0$: $1=C$ [M1] $y=\ln\left(1+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $y=\ln 3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Move all the $y$ terms to one side before integrating. Apply the initial condition before taking the logarithm, as it keeps the arithmetic simple.

subtopic: Separable equation with a trigonometric squared term
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y\sin^2 x$, where $y>0$ and $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [6] (b) Explain why $y$ is a non-decreasing function of $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int 2\sin^2 x\,dx$ [M1] Using $2\sin^2 x=1-\cos 2x$ [M1] $\ln y=x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $C=\ln 2$ [M1] $y=2e^{\,x-\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x}$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y\sin^2 x\ge 0$ because $y>0$ and $\sin^2 x\ge 0$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A squared trigonometric function must be rewritten with a double-angle identity before it can be integrated. Do not forget the factor $\frac12$ when integrating $\cos 2x$.

subtopic: Separable equation with partial fractions in x
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{(x+1)(x+3)}$, where $x>-1$, $y>0$ and $y=\sqrt{3}$ when $x=0$. (a) Express $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Hence show that $y=3\sqrt{\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}}$. [5] (c) Write down the value that $y$ approaches as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x+3}$ so $1=A(x+3)+B(x+1)$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}-\dfrac{1}{2(x+3)}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}-\dfrac{1}{2(x+3)}\right)dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+1)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+3)+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=\sqrt3$ when $x=0$: $\dfrac12\ln 3=-\dfrac12\ln 3+C$, so $C=\ln 3$ [M1] $\ln y=\ln 3+\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}$ [A1] $y=3\sqrt{\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $y\to 3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Partial fractions turn an awkward integral into two logarithms. Combine the logarithms only at the end, once the constant has been found.

subtopic: Linear first-order equation with integrating factor e^x
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=x$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Write down an integrating factor for this differential equation. [1] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [6]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int 1\,dx}=e^{x}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{x}\right)=xe^{x}$ [M1] $ye^{x}=\int xe^{x}\,dx$. By parts: $\int xe^{x}\,dx=xe^{x}-e^{x}$ [M1][A1] $ye^{x}=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $1=-1+C$, so $C=2$ [M1] $y=x-1+2e^{-x}$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Once multiplied by the integrating factor, the left side is the derivative of $ye^{x}$. Integration by parts on $xe^{x}$ is expected, so choose $u=x$ and $dv=e^{x}dx$.

subtopic: Recognizing a product derivative with a 1/x coefficient
statement: Consider the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=\ln x$, where $x>0$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Show that the differential equation can be written as $\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)=\ln x$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)=x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y$ by the product rule [M1] $=\ln x$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $xy=\int\ln x\,dx$ [M1] $=x\ln x-x+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=1$: $0=-1+C$, so $C=1$ [M1] $y=\ln x-1+\dfrac1x$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Look for the product rule hiding on the left side before reaching for an integrating factor. You may need to recall that $\int \ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x+C$.

subtopic: Linear equation with a tan x coefficient and a maximum value
statement: The function $y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sec x$, for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this differential equation is $\sec x$. [2] (b) Hence show that $y=\sin x+2\cos x$. [4] (c) Find the exact maximum value of $y$ on the given domain. [2]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int\tan x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\sec x|}$ [M1] $=\sec x$ since $\sec x>0$ on the domain [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\sec x\right)=\sec^2 x$ [M1] $y\sec x=\tan x+C$ [A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $C=2$ [M1] $y=\sin x+2\cos x$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x-2\sin x=0$ gives $\tan x=\dfrac12$, which lies in the domain [M1] Then $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos x=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, so $y_{\max}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5$ [A1] Alternatively write $y=\sqrt5\sin(x+\alpha)$. [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying the whole equation by $\sec x$ gives $\sec x\,y'+\sec x\tan x\,y$, which is the derivative of $y\sec x$. In (c), check that the stationary point lies inside the stated domain.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation whose solution is a circle
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y^2-x^2}{2xy}$, where $x>0$, $y>0$ and $y=1$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $x^2+y^2=2x$. [4] (c) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$, and state the set of values of $x$ for which the solution is defined (the endpoints are excluded). [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{v^2x^2-x^2}{2vx^2}=\dfrac{v^2-1}{2v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{v^2-1}{2v}-v=\dfrac{v^2-1-2v^2}{2v}=-\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{2v}{1+v^2}\,dv=-\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln(1+v^2)=-\ln x+C$ [A1] Using $v=1$ when $x=1$: $C=\ln 2$ [M1] $x(1+v^2)=2$, so $x+\dfrac{y^2}{x}=2$, hence $x^2+y^2=2x$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $y=\sqrt{2x-x^2}$ (positive root since $y>0$) [A1] Defined for the open interval $0<x<2$, since $x>0$ is given and $y>0$ excludes $x=2$ where $y=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: After substituting $y=vx$ every $x$ cancels from the right-hand side, which is the test of a homogeneous equation. Separate the variables $v$ and $x$ before integrating. Complete the square if you want to recognize the final curve.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation with an exponential of y/x
statement: A curve $y=y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x}+e^{y/x}$, where $0<x<e$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ to show that $x\dfrac{du}{dx}=e^{u}$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $y=ux$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=u+x\dfrac{du}{dx}$ [M1] $u+x\dfrac{du}{dx}=u+e^{u}$, so $x\dfrac{du}{dx}=e^{u}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\int e^{-u}\,du=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $-e^{-u}=\ln x+C$ [A1] Using $u=0$ when $x=1$: $-1=C$ [M1] $e^{-u}=1-\ln x$ [A1] $u=-\ln(1-\ln x)$, so $y=-x\ln(1-\ln x)$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The substitution is given in the question, so use it exactly as stated. The condition $x<e$ guarantees that $1-\ln x>0$ so the logarithm in the answer exists.

subtopic: Euler method by hand and sign of the second derivative
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $h=0.2$ to find an approximation for $y(0.6)$. [3] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $y=e^{x^2/2}$. [4] (c) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=(1+x^2)y$, and hence explain why your answer to part (a) is an underestimate of $y(0.6)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.2\,x_ny_n$ [M1] $y(0.2)\approx 1+0.2(0)(1)=1$, $y(0.4)\approx 1+0.2(0.2)(1)=1.04$ [A1] $y(0.6)\approx 1.04+0.2(0.4)(1.04)=1.1232$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac1y\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $C=0$ [M1] $y=e^{x^2/2}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y+x^2y=(1+x^2)y$ [M1] This is positive, so the solution curve is concave up, the tangent lines used by Euler's method lie below the curve and the estimate is an underestimate [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the recursion $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$ and keep exact decimals at each step. The sign of $y''$ tells you which side of the curve the tangent lines lie on.

subtopic: Euler method with GDC and convexity
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sqrt{x+y}$, where $y=2$ when $x=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $0.1$ to find an estimate for $y(1.5)$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [4] (b) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{1+\frac{dy}{dx}}{2\sqrt{x+y}}$. [2] (c) Hence state, with a reason, whether your estimate in part (a) is greater than or less than the true value of $y(1.5)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1\sqrt{x_n+y_n}$ [M1] $$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline 1.0 & 2 \\ \hline 1.1 & 2.1732 \\ \hline 1.2 & 2.3541 \\ \hline 1.3 & 2.5426 \\ \hline 1.4 & 2.7387 \\ \hline 1.5 & 2.9421 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ [A1][A1] $y(1.5)\approx 2.94$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(x+y)^{1/2}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac12(x+y)^{-1/2}\left(1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=\dfrac{1+\frac{dy}{dx}}{2\sqrt{x+y}}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}>0$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ and the solution is concave up [R1] The tangent lines lie below the curve, so the estimate is less than the true value [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the table or sequence feature of your GDC to avoid arithmetic slips, and do not round intermediate values. Convexity of the solution tells you the direction of the Euler error without solving the equation.

subtopic: Newton warming law with two data points
statement: A bottle of water at $4^\circ$C is placed in a room kept at $24^\circ$C. The temperature $T$ of the water, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the bottle is placed in the room satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-24)$, where $k>0$. (a) Show that $T=24-20e^{-kt}$. [3] After 10 minutes the temperature of the water is $10^\circ$C. (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the water to reach $20^\circ$C. Give your answer in minutes to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Keep $k$ unrounded in your calculator memory for part (c). The constant $24$ is the long-term temperature, so the solution tends to $24$ from below.

subtopic: Mixing problem with brine entering a tank
statement: A tank contains $100$ liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.2$ kg of salt per liter flows into the tank at $5$ liters per minute. The solution is kept well mixed and flows out of the tank at $5$ liters per minute. Let $S$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=1-\dfrac{S}{20}$. [2] (b) Solve this differential equation to find $S$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the exact time at which the concentration of salt in the tank first reaches $0.1$ kg per liter. [2]
markscheme: (a) Rate of salt in $=0.2\times 5=1$ kg per minute [A1] Rate of salt out $=\dfrac{S}{100}\times 5=\dfrac{S}{20}$ kg per minute [A1] $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=1-\dfrac{S}{20}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1}{20-S}\,dS=\int\dfrac{1}{20}\,dt$ [M1] $-\ln(20-S)=\dfrac{t}{20}+C$ [A1] Using $S=0$ when $t=0$: $C=-\ln 20$ [M1] $S=20\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Concentration $0.1$ means $S=10$ [M1] $e^{-t/20}=\dfrac12$, so $t=20\ln 2$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The volume stays at $100$ liters because inflow and outflow rates are equal, so the concentration is simply $S/100$. Note that $S<20$ throughout, so $20-S>0$ and no modulus is needed.

subtopic: Logistic growth with partial fractions
statement: The size $P$ of a population of birds on an island, $t$ years after observation begins, satisfies the logistic differential equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.1P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{200}\right)$, where $P=50$ when $t=0$. (a) Express $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Hence show that $P=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$. [5] (c) Find the exact time at which the population reaches $100$. [2] (d) Find the maximum rate of growth of the population, and the population size when this occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}=\dfrac{A}{P}+\dfrac{B}{200-P}$ so $1=A(200-P)+BP$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}=\dfrac{1}{200}\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac{1}{200-P}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(200-P)}{2000}$ so $\int\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}\,dP=\int\dfrac{1}{2000}\,dt$ [M1] $\ln P-\ln(200-P)=\dfrac{t}{10}+C$ [A1] Using $P=50$ when $t=0$: $C=\ln\dfrac13$ [M1] $\dfrac{P}{200-P}=\dfrac13e^{t/10}$ [A1] $3P=e^{t/10}(200-P)$, so $P\left(3+e^{t/10}\right)=200e^{t/10}$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $100=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$ so $3e^{-t/10}=1$ [M1] $t=10\ln 3$ years [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(200-P)}{2000}$ is a quadratic in $P$ with maximum at $P=100$ [M1] Maximum rate $=\dfrac{100\times100}{2000}=5$ birds per year [A1] Population size $100$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (d) work with $dP/dt$ as a function of $P$, not of $t$. The growth rate of a logistic model is greatest when the population is half of the limiting value.

subtopic: Second-order chemical reaction rate
statement: In a chemical reaction the concentration $x$ mol/L of a product after $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.015(4-x)^2$, where $x=0$ when $t=0$ and $x<4$. (a) Show that $x=4-\dfrac{1}{0.25+0.015t}$. [4] (b) Find the concentration after $20$ minutes. [1] (c) Find the time taken for the concentration to reach $3.5$ mol/L. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) Write down the limiting value of $x$ as $t\to\infty$. [1]
tips: Integrating $(4-x)^{-2}$ gives $(4-x)^{-1}$ with a positive sign, as $\frac{d}{dx}(4-x)^{-1}=(4-x)^{-2}$. Check your answer against the initial condition and the limiting behavior.

subtopic: Drug elimination with a second dose
statement: The amount $A$ mg of a drug in a patient's body satisfies $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-kA$, where $t$ is the time in hours and $k>0$. The drug has a half-life of $6$ hours. A first dose gives $A=200$ at $t=0$. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$. [3] A second dose of $150$ mg is taken at $t=4$, which increases the amount in the body by exactly $150$ mg. (b) Find the amount of the drug in the body immediately before the second dose is taken. [2] (c) Find the amount of the drug in the body at $t=10$. [2] (d) Find the time at which the amount of the drug first falls to $50$ mg. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=200e^{-kt}$ [M1] Half-life: $100=200e^{-6k}$ [M1] $e^{-6k}=\dfrac12$ so $-6k=-\ln 2$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $A(4)=200e^{-4k}$ [M1] $=126$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (c) Amount just after second dose $=126+150=276$ [M1] After a further $6$ hours (one half-life): $\dfrac{276}{2}=138$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (d) $276e^{-ks}=50$ where $s=t-4$ [M1] $s=\dfrac{\ln 5.52}{k}=14.8$ [M1] $t=18.8$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Restart the exponential decay from the new amount after the second dose, measuring time from $t=4$. Use the unrounded value of $A(4)$ in later parts to avoid a rounding error in your final answer.

subtopic: Isoclines and a solution curve that is also an isocline
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x$. (a) An isocline is the set of all points $(x,y)$ at which solution curves have the same gradient $m$. Describe the isocline for gradient $m$ in terms of its equation, and describe what the isoclines look like as $m$ varies. [2] (b) Show that the line $y=x+1$ is a solution curve of the differential equation, and that it is also an isocline. [3] (c) Find the solution of the differential equation for which $y=3$ when $x=0$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Isocline: $y-x=m$, that is $y=x+m$ [M1] These are parallel straight lines with gradient $1$ and $y$-intercept $m$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) For $y=x+1$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$ [M1] and $y-x=1$, so the equation is satisfied [A1] The isocline for $m=1$ is $y-x=1$, which is the line $y=x+1$ itself, and the gradient of this line is $1=m$, so the solution curve through it follows the isocline [R1] [3 marks] (c) Write as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=-x$ with integrating factor $e^{-x}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{-x}\right)=-xe^{-x}$ [A1] $ye^{-x}=xe^{-x}+e^{-x}+C$ [M1][A1] Using $y=3$ when $x=0$: $3=1+C$, so $C=2$ and $y=x+1+2e^{x}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: An isocline is a curve of constant slope, found by setting $\frac{dy}{dx}=m$ in the equation. In (c) the coefficient of $y$ is $-1$, so the integrating factor is $e^{-x}$.

subtopic: Euler method compared with an exact solution
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y-x$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $0.1$ to find an estimate for $y(0.5)$. Give your answer to four significant figures. [4] (b) Show that the exact solution is $y=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e^{2x}$. [5] (c) Find the percentage error of your estimate in part (a), to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1(2y_n-x_n)$ [M1] $$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0.1 & 1.2 \\ \hline 0.2 & 1.43 \\ \hline 0.3 & 1.696 \\ \hline 0.4 & 2.0052 \\ \hline 0.5 & 2.36624 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ [A1][A1] $y(0.5)\approx 2.366$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2y=-x$, integrating factor $e^{-2x}$ [M1] $ye^{-2x}=-\int xe^{-2x}\,dx$. By parts [M1] $\int xe^{-2x}\,dx=-\dfrac{x}{2}e^{-2x}-\dfrac14e^{-2x}$ [A1] $ye^{-2x}=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{-2x}+\dfrac14e^{-2x}+C$, so $y=\dfrac x2+\dfrac14+Ce^{2x}$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $1=\dfrac14+C$, so $C=\dfrac34$ [M1] $y=\dfrac x2+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e^{2x}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) Exact $y(0.5)=\dfrac14+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e=2.5387$ [M1] Percentage error $=\dfrac{2.5387-2.36624}{2.5387}\times100=6.79\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Enter the recursion in your GDC as a sequence in $(x_n,y_n)$ so that you can read off each row. The Euler estimate is below the exact value here because the solution is concave up.

subtopic: Bernoulli-type equation solved by the substitution u = 1/y
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{x}=xy^2$, where $x>0$, $y>0$ and $y=\dfrac12$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $u=\dfrac1y$ to show that $\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac{u}{x}=-x$. [3] (b) Find an integrating factor for this equation and hence show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac ux\right)=-1$, and find the general solution for $u$. [4] (c) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [3] (d) State the set of values of $x$ for which this solution is positive. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y=\dfrac1u$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\dfrac{du}{dx}$ [M1] $-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\dfrac{du}{dx}+\dfrac{1}{xu}=\dfrac{x}{u^2}$ [M1] Multiplying by $-u^2$: $\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac ux=-x$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) Integrating factor $=e^{-\int\frac1x\,dx}$ [M1] $=e^{-\ln x}=\dfrac1x$ [A1] $\dfrac1x\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac{u}{x^2}=-1$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac ux\right)=-1$ [A1] $\dfrac ux=-x+C$, so $u=Cx-x^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=\dfrac12$ when $x=1$ gives $u=2$, so $2=C-1$ and $C=3$ [M1] $u=3x-x^2$ [A1] $y=\dfrac{1}{3x-x^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $y>0$ when $0<x<3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When a substitution is given, differentiate it carefully using the chain rule: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{u^2}\frac{du}{dx}$. Remember to check where the final formula is defined and positive.

subtopic: Population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish farm models its stock of fish by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.05P-30$, where $P$ is the number of fish and $t$ is the time in years since the start of harvesting. Initially there are $500$ fish. (a) Show that $P=600-100e^{0.05t}$. [4] (b) Find the number of fish after $10$ years. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. [1] (c) Show that the stock of fish is exhausted after $20\ln 6$ years, and evaluate this time to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Factor the right-hand side as $0.05(P-600)$ to see the equilibrium value $600$. Since the initial population is below $600$, the stock decreases and eventually reaches zero.

subtopic: Induction for a weighted sum with powers of 2
statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\,2^{r-1}=(n-1)2^{n}+1$$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [7]
markscheme: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\,2^{r-1}=(n-1)2^{n}+1$. Base case $n=1$: LHS $=1\cdot 2^0=1$ [M1] RHS $=(0)2+1=1$, so $P(1)$ is true [A1] Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [M1] Consider $n=k+1$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r\,2^{r-1}=(k-1)2^{k}+1+(k+1)2^{k}$ [M1] $=2k\cdot 2^{k}+1$ [A1] $=k\,2^{k+1}+1=\left((k+1)-1\right)2^{k+1}+1$ [A1] So $P(k)$ true implies $P(k+1)$ true. Since $P(1)$ is true, $P(n)$ is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the induction hypothesis clearly and add the $(k+1)$th term to the right-hand side of the assumption. Finish with a full concluding sentence, as this earns a mark.

subtopic: Induction for the nth derivative of a product
statement: Let $f(x)=x\,e^{2x}$. Use mathematical induction to prove that the $n$th derivative of $f$ is $$f^{(n)}(x)=2^{\,n-1}(2x+n)\,e^{2x},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}^+.$$ [7]
markscheme: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $f^{(n)}(x)=2^{n-1}(2x+n)e^{2x}$. Base case $n=1$: $f'(x)=e^{2x}+2xe^{2x}=(2x+1)e^{2x}$ [M1] This equals $2^{0}(2x+1)e^{2x}$, so $P(1)$ is true [A1] Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [M1] $f^{(k+1)}(x)=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[2^{k-1}(2x+k)e^{2x}\right]$ [M1] $=2^{k-1}\left[2e^{2x}+2(2x+k)e^{2x}\right]$ [A1] $=2^{k-1}\cdot 2\,e^{2x}\left(2x+k+1\right)=2^{k}\left(2x+(k+1)\right)e^{2x}$ [A1] So $P(k)$ true implies $P(k+1)$ true. Since $P(1)$ is true, $P(n)$ is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Use the product rule on $2^{k-1}(2x+k)e^{2x}$ and factor out $2^{k-1}\cdot 2\,e^{2x}$ to reach the target form. The target for $n=k+1$ is $2^{k}(2x+k+1)e^{2x}$, so keep it in view.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction that a logarithm is irrational
statement: Prove by contradiction that $\log_2 3$ is irrational. [6]
markscheme: Assume that $\log_2 3$ is rational, so $\log_2 3=\dfrac pq$ for some integers $p,q$ with $q\ne 0$ [M1] Since $\log_2 3>0$, we may take $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [A1] Then $2^{p/q}=3$, so $2^{p}=3^{q}$ [M1] $2^{p}$ is even since $p\ge 1$ [R1] $3^{q}$ is odd since $q\ge 1$ and a product of odd numbers is odd [R1] An even number cannot equal an odd number, which is a contradiction, so $\log_2 3$ is irrational [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Start with the assumption that the number equals $p/q$ and convert the logarithm to an exponential equation. Contradictions with parity of even and odd integers are the standard route.

subtopic: Direct proof that a product of four consecutive integers plus one is a square
statement: Prove that for every positive integer $n$, the number $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)+1$ is the square of an integer. [5]
markscheme: $n(n+3)=n^2+3n$ and $(n+1)(n+2)=n^2+3n+2$ [M1] Let $m=n^2+3n$. Then the expression is $m(m+2)+1$ [M1][A1] $=m^2+2m+1=(m+1)^2$ [A1] $=\left(n^2+3n+1\right)^2$, and $n^2+3n+1$ is an integer, so the number is a perfect square [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Pair the outer factors and the inner factors so that both pairs contain the same expression $n^2+3n$. A substitution then reveals the perfect square.

subtopic: Induction: sum of squares
statement: Show, using mathematical induction, that the sum of the first $n$ squares satisfies $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: For $n=1$: LHS $=1$ and RHS $=\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3}{6}=1$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k} r^2=\frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}$ [M1] Then $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r^2=\frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}+(k+1)^2$ [M1] $=\frac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\right]}{6}$ [A1] $=\frac{(k+1)(2k^2+7k+6)}{6}=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{6}$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+1$. True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Factor out $(k+1)$ early rather than expanding everything, so the target $(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)$ is easy to reach. Always finish with the full conclusion sentence.

subtopic: Direct proof of arithmetic and geometric series formulas
statement: (a) The arithmetic series with first term $a$ and common difference $d$ has $n$ terms, with sum $S_n$. By writing $S_n$ forwards and then backwards, show that $S_n=\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$. [3] (b) The geometric series $T_n=a+ar+ar^2+\dots+ar^{n-1}$ has common ratio $r\neq1$. By considering $T_n-rT_n$, show that $T_n=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=a+(a+d)+\dots+(a+(n-1)d)$ and, reversed, $S_n=(a+(n-1)d)+(a+(n-2)d)+\dots+a$ [M1] Adding the terms in matching positions, each pair sums to $2a+(n-1)d$ [A1] There are $n$ such pairs, so $2S_n=n\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ [M1] $S_n=\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $rT_n=ar+ar^2+\dots+ar^{n}$ [M1] $T_n-rT_n=a-ar^n$, since all middle terms cancel [M1][A1] So $(1-r)T_n=a(1-r^n)$ and, since $r\neq1$, $T_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: In both derivations the idea is to line up terms so that almost everything cancels or pairs up. Write out at least three terms and the last term of each line so the cancellation is visible.

subtopic: Direct proof: n cubed minus n is divisible by 6
statement: Let $n$ be an integer. (a) Show that $n^3-n=(n-1)n(n+1)$. [2] (b) Hence prove that $n^3-n$ is divisible by $6$. [3] (c) Hence prove that $n^3+5n$ is divisible by $6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n^3-n=n(n^2-1)$ [M1] $=n(n-1)(n+1)$ using the difference of two squares [A1] $=(n-1)n(n+1)$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers [M1] Among any three consecutive integers at least one is even, so the product is divisible by $2$ [R1] Exactly one of any three consecutive integers is a multiple of $3$, so the product is divisible by $3$. As $2$ and $3$ have no common factor, the product is divisible by $6$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $n^3+5n=(n^3-n)+6n$ [M1] Both $n^3-n$ and $6n$ are divisible by $6$, so their sum is divisible by $6$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For divisibility by a composite number, justify divisibility by its coprime factors separately. Look for a way to write the new expression as the old one plus an obvious multiple.

subtopic: Induction: Bernoulli's inequality
statement: (a) Prove by mathematical induction that $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, where $x>-1$ is a fixed real number. [7] (b) Hence show that $(1.003)^{400}>2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) For $n=1$: both sides equal $1+x$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $(1+x)^k\ge1+kx$ [M1] Since $x>-1$, we have $1+x>0$, so multiplying both sides of the inequality by $1+x$ preserves it [R1] $(1+x)^{k+1}\ge(1+kx)(1+x)$ [M1] $=1+(k+1)x+kx^2$ [A1] Since $kx^2\ge0$, $1+(k+1)x+kx^2\ge1+(k+1)x$, hence $(1+x)^{k+1}\ge1+(k+1)x$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [R1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks] (b) Use $x=0.003$ and $n=400$ (valid since $x>-1$) [M1] $(1.003)^{400}\ge1+400\times0.003=2.2>2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When an inequality is multiplied by an expression, state why that expression is positive; this is where the condition $x>-1$ is used and it earns a reasoning mark.

subtopic: Induction with a second-order recurrence
statement: A sequence is defined by $u_1=1$, $u_2=5$ and $u_{n+2}=5u_{n+1}-6u_n$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. (a) Find $u_3$. [1] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $u_n=3^n-2^n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $u_3=5\times5-6\times1=19$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) For $n=1$: $3-2=1=u_1$ and for $n=2$: $9-4=5=u_2$, so true for $n=1$ and $n=2$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$ and $n=k+1$: $u_k=3^k-2^k$ and $u_{k+1}=3^{k+1}-2^{k+1}$ [M1] Then $u_{k+2}=5\left(3^{k+1}-2^{k+1}\right)-6\left(3^k-2^k\right)$ [M1] $=3^k(15-6)-2^k(10-6)$ [A1] $=9\cdot3^k-4\cdot2^k=3^{k+2}-2^{k+2}$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+2$. True for $n=1,2$, and true for $n=k,k+1$ implies true for $n=k+2$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: A two-term recurrence needs two base cases and an assumption for two consecutive values. Express every power in terms of $3^k$ and $2^k$ before collecting.

subtopic: Induction on higher derivatives of ln(1+x)
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$ for $x>-1$. (a) Find $f'(x)$, $f''(x)$ and $f'''(x)$. [3] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac{(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!}{(1+x)^n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, where $f^{(n)}$ is the $n$th derivative of $f$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}$ [A1] $f''(x)=-\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}$ [A1] $f'''(x)=\frac{2}{(1+x)^3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $n=1$: $\frac{(-1)^0\,0!}{(1+x)^1}=\frac{1}{1+x}=f'(x)$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $f^{(k)}(x)=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(1+x)^{-k}$ [M1] Differentiating: $f^{(k+1)}(x)=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\cdot(-k)(1+x)^{-k-1}$ [M1] $=(-1)^{k}\,k!\,(1+x)^{-(k+1)}$ using $(-1)^{k-1}\cdot(-1)=(-1)^k$ and $(k-1)!\,k=k!$ [A1] $=\frac{(-1)^{(k+1)-1}\left((k+1)-1\right)!}{(1+x)^{k+1}}$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [A1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Part (a) shows the pattern you are trying to prove; use it to check the formula for $n=1,2,3$ before starting the induction. Keep track of the sign factor $(-1)^{k}$ carefully when differentiating.

subtopic: Induction: powers of a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{A}^2$. [1] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $\mathbf{A}^n=\begin{pmatrix} 2^n & n\cdot2^{n-1} \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) For $n=1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2^1 & 1\cdot2^0 \\ 0 & 2^1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{A}$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\mathbf{A}^k=\begin{pmatrix} 2^k & k\cdot2^{k-1} \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{k+1}=\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2^k & k\cdot2^{k-1} \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2^{k+1} & 2^k+k\cdot2^k \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2^{k+1} & (k+1)2^k \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [A1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Multiply the assumed form of $\mathbf{A}^k$ by $\mathbf{A}$ entry by entry and only then simplify powers of $2$. State clearly which matrix product you are using ($\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^k$).

subtopic: Proof of de Moivre's theorem by induction
statement: (a) Prove by mathematical induction that $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$. [6] (b) Hence show that $(1+\mathrm{i})^8=16$. [2]
markscheme: (a) For $n=1$: both sides equal $\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^k=\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta$ [M1] $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{k+1}=(\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)$ [M1] $=(\cos k\theta\cos\theta-\sin k\theta\sin\theta)+\mathrm{i}(\sin k\theta\cos\theta+\cos k\theta\sin\theta)$ [A1] $=\cos(k+1)\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin(k+1)\theta$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+1$. True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks] (b) $1+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] $(1+\mathrm{i})^8=(\sqrt{2})^8\left(\cos2\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin2\pi\right)$ [M1] $=16(1+0)=16$ [AG] [2 marks]
tips: The key step is recognizing the compound-angle formulas for $\cos(k+1)\theta$ and $\sin(k+1)\theta$ in the expanded product. In part (b), convert to modulus-argument form first.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction that root 2 is irrational
statement: (a) Prove that if $a$ is an integer and $a^2$ is even, then $a$ is even. [3] (b) Hence prove by contradiction that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. [5]
markscheme: (a) Prove the contrapositive: if $a$ is odd then $a^2$ is odd. Let $a=2k+1$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $a^2=4k^2+4k+1=2\left(2k^2+2k\right)+1$ [A1] which is odd. So if $a^2$ is even then $a$ is even [R1] [3 marks] (b) Assume $\sqrt{2}$ is rational, so $\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}$ with $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ having no common factor [M1] Then $p^2=2q^2$ [A1] So $p^2$ is even, hence $p$ is even by part (a) [R1] Let $p=2m$: $4m^2=2q^2$, so $q^2=2m^2$ [M1] So $q^2$ is even, hence $q$ is even. Then $p$ and $q$ share the factor $2$, contradicting the assumption. Hence $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Begin every contradiction proof with an explicit assumption (here: lowest terms). The contradiction must be stated clearly at the end, and part (a) should be quoted by name when used.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction: infinitely many primes
statement: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers. [6]
markscheme: Assume there are only finitely many primes, $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n$ [M1] Let $N=p_1p_2\cdots p_n+1$ [M1] Dividing $N$ by any $p_i$ leaves remainder $1$, so no $p_i$ divides $N$ [A1] Since $N>1$, $N$ has at least one prime factor [R1] This prime factor is not in the list $p_1,\dots,p_n$, contradicting the assumption that the list contains all primes [R1] Hence there are infinitely many primes [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Be precise: the contradiction is not that $N$ is prime, but that $N$ has a prime factor missing from the list. State that every integer greater than $1$ has a prime factor.

subtopic: Direct proof: product of two sums of two squares
statement: Let $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=(ac-bd)^2+(ad+bc)^2$. [3] (b) Hence write $13\times25$ as the sum of two squares of integers, by using $13=2^2+3^2$ and $25=3^2+4^2$. [2] (c) Find a way of writing $325$ as the sum of two squares of positive integers that is different from both $6^2+17^2$ and $1^2+18^2$. [2]
tips: In "show that" identities, expand each side separately and compare. Re-using an identity with a different assignment of the variables is a quick way to get a second solution in part (c).

subtopic: Direct proof: sum of four consecutive integers
statement: Let $n$ be an integer. (a) Show that the sum of the four consecutive integers $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$ is $4n+6$. [1] (b) Hence prove that the sum of four consecutive integers is never divisible by $4$. [2] (c) Given that every perfect square is of the form $4k$ or $4k+1$ for some integer $k$, prove that the sum of four consecutive integers is never a perfect square. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n+(n+1)+(n+2)+(n+3)=4n+6$ [M1] [AG] [1 mark] (b) $4n+6=4(n+1)+2$ [M1] So the sum leaves remainder $2$ when divided by $4$, hence is never divisible by $4$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) The sum is of the form $4m+2$ with $m=n+1\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] This is neither of the form $4k$ nor $4k+1$, so it is never a perfect square [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite the sum in the form $4m+r$ so the remainder is visible. A statement about remainders can be used to rule out whole families of values.

subtopic: Completing the square to prove a strict inequality
statement: Let $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Express $x^2+y^2-6x+10y+40$ in the form $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+c$, where $a,b,c$ are constants to be found. [3] (b) Hence prove that $x^2+y^2-6x+10y+40>0$ for all real $x$ and $y$, and state the minimum value of the expression. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9$ and $y^2+10y=(y+5)^2-25$ [M1] Expression $=(x-3)^2+(y+5)^2-9-25+40$ [A1] $=(x-3)^2+(y+5)^2+6$ so $a=3$, $b=-5$, $c=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Since $(x-3)^2\ge0$ and $(y+5)^2\ge0$, the expression is $\ge6>0$ for all real $x,y$ [R1] The minimum value is $6$, attained at $x=3$, $y=-5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A sum of squares plus a positive constant is always positive. Completing the square on each variable separately is the standard route to this type of result.

subtopic: Disproving claims with counterexamples
statement: Each of the following statements is false. In each case, give a counterexample, showing your working. (a) "For every positive integer $n$, the number $n^2-79n+1601$ is prime." [3] (b) "For all real numbers $a$ and $b$, if $a>b$ then $a^2>b^2$." [2] (c) "The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational." You may assume that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. [2]
markscheme: (a) Try $n=80$: $80^2-79\times80+1601=6400-6320+1601$ [M1] $=1681=41^2$ [A1] which is not prime (it has the factor $41$), so the claim is false [R1] [3 marks] (b) For example $a=1$, $b=-2$: $a>b$ [A1] but $a^2=1<4=b^2$, so the claim is false [R1] [2 marks] (c) Take $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$, both irrational (if $-\sqrt{2}$ were rational then so would be $\sqrt{2}$) [A1] Their sum is $0$, which is rational, so the claim is false [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A single valid counterexample disproves a universal claim. Verify your counterexample fully (here, show that $1681$ has a factor other than $1$ and itself) and state that it contradicts the claim.

subtopic: Converse and contrapositive with odd squares
statement: Let $S$ be the statement: "If $n$ is an odd integer, then $n^2-1$ is divisible by $8$." (a) Prove that $S$ is true. [3] (b) Write down the converse of $S$. [1] (c) Prove the converse of $S$ by proving its contrapositive. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $n=2k+1$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $n^2-1=4k^2+4k=4k(k+1)$ [A1] $k(k+1)$ is a product of two consecutive integers, so it is even, hence $4k(k+1)$ is divisible by $8$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) If $n^2-1$ is divisible by $8$, then $n$ is an odd integer [A1] [1 mark] (c) The contrapositive is: if $n$ is even, then $n^2-1$ is not divisible by $8$ [A1] Let $n=2m$: $n^2-1=4m^2-1=2\left(2m^2\right)-1$ [M1] which is odd, so it is not divisible by $2$ and hence not by $8$. The contrapositive is true, so the converse is true [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion; the contrapositive negates and swaps them. A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, but a statement and its converse are not.

subtopic: Number theory: remainders of powers
statement: An integer $N$ leaves remainder $3$ when divided by $7$. (a) Show that $N^2$ leaves remainder $2$ when divided by $7$. [3] (b) Show that $N^3$ leaves remainder $6$ when divided by $7$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N=7k+3$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $N^2=49k^2+42k+9=7\left(7k^2+6k+1\right)+2$ [A1] Since $7k^2+6k+1$ is an integer, the remainder is $2$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) $N^3=(7k+3)^3=343k^3+441k^2+189k+27$ [M1] $=7\left(49k^3+63k^2+27k+3\right)+6$ [A1] Since $49k^3+63k^2+27k+3$ is an integer, the remainder is $6$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the integer as $7k+3$, expand, and split off a multiple of $7$ so the remainder is clear. In part (b) you could also use $N^3=N\cdot N^2$.

subtopic: Proving a triple-angle identity and a cubic root
statement: (a) Prove that $\cos3\theta\equiv4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$. [3] (b) Hence show that $x=\cos20^\circ$ is a root of the equation $8x^3-6x-1=0$. [2] (c) Write down the other two roots of $8x^3-6x-1=0$ in the form $\cos\alpha$, where $0^\circ<\alpha<180^\circ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos3\theta=\cos(2\theta+\theta)=\cos2\theta\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\sin\theta$ [M1] $=(2\cos^2\theta-1)\cos\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta$ [A1] $=(2\cos^2\theta-1)\cos\theta-2(1-\cos^2\theta)\cos\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$ [M1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) With $\theta=20^\circ$: $4\cos^320^\circ-3\cos20^\circ=\cos60^\circ=\frac{1}{2}$ [M1] Multiplying by $2$: $8\cos^320^\circ-6\cos20^\circ=1$ [A1] so $x=\cos20^\circ$ is a root of $8x^3-6x-1=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $8x^3-6x-1=0$ with $x=\cos\theta$ gives $\cos3\theta=\frac{1}{2}$, so $3\theta=60^\circ,300^\circ,420^\circ$, giving $\theta=20^\circ,100^\circ,140^\circ$ [M1] The other roots are $\cos100^\circ$ and $\cos140^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the compound angle formula with $2\theta+\theta$ and the double angle formulas. A cubic has at most three roots, so once you have three distinct values of $\cos\theta$ you have them all.

subtopic: Complex numbers: proof of the parallelogram law
statement: Let $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Show that $|z_1+z_2|^2+|z_1-z_2|^2=2|z_1|^2+2|z_2|^2$. [4] (b) Given that $|z_1|=3$, $|z_2|=5$ and $|z_1+z_2|=7$, find the exact value of $|z_1-z_2|$. [2]
tips: Replace each modulus squared by $zz^*$ and expand like ordinary brackets, remembering that $(z_1+z_2)^*=z_1^*+z_2^*$. Look for cross terms that cancel when adding.

subtopic: Arrangements in a row with adjacency restrictions
statement: Five boys and three girls stand in a line for a photograph. (a) Find the number of possible arrangements with no restrictions. [1] (b) Find the number of arrangements in which the three girls stand together. [2] (c) Find the number of arrangements in which no two girls stand next to each other. [3]
markscheme: (a) $8!=40320$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Treat the three girls as one block: $6!$ arrangements of the $6$ objects, and $3!$ orders within the block [M1] $6!\times3!=720\times6=4320$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Arrange the boys first: $5!=120$ ways [M1] This creates $6$ gaps; choose $3$ of them for the girls and order the girls: $\binom{6}{3}\times3!=20\times6=120$ [M1] Total $=120\times120=14400$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For "no two adjacent", place the unrestricted people first and then slot the others into the gaps between them (including the ends). For "together", glue into a block and multiply by the internal arrangements.

subtopic: Committees with a pair that cannot serve together
statement: A student club has $9$ members, of whom $4$ are first-year students. A committee of $5$ members is to be chosen. (a) Find the number of committees containing exactly two first-year students. [2] (b) Find the number of committees containing at most one first-year student. [2] (c) Bella and Carl are two members who are not first-year students. They refuse to serve on the committee together. Find the number of possible committees (with any number of first-year students) that respect this condition. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\binom{4}{2}\times\binom{5}{3}$ [M1] $=6\times10=60$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Zero first-years: $\binom{5}{5}=1$; one first-year: $\binom{4}{1}\binom{5}{4}=20$ [M1] Total $=1+20=21$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) All committees: $\binom{9}{5}=126$ [M1] Committees containing both Bella and Carl: choose the other $3$ from the remaining $7$: $\binom{7}{3}=35$ [M1] Valid committees $=126-35=91$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For "at most" or "not both", split into cases or subtract the forbidden selections from the total. Check that your cases cover everything without overlap.

subtopic: Counting codes with repeated digits
statement: A security code consists of five digits chosen from $0,1,2,\dots,9$, and a code may begin with $0$. (a) Find the number of possible codes if digits may be repeated. [1] (b) Find the number of codes in which no digit is repeated. [2] (c) Find the number of codes that contain exactly two digits equal to $7$ (and the other three digits are not $7$, but may otherwise repeat). [3]
markscheme: (a) $10^5=100\,000$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $10\times9\times8\times7\times6$ [M1] $=30\,240$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Choose the positions of the two $7$s: $\binom{5}{2}=10$ [M1] Each of the other three positions has $9$ choices (not $7$): $9^3=729$ [M1] Total $=10\times729=7290$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Decide first whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed. For "exactly $k$ of a digit", choose their positions with a combination, then fill the remaining places.

subtopic: Circular arrangements of married couples
statement: Four married couples (eight people) are seated at a round table. Two seatings are considered the same if one can be obtained from the other by rotation. (a) Find the total number of different seatings. [1] (b) Find the number of seatings in which men and women alternate. [3] (c) Find the number of seatings in which each husband sits next to his wife. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(8-1)!=5040$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Seat the four men around the table: $(4-1)!=6$ ways [M1] The four women take the four gaps between the men: $4!=24$ ways [M1] Total $=6\times24=144$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Treat each couple as a unit: $(4-1)!=6$ circular arrangements of the four units [M1] Each couple can sit in $2$ orders: $2^4=16$ [M1] Total $=6\times16=96$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Fix the rotation by counting circular arrangements of $n$ objects as $(n-1)!$. For alternating patterns, seat one group first and then place the other group into the gaps.

subtopic: Multiplication principle with optional courses
statement: A restaurant offers 4 starters, 6 main courses and 3 desserts. (a) A diner chooses one starter, one main course and one dessert. Find the number of different meals possible. [2] (b) Another diner must choose one main course but may choose to have no starter and/or no dessert. Find the number of different meals possible for this diner. [2]
markscheme: (a) Number of meals $=4\times6\times3$ [M1] $=72$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Starter options: $4+1=5$ and dessert options: $3+1=4$ [M1] Number of meals $=5\times6\times4=120$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the multiplication principle when choices are made one after another. Treating "no starter" as an extra option is a quick way to handle optional courses.

subtopic: Number of diagonals of a convex polygon
statement: (a) Find the number of diagonals of a convex polygon with 10 sides. [2] (b) A convex polygon with $n$ sides has 44 diagonals. (i) Show that $n^2-3n-88=0$. [3] (ii) Hence find the value of $n$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Number of line segments joining pairs of vertices $=\binom{10}{2}=45$ [M1] Subtract the 10 sides: $45-10=35$ [A1] [2 marks] (b)(i) Number of diagonals $=\binom{n}{2}-n$ [M1] $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}-n=44$ [A1] $n^2-n-2n=88$, so $n^2-3n-88=0$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (ii) $(n-11)(n+8)=0$ so $n=11$ (reject $n=-8$) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A diagonal is a line joining two vertices that is not a side, so count all pairs of vertices and subtract the sides. Reject any negative root when $n$ is a number of sides.

subtopic: Word arrangements with vowels together or separated
statement: The eight letters of the word TRIANGLE are arranged in a line. (a) Find the total number of different arrangements. [1] (b) Find the number of arrangements in which the three vowels are together. [3] (c) Find the number of arrangements in which no two vowels are next to each other. [4]
markscheme: (a) $8!=40320$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Treat the vowels I, A, E as one block: $6!$ arrangements of the block and 5 consonants [M1] Vowels within the block can be ordered in $3!$ ways [M1] Number $=6!\times3!=720\times6=4320$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Arrange the 5 consonants: $5!=120$ ways [M1] This creates 6 gaps (including both ends) [A1] Place the 3 vowels in different gaps in order: $^6P_3=6\times5\times4=120$ [M1] Number $=120\times120=14400$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For "together" questions, glue the items into one block and multiply by the internal orderings. For "not adjacent" questions, arrange the other items first and place the restricted items in the gaps.
