subtopic: Arrangements of letters with repeats and restrictions
statement: The nine letters of the word COMMITTEE are arranged in a line. (a) Find the number of distinct arrangements. [2] (b) Find the number of distinct arrangements that begin and end with the letter E. [3] (c) Find the number of distinct arrangements in which the two letters M are next to each other. [3]
markscheme: (a) The letters M, T, E each appear twice [M1] Number $=\dfrac{9!}{2!\,2!\,2!}=\dfrac{362880}{8}=45360$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Place E at each end; the remaining letters are C, O, M, M, I, T, T [M1] Number of arrangements $=\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!}$ [M1] $=1260$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Treat MM as one object; there are 8 objects with T and E each repeated twice [M1] Number $=\dfrac{8!}{2!\,2!}$ [M1] $=10080$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide by the factorial of each repeated letter count. After fixing or gluing letters, recount which letters are still repeated.

subtopic: Four-digit numbers with distinct digits and a multiple of 5
statement: Four-digit positive integers are formed using the digits 0 to 9, with no digit used more than once in any integer. (a) Find the number of such integers that are greater than 5000 and are multiples of 5. [5] (b) Find the total number of such four-digit integers, and hence find the probability that one of them, chosen at random, is greater than 5000 and a multiple of 5. [2]
markscheme: (a) Multiple of 5 so the last digit is 0 or 5 [M1] Last digit 0: first digit from $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$ gives 5 choices [A1] then $8\times7=56$ choices for the middle digits, giving $5\times56=280$ [A1] Last digit 5: first digit from $\{6,7,8,9\}$ gives 4 choices, then $8\times7=56$, giving $4\times56=224$ [A1] Total $=280+224=504$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) Total number $=9\times9\times8\times7=4536$ [A1] Probability $=\dfrac{504}{4536}=\dfrac19$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Split into cases by the last digit because the restriction on the first digit differs. Fill the most restricted positions first.

subtopic: Handshakes between pairs of people
statement: (a) At a meeting, every person shakes hands exactly once with every other person. There are 66 handshakes in total. Find the number of people at the meeting. [3] (b) At a party there are 8 married couples. Each person shakes hands exactly once with every other person except his or her own partner. Find the total number of handshakes. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let there be $n$ people; handshakes $=\binom n2=66$ [M1] $n(n-1)=132$ so $n^2-n-132=0$ [A1] $(n-12)(n+11)=0$ so $n=12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) 16 people so $\binom{16}{2}=120$ possible pairs [M1] Subtract the 8 couples [M1] $120-8=112$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A handshake is an unordered pair, so use $\binom n2$ and not $n(n-1)$. In part (b) count all pairs first, then remove the forbidden ones.

subtopic: Lattice paths through a given point
statement: A path on a grid goes from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(6,4)$. Each step is either one unit to the right or one unit up. (a) Find the number of different paths from $(0,0)$ to $(6,4)$. [2] (b) Find the number of these paths that pass through the point $(3,2)$. [3] (c) Find the number of these paths that do not pass through $(3,2)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Each path has 10 steps, of which 4 are up [M1] Number $=\binom{10}{4}=210$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Paths from $(0,0)$ to $(3,2)$: $\binom52=10$ [M1] Paths from $(3,2)$ to $(6,4)$ (3 right, 2 up): $\binom52=10$ [A1] Number $=10\times10=100$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $210-100$ [M1] $=110$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Choose which of the steps are "up" steps. To pass through a point, multiply the number of paths to the point by the number of paths onward from it.

subtopic: Pascal's identity for binomial coefficients
statement: (a) Show that $\dbinom{n}{r-1}+\dbinom{n}{r}=\dbinom{n+1}{r}$, where $1\le r\le n$. [3] It is given that $\dbinom{15}{5}=3003$, $\dbinom{15}{6}=5005$ and $\dbinom{15}{7}=6435$. (b) Find the value of $\dbinom{16}{6}$ and the value of $\dbinom{16}{7}$. [2] (c) Hence find the value of $\dbinom{17}{7}$. [2]
tips: In part (a) factor out the common factorial terms before adding fractions. Pascal's identity builds each row from the row above, so apply it in the right index pairs.

subtopic: Identity k times nCk and the sum of k nCk
statement: (a) Show that $k\dbinom{n}{k}=n\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}$ for $1\le k\le n$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\dbinom{n}{k}=n\times2^{n-1}$. [3] (c) Given that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\dbinom{n}{k}=2304$, find the value of $n$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $k\dbinom nk=\dfrac{k\cdot n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}$ [A1] $=n\cdot\dfrac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!\,[(n-1)-(k-1)]!}=n\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\dbinom nk=n\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}$ [M1] $=n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\dbinom{n-1}{j}$ [M1] $=n(1+1)^{n-1}$ by the binomial theorem $=n\times2^{n-1}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) $n\times2^{n-1}=2304$ and $2304=9\times2^8$ [M1] $n=9$ (since $n\times2^{n-1}$ is increasing, this is the only solution) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write binomial coefficients in factorial form and cancel the extra factor of $k$. For the sum, shift the index so the terms become the coefficients of $(1+1)^{n-1}$.

subtopic: Circular seating of couples
statement: Four married couples are to be seated around a circular table. Two seatings are considered the same if one can be rotated to give the other. (a) Find the total number of different seatings. [1] (b) Find the number of seatings in which each husband sits next to his wife. [3] (c) Find the number of seatings in which men and women sit in alternate seats. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(8-1)!=5040$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Treat each couple as one block; 4 blocks in a circle: $(4-1)!=6$ [M1] Each couple can be ordered in 2 ways: $2^4=16$ [M1] Number $=6\times16=96$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Seat the 4 men around the table: $(4-1)!=6$ [M1] The 4 women fill the 4 gaps between the men: $4!=24$ [M1] Number $=6\times24=144$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In a circular arrangement, fix one object (or divide by the number of rotations) so that each seating is counted once. After the men are placed, the seats for the women are fixed gaps.

subtopic: Distributing distinct objects among people
statement: Six different books are given to three children, Ana, Ben and Cy. Each book is given to exactly one child, and a child may receive no books. (a) Find the total number of ways of giving out the books. [1] (b) Find the number of ways in which Ana receives no books. [1] (c) Find the number of ways in which each child receives at least one book. [4] (d) The books are given out at random, with all ways equally likely. Find the probability that each child receives at least one book. [2]
markscheme: (a) Each book has 3 choices: $3^6=729$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Each book goes to Ben or Cy: $2^6=64$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Number with at least one child receiving nothing: use inclusion-exclusion [M1] One child receives nothing: $3\times2^6=192$ [A1] Two children receive nothing (all books to one child): $3\times1=3$ [A1] Number with each child receiving at least one $=729-192+3=540$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Probability $=\dfrac{540}{729}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20}{27}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When objects are distinct, count by choosing a recipient for each object. For "at least one each", subtract the cases where someone gets nothing and add back the double-counted cases.

subtopic: Splitting a group into two unlabeled teams
statement: Ten players are to be divided into two teams of five. The teams are not labeled. (a) Find the number of different ways of dividing the players into two teams. [3] Two of the players, Kim and Lee, are the best players. (b) Find the number of ways in which Kim and Lee are in the same team. [2] (c) Find the number of ways in which Kim and Lee are in different teams. [2]
markscheme: (a) Choose the 5 players for one particular team: $\binom{10}{5}=252$ [M1] Each division is counted twice (once for each team) [M1] Number $=\dfrac{252}{2}=126$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Kim and Lee are together, so choose the other 3 members of their team from the remaining 8 players [M1] $\binom83=56$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $126-56$ [M1] $=70$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If the groups are not labeled, divide by the number of ways to order the groups. For "different teams", subtracting from the total is usually faster than counting directly.

subtopic: Inclusion-exclusion with three divisibility conditions
statement: Let $S$ be the set of integers $1,2,3,\dots,210$. (a) Find the number of integers in $S$ that are divisible by (i) 6; (ii) 42. [2] (b) Use the inclusion-exclusion principle to find the number of integers in $S$ that are divisible by at least one of 2, 3 and 7. [4] (c) An integer is chosen at random from $S$. Find the probability that it is divisible by none of 2, 3 and 7. [2]
markscheme: (a) (i) $\dfrac{210}{6}=35$ [A1] (ii) $\dfrac{210}{42}=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $n(A\cup B\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\cap B)-n(A\cap C)-n(B\cap C)+n(A\cap B\cap C)$ [M1] $n(A)+n(B)+n(C)=105+70+30=205$ [A1] $n(A\cap B)+n(A\cap C)+n(B\cap C)=35+15+10=60$ [A1] $205-60+5=150$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Number divisible by none $=210-150=60$ [M1] Probability $=\dfrac{60}{210}=\dfrac27$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For three sets, the three pairwise overlaps are subtracted and the triple overlap is added back. Intersections of divisibility sets correspond to the least common multiple.

subtopic: Hat problem: derangements of four objects
statement: Four guests each leave a hat in a cloakroom. When they leave, the four hats are returned to the guests in a random order, with all $4!$ orders equally likely. (a) Write down the total number of ways in which the hats can be returned. [1] (b) Find the number of ways in which exactly two guests receive their own hat. [2] (c) Explain why it is impossible for exactly three guests to receive their own hat. [1] (d) Given that there are 2 ways of returning three hats to three guests so that none receives their own hat, find the number of ways in which exactly one guest receives their own hat. [2] (e) Hence find the number of ways in which no guest receives their own hat, and the probability that no guest receives their own hat. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4!=24$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Choose the 2 guests who receive their own hat: $\binom42=6$ [M1] The other two must swap hats: 1 way, so number $=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) If three guests have their own hats, the fourth hat can only be the fourth guest's own hat, so all four are correct [R1] [1 mark] (d) Choose the guest with the correct hat: 4 ways [M1] The other three guests all receive wrong hats in 2 ways, so number $=4\times2=8$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Exactly four correct: 1; exactly three: 0; exactly two: 6; exactly one: 8 [M1] Number with none correct $=24-1-0-6-8=9$ [A1] Probability $=\dfrac{9}{24}=\dfrac38$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Classify outcomes by how many items are in the correct place, then subtract from the total. Check your classes cover every case exactly once.

subtopic: Selections with at most or at least conditions
statement: A basket contains 5 different apples and 4 different oranges. Five pieces of fruit are chosen at random from the basket. (a) Find the total number of different selections of five pieces of fruit. [1] (b) Find the number of selections that contain at most two oranges. [3] (c) Find the probability that a randomly chosen selection contains at most two oranges. [1] (d) Given that a selection contains at most two oranges, find the probability that it contains exactly two oranges. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\binom95=126$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) 0 oranges: $\binom55=1$; 1 orange: $\binom41\binom54=20$; 2 oranges: $\binom42\binom53=60$ [M1] [A1] Total $=1+20+60=81$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{81}{126}=\dfrac{9}{14}\ (=0.643)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{P(\text{exactly 2})}{P(\text{at most 2})}=\dfrac{60}{81}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20}{27}\ (=0.741)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For "at most", add the cases from zero up to the limit. For conditional probability, restrict the sample space to the given condition: use $81$, not $126$, as the denominator.

subtopic: PIN codes with repeated digits
statement: A four-digit PIN is formed by choosing each digit from 0 to 9. Digits may be repeated and a PIN may start with 0. (a) Find the number of possible PINs. [1] (b) Find the number of PINs in which all four digits are different. [2] (c) Find the number of PINs in which exactly two of the digits are the same, and the other two digits are different from this digit and from each other. [3] (d) A PIN is chosen at random. Find the probability that it contains at least two digits that are the same. [1]
markscheme: (a) $10^4=10000$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $10\times9\times8\times7$ [M1] $=5040$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Choose the 2 positions for the repeated digit: $\binom42=6$ [M1] Repeated digit: 10 choices; third digit: 9 choices; fourth digit: 8 choices [M1] Number $=6\times10\times9\times8=4320$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $1-\dfrac{5040}{10000}$ $=0.496$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Decide where the repeated digit goes first, then fill the remaining positions with choices that avoid earlier digits. "At least two the same" is the complement of "all different".

subtopic: Triangles formed from the vertices of a regular polygon
statement: Triangles are formed by choosing three of the 12 vertices of a regular 12-sided polygon. (a) Find the total number of triangles that can be formed. [1] (b) Find the number of triangles that have exactly two sides that are also sides of the polygon. [2] (c) Find the number of triangles that have exactly one side that is also a side of the polygon. [3] (d) Hence find the number of triangles that have no side in common with the polygon. [2] (e) A triangle is chosen at random from all the triangles in part (a). Find the probability that it has no side in common with the polygon. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\binom{12}{3}=220$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Two polygon sides share a vertex, so the triangle is formed by three consecutive vertices [M1] There are 12 such triangles [A1] [2 marks] (c) Choose the polygon side: 12 ways [M1] The third vertex must not be either endpoint, nor adjacent to either endpoint [M1] So $12-4=8$ choices, and number $=12\times8=96$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $220-12-96$ [M1] $=112$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{112}{220}=\dfrac{28}{55}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Classify triangles by how many polygon sides they use. In (c), check which third vertices would create a second polygon side, and exclude them.

subtopic: Lottery combinations and probability
statement: In a lottery, a player chooses 6 different numbers from the numbers 1 to 45. Six winning numbers are then drawn at random from the numbers 1 to 45, without replacement. (a) Find the number of different ways to choose 6 numbers. [1] (b) Find the probability that a player's choice matches all six winning numbers. [1] (c) Find the probability that a player's choice matches exactly four of the winning numbers. [3] (d) Find the probability that a player's choice matches at least five of the winning numbers. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\binom{45}{6}=8145060$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{1}{8145060}=1.23\times10^{-7}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Choose 4 of the 6 winning numbers: $\binom64=15$ [M1] Choose the other 2 numbers from the 39 non-winning numbers: $\binom{39}{2}=741$ [M1] Probability $=\dfrac{15\times741}{8145060}=\dfrac{11115}{8145060}=0.00136$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Exactly five: $\binom65\binom{39}{1}=6\times39=234$ [M1] Exactly six: 1 [M1] Probability $=\dfrac{234+1}{8145060}=\dfrac{235}{8145060}=2.89\times10^{-5}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split the player's numbers into those from the winning set and those from the non-winning set, and multiply the two combination counts. Always divide by the total number of possible choices.

subtopic: Passwords with at least one digit
statement: A password has 8 characters. Each character is one of the 26 lowercase letters or one of the 10 digits 0 to 9, and characters may be repeated. (a) Find the total number of possible passwords. [1] (b) Find the number of passwords that contain at least one digit. [2] (c) A password is chosen at random. Find the probability that it contains at least one digit. [1] (d) Find the probability that a randomly chosen password contains exactly two digits. [3] (e) A program tests $5\times10^8$ passwords per second. Find the maximum time, in hours, that it needs to test all passwords that contain at least one digit. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: "At least one" is easiest as total minus none. For exactly $k$ of a type, choose the positions first, then count the choices for each position.

subtopic: Bridge hand probabilities from combinations
statement: A bridge hand consists of 13 cards dealt at random from a standard pack of 52 cards. The pack contains 13 spades and 4 aces. (a) Find the total number of different bridge hands. [1] (b) Find the probability that a hand contains exactly five spades. [3] (c) Find the probability that a hand contains no aces. [2] (d) Find the probability that a hand contains at least one ace. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\binom{52}{13}=635013559600\approx6.35\times10^{11}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Choose 5 spades from 13: $\binom{13}{5}$ [M1] Choose 8 non-spades from 39: $\binom{39}{8}$ [M1] Probability $=\dfrac{\binom{13}{5}\binom{39}{8}}{\binom{52}{13}}=0.125$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\binom{48}{13}}{\binom{52}{13}}$ [M1] $=0.304$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $1-0.3038=0.696$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the nCr function on your GDC and keep full accuracy until the final rounding. "At least one" is the complement of "none".

subtopic: Arrangements with no two identical letters adjacent
statement: The eleven letters of the word MISSISSIPPI are arranged in a line. (a) Find the number of distinct arrangements. [2] (b) Find the number of distinct arrangements in which no two of the letter S are next to each other. [4] (c) Find the number of distinct arrangements in which the first letter is M and no two of the letter S are next to each other. [3]
markscheme: (a) The letters are M(1), I(4), S(4), P(2) [M1] $\dfrac{11!}{4!\,4!\,2!}=34650$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Arrange the 7 letters that are not S: M, I, I, I, I, P, P: $\dfrac{7!}{4!\,2!}=105$ [M1] [A1] These create 8 gaps (including the ends) [A1] Choose 4 gaps for the S's: $\binom84=70$, so number $=105\times70=7350$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The other six letters I, I, I, I, P, P: $\dfrac{6!}{4!\,2!}=15$ arrangements [M1] The S's can go after M, between any two of the six letters, or at the end, which gives 7 gaps [A1] Number $=15\times\binom74=15\times35=525$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Arrange the unrestricted letters first, then choose gaps for the restricted ones. In (c), the gap right after the fixed M is allowed, but the gap before M is not available.

subtopic: Numbers with strictly increasing or decreasing digits
statement: A three-digit positive integer is formed using the digits 0 to 9. (a) Find the number of such integers whose digits are in strictly increasing order from left to right, for example 148. [3] (b) Find the number of such integers whose digits are in strictly decreasing order from left to right, for example 730. [3]
markscheme: (a) Any choice of three different digits gives exactly one increasing arrangement [M1] The digit 0 would have to be first, which is not allowed, so choose the digits from 1 to 9 [A1] Number $=\binom93=84$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Any choice of three different digits gives exactly one decreasing arrangement [M1] The digit 0 would then be last, which is allowed, so choose from the 10 digits 0 to 9 [A1] Number $=\binom{10}{3}=120$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When the order is forced, count the selections of digits instead of arrangements. Check separately whether the digit 0 is allowed in the forced position.

subtopic: Quota sampling by age group
statement: A town has 4800 adult residents: 2000 aged 18 to 34, 1700 aged 35 to 59 and 1100 aged 60 or over. A researcher wants a sample of 240 residents, using quota sampling by age group. (a) Find the quota for each age group. [3] (b) The researcher interviews people outside a shopping center on a weekday morning until every quota is filled. State one advantage of quota sampling compared with simple random sampling, and one reason the sample may still be biased. [2]
markscheme: (a) Sampling fraction $=\dfrac{240}{4800}=\dfrac{1}{20}$ [M1] 18 to 34: $\dfrac{2000}{20}=100$ [A1] 35 to 59: $85$ and 60 or over: $55$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Advantage, for example: no sampling frame (list of all residents) is needed, so it is quicker and cheaper [A1] Bias, for example: only people at the shopping center on weekday mornings are reached, so working residents or those who rarely shop there are under-represented [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Quotas are proportional to group size. Note that quota sampling is non-random: within each quota the interviewer chooses who is asked, which can introduce bias.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation of grouped heights
statement: The heights of 70 students are summarized in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Height } h \text{ (cm)} & 140\le h<150 & 150\le h<160 & 160\le h<170 & 170\le h<180 & 180\le h<190 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 14 & 25 & 18 & 7 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Use midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean height. [2] (b) Estimate the population standard deviation of the heights. [2] (c) Each height is converted from centimeters to inches by dividing by 2.54. Write down the estimated mean and standard deviation of the heights in inches. [2] (d) Explain why the answers to (a) and (b) are only estimates. [1]
markscheme: (a) Midpoints 145, 155, 165, 175, 185 [M1] Mean $=\dfrac{6(145)+14(155)+25(165)+18(175)+7(185)}{70}=\dfrac{11610}{70}=165.857\ldots\approx166$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Using the GDC, correct GDC list entry or sum of squares [M1] population standard deviation $\sigma=10.9$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Mean $=\dfrac{165.857}{2.54}=65.3$ inches [A1] Population standard deviation $=\dfrac{10.92}{2.54}=4.30$ inches [A1] [2 marks] (d) The exact heights within each class are unknown, so the midpoint is used to represent every value in the class [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Enter midpoints and frequencies in a GDC list and read $\bar{x}$ and $\sigma$. Dividing every value by a constant divides both the mean and the standard deviation by that constant.

subtopic: Outliers preserved under a positive linear transformation
statement: A data set $x$ has lower quartile $Q_1=20$ and upper quartile $Q_3=32$. A value is an outlier if it is less than $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or greater than $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$. (a) Find the lower and upper limits for outliers in the data set $x$. [3] A new data set $y$ is formed using $y=3x-4$. (b) Find the quartiles and interquartile range of $y$, and hence find the lower and upper limits for outliers in $y$. [3] (c) More generally, let $y=ax+b$ where $a>0$. Show that a value $x_0$ is an outlier in the data set $x$ if and only if the corresponding value $ax_0+b$ is an outlier in the data set $y$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\text{IQR}=32-20=12$ [A1] $20-1.5\times12=2$ [A1] $32+1.5\times12=50$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $Q_1=3(20)-4=56$ and $Q_3=3(32)-4=92$ [A1] $\text{IQR}=36$ [A1] Limits: $56-54=2$ and $92+54=146$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1'=aQ_1+b$, $Q_3'=aQ_3+b$ so $\text{IQR}'=a\,\text{IQR}$ [M1] Lower limit for $y$: $aQ_1+b-1.5a\,\text{IQR}=a(Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR})+b$, and similarly the upper limit is $a(Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR})+b$, so both limits for $y$ are the images of the limits for $x$ [A1] Since $a>0$, $x\mapsto ax+b$ preserves order, so $x_0$ is below (or above) the limit for $x$ if and only if $ax_0+b$ is below (or above) the corresponding limit for $y$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A positive linear transformation scales the IQR by $a$ and shifts the quartiles with the data. In part (c), use $a>0$ explicitly when preserving the direction of an inequality.

subtopic: Radian conversion, arc length and sector area
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $6$ cm and a central angle of $150^\circ$. (a) Write the angle $150^\circ$ in radians, in terms of $\pi$. [1] (b) Find the exact length of the arc of the sector. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $150\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Arc length $=r\theta=6\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=5\pi$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area $=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12(36)\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ [M1] $=15\pi\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The formulas $s=r\theta$ and $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ only work when $\theta$ is in radians, so convert first. Leave $\pi$ in your answer when an exact value is requested.

subtopic: Exact trigonometric values in radians
statement: (a) Write down the exact values of $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ and $\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] $\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [M1] $=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use a reference angle in the correct quadrant and decide the sign with the unit circle. Rationalizing denominators makes products like the one in (b) quicker to simplify.

subtopic: Cosine rule leading to a quadratic in x
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=x$ cm, $AC=(x+3)$ cm, $BC=7$ cm and angle $BAC=60^\circ$. (a) Show that $x^2+3x-40=0$. [3] (b) Hence find the value of $x$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $7^2=x^2+(x+3)^2-2x(x+3)\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $49=x^2+x^2+6x+9-x(x+3)$ [A1] $49=x^2+3x+9$, so $x^2+3x-40=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(x+8)(x-5)=0$ [M1] $x=5$ (reject $x=-8$ since a length is positive) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $AC=8$, so area $=\tfrac12(5)(8)\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=10\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute $\cos60^\circ=\tfrac12$ before expanding, and always reject any root that gives a negative length.

subtopic: Ambiguous case with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$, $AC=5$ and angle $ABC=30^\circ$. (a) Show that $\sin C=\dfrac45$. [2] (b) Find the two possible exact values of $\cos C$. [2] (c) Hence find the two possible exact values of $BC$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin C}{8}=\dfrac{\sin30^\circ}{5}$ [M1] $\sin C=\dfrac{8\times\frac12}{5}=\dfrac45$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos^2C=1-\dfrac{16}{25}=\dfrac{9}{25}$ [M1] $\cos C=\dfrac35$ or $\cos C=-\dfrac35$ (angle $C$ may be acute or obtuse) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=180^\circ-30^\circ-C=150^\circ-C$, so $\sin A=\sin150^\circ\cos C-\cos150^\circ\sin C=\tfrac12\cos C+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\dfrac45$ [M1] Sine rule: $\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}=\dfrac{5}{\sin30^\circ}$ gives $BC=10\sin A$ [M1] When $\cos C=\dfrac35$: $BC=10\left(\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{5}\right)=3+4\sqrt3$ [A1] When $\cos C=-\dfrac35$: $BC=10\left(-\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{5}\right)=4\sqrt3-3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The ambiguous case arises when the side opposite the given angle is shorter than the other given side. Write $\sin A$ as $\sin(150^\circ-C)$ and expand with the compound angle formula to stay exact.

subtopic: Bearings forming a right-angled triangle
statement: A boat leaves a harbor $H$ and sails $12$ km on a bearing of $035^\circ$ to a buoy $B$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $125^\circ$ to a point $C$. (a) Show that angle $HBC=90^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $HC$. [2] (c) Find the bearing of $C$ from $H$, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) The bearing of $H$ from $B$ is $035^\circ+180^\circ=215^\circ$ [M1] The bearing of $C$ from $B$ is $125^\circ$, and $215^\circ-125^\circ=90^\circ$, so angle $HBC=90^\circ$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $HC=\sqrt{12^2+9^2}$ [M1] $=15$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) Angle $BHC=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right)=36.87^\circ$ [M1] $C$ lies clockwise from $B$ as seen from $H$, so the bearing is $35^\circ+36.87^\circ$ [M1] $=71.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use alternate (back) bearings by adding or subtracting $180^\circ$. A quick sketch with a north line at each point prevents sign errors.

subtopic: Diagonals and angles in a cuboid
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$ with $AB=4$ cm and $AD=3$ cm. The vertical edges $AE$, $BF$, $CG$ and $DH$ each have length $12$ cm, with $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ directly above $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ respectively. (a) Show that the space diagonal $AG=13$ cm. [2] (b) Find the exact value of the sine of the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\cos\angle AGE$, where $E$ is directly above $A$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ [M1] $AG=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ cm [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) The angle between $AG$ and the base is $\angle GAC$, in the right-angled triangle $ACG$ with $CG=12$ [M1] $\sin\angle GAC=\dfrac{CG}{AG}=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $EG=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ and $AE\perp EG$, so triangle $AEG$ is right-angled at $E$ [M1] $\cos\angle AGE=\dfrac{EG}{AG}=\dfrac{5}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In 3D problems, identify a right-angled triangle that contains the required angle and write down its sides before using any ratio. The angle between a line and a plane is measured to its projection onto the plane.

subtopic: Wedge: angles between lines and planes
statement: A solid wedge has a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ m and $AD=8$ m. The point $E$ is $5$ m vertically above $D$, and the point $F$ is $5$ m vertically above $C$. The top face $ABFE$ is a sloping rectangle, the face $DCFE$ is a vertical rectangle, and the triangles $ADE$ and $BCF$ are vertical triangular ends. (a) Find $AC$. [2] (b) Find the exact length of $AF$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $AF$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (d) Find the angle between the sloping face $ABFE$ and the base $ABCD$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $=10$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AF=\sqrt{AC^2+CF^2}=\sqrt{100+25}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{125}=5\sqrt5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) The angle is $\angle FAC$, so $\tan\angle FAC=\dfrac{5}{10}$ [M1] $=26.6^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The faces meet along $AB$. $AD\perp AB$ and $AE$ lies in the sloping face, with $DE\perp AD$, so the angle is $\angle EAD$ with $\tan\angle EAD=\dfrac58$ [M1] $=32.0^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For the angle between two planes, find a line in each plane perpendicular to their common edge. Check that the triangle you pick for the angle is right-angled.

subtopic: Sprinkler sector: radians, area and perimeter
statement: A garden sprinkler waters a sector of a circle of radius $7.5$ m, with central angle $110^\circ$. (a) Write $110^\circ$ in radians, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (b) Find the area watered. [2] (c) Find the length of fencing needed to enclose the sector, that is, the perimeter of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $110\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=1.92$ radians [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(7.5)^2\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{18}\right)$ [M1] $=54.0\text{ m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Arc length $=7.5\times1.9199=14.399$ [M1] Perimeter $=2(7.5)+14.399=29.4$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not round the angle until the end of a calculation; store the unrounded value on your GDC. Remember the perimeter includes both straight radii.

subtopic: Optimizing a sector with a restricted angle
statement: A piece of wire of length $40$ cm is bent to form the boundary of a sector of a circle of radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians. (a) Show that the area $A\text{ cm}^2$ of the sector is $A=20r-r^2$. [3] (b) Ignoring any restriction on $\theta$, find the value of $r$ for which $A$ is greatest, and the greatest value of $A$. [3] (c) It is now required that $\theta\le\dfrac32$. Find the greatest possible area of the sector, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [4]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter: $2r+r\theta=40$, so $r\theta=40-2r$ [M1] $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12r(40-2r)$ [M1] $=20r-r^2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=20-2r=0$ [M1] $r=10$ [A1] $A=200-100=100\text{ cm}^2$ (a maximum since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-2<0$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\theta=\dfrac{40-2r}{r}\le\dfrac32$ [M1] $80-4r\le3r$, so $r\ge\dfrac{80}{7}$ [A1] When $r=10$, $\theta=2>\dfrac32$, so the unrestricted maximum is not allowed; $A$ is decreasing for $r>10$, so the maximum occurs at $r=\dfrac{80}{7}$ [R1] $A=20\left(\dfrac{80}{7}\right)-\left(\dfrac{80}{7}\right)^2=\dfrac{11200-6400}{49}=\dfrac{4800}{49}\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: When a constraint rules out the stationary point, the optimum lies at the boundary of the allowed interval. State clearly why the function is monotonic on that interval.

subtopic: Area of a segment with exact values
statement: $O$ is the center of a circle of radius $2\sqrt2$ cm. The chord $AB$ subtends an angle of $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ at $O$. (a) Find the exact area of the sector $OAB$. [2] (b) Find the exact area of triangle $OAB$. [2] (c) Hence find the exact area of the minor segment cut off by the chord $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Area $=\tfrac12(2\sqrt2)^2\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$ [M1] $=\tfrac12(8)\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)=3\pi\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(8)\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [M1] $=4\times\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=2\sqrt2\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Segment $=3\pi-2\sqrt2\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A segment is a sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. Evaluate $\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ with a reference angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

subtopic: Chords of a circle and parallel chords
statement: A circle has center $O$ and radius $13$. The chord $AB$ has length $24$. (a) Find the distance from $O$ to the chord $AB$. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $\cos\angle AOB$. [3] A second chord $CD$ is parallel to $AB$ and lies on the opposite side of $O$ from $AB$, at a distance $12$ from $O$. (c) Find the length of $CD$. [2] (d) The four endpoints $A$, $B$, $D$, $C$ form a trapezium whose parallel sides are $AB$ and $CD$. Find its area. [2]
markscheme: (a) The perpendicular from $O$ to a chord bisects it, so the half-chord is $12$ [M1] Distance $=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $\alpha=\angle AOB$; $\sin\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [M1] $\cos\alpha=1-2\sin^2\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ [M1] $=1-2\left(\dfrac{144}{169}\right)=-\dfrac{119}{169}$ [A1] [3 marks] Alternatively, use the cosine rule in triangle $AOB$: $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{169+169-576}{2(169)}=-\dfrac{119}{169}$. (c) Half-length of $CD=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$ [M1] $CD=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The perpendicular distance between the chords is $5+12=17$ [M1] Area $=\tfrac12(24+10)(17)=289$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects the chord, giving a right-angled triangle with the radius as hypotenuse. Remember the chords are on opposite sides of the center when adding their distances.

subtopic: Cone volume, surface area and a frustum by subtraction
statement: A solid cone has base radius $5$ cm and slant height $13$ cm. (a) Find the perpendicular height of the cone. [2] (b) Find the exact volume of the cone. [2] (c) Find the exact total surface area of the cone, including its base. [2] A smaller cone is cut off from the top of the cone by a plane parallel to the base, at a perpendicular distance of $6$ cm from the apex. (d) Find the exact volume of the remaining solid, which is a frustum. [3]
markscheme: (a) $h=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}$ [M1] $=12$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\tfrac13\pi(5^2)(12)$ [M1] $=100\pi\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Curved surface $=\pi rl=65\pi$ [M1] Total $=65\pi+\pi(25)=90\pi\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The small cone has height $6$, which is half of $12$, so its radius is $\dfrac52$ [M1] $V_{small}=\tfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac{25}{4}\right)(6)=\dfrac{25\pi}{2}$ [A1] Frustum $=100\pi-\dfrac{25\pi}{2}=\dfrac{175\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Similar cones have lengths in the same ratio, so a cut at half the height halves the radius. Find a frustum by subtracting the small cone from the large one.

subtopic: Composite solid: cone with hemisphere
statement: A frozen dessert is made in the shape of a cone with a hemisphere on top. The cone has base radius $3$ cm and perpendicular height $10$ cm, and the hemisphere has radius $3$ cm with its flat face joined exactly to the base of the cone. (a) Find the total volume of the dessert. [3] (b) Find the total outer surface area of the dessert. [3] (c) The outer surface is coated with chocolate costing \$0.004 per $\text{cm}^2$. Find the cost of the chocolate, to the nearest cent. [2]
markscheme: (a) Cone: $\tfrac13\pi(3^2)(10)=30\pi$ [M1] Hemisphere: $\tfrac23\pi(3^3)=18\pi$ [M1] Total $=48\pi=151\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Slant height $=\sqrt{3^2+10^2}=\sqrt{109}$ [M1] Curved cone surface $=\pi(3)\sqrt{109}$ and hemisphere surface $=2\pi(3^2)=18\pi$ [M1] Total $=18\pi+3\pi\sqrt{109}=155\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Cost $=154.95\times0.004$ [M1] $=\$0.62$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The flat face where the two solids join is not part of the outer surface. Keep unrounded values in your GDC until the final cost.

subtopic: Sliding ladder and its midpoint
statement: A ladder of length $6$ m rests with its top on a vertical wall and its foot on horizontal ground. The ladder makes an angle $\theta$ with the ground. (a) When $\theta=60^\circ$, find the exact height of the top of the ladder and the exact distance of its foot from the wall. [2] (b) The foot is pulled away from the wall until the top of the ladder is at a height of $3\sqrt2$ m. Find the exact distance the foot has moved. [3] (c) Let $M$ be the midpoint of the ladder and $O$ the point where the wall meets the ground. By taking $O$ as the origin, show that $OM$ has the same length for every value of $\theta$, and state this length. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height $=6\sin60^\circ=3\sqrt3$ m [A1] Distance of foot $=6\cos60^\circ=3$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $6\sin\theta=3\sqrt2$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\theta=45^\circ$ [M1] Foot distance $=6\cos45^\circ=3\sqrt2$ [A1] Distance moved $=3\sqrt2-3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) The foot is at $(6\cos\theta,0)$ and the top at $(0,6\sin\theta)$, so $M=(3\cos\theta,3\sin\theta)$ [M1] $OM^2=9\cos^2\theta+9\sin^2\theta=9$ [A1] So $OM=3$ m for every $\theta$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Place the corner at the origin and write coordinates using $6\cos\theta$ and $6\sin\theta$. The identity $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ turns the midpoint problem into a one-line proof.

subtopic: Angles of depression to boats on different bearings
statement: An observer stands at the top $T$ of a vertical lighthouse of height $60$ m, whose base $O$ is at sea level. Boat $A$ is due east of the lighthouse and the angle of depression from $T$ to $A$ is $12^\circ$. Boat $B$ is on a bearing of $150^\circ$ from the lighthouse, and the angle of depression from $T$ to $B$ is $25^\circ$. (a) Find the horizontal distance $OA$. [2] (b) Find the horizontal distance $OB$. [2] (c) Find the distance $AB$ between the two boats. [3]
tips: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the boat (alternate angles). Work with the horizontal triangle $OAB$ for the distance between the boats.

subtopic: Track perimeter constraint and maximum area
statement: The inner boundary of a running track consists of two parallel straight sections, each of length $L$ m, joined by two semicircular ends, each of radius $r$ m. The total length of the boundary is $400$ m. (a) Show that the area $A\text{ m}^2$ enclosed by the boundary is $A=400r-\pi r^2$. [3] (b) Each straight section must be at least $90$ m long. Show that $r\le\dfrac{110}{\pi}$. [2] (c) Find the largest possible value of $A$ and the value of $r$ at which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter: $2L+2\pi r=400$, so $L=200-\pi r$ [M1] Area $=2rL+\pi r^2$ (rectangle plus two semicircles) [M1] $=2r(200-\pi r)+\pi r^2=400r-\pi r^2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $L\ge90$ gives $200-\pi r\ge90$ [M1] $\pi r\le110$, so $r\le\dfrac{110}{\pi}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=400-2\pi r$ [M1] This is zero at $r=\dfrac{200}{\pi}\approx63.7>\dfrac{110}{\pi}$, so $A$ is increasing throughout the allowed interval [R1] The maximum occurs at $r=\dfrac{110}{\pi}=35.0$ m [A1] $A=400(35.014)-\pi(35.014)^2=10\,200\text{ m}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Check whether the stationary point lies in the allowed interval before concluding it is the maximum. If it does not, evaluate at the endpoint.

subtopic: Cosine rule with 4, 5, 6 triangle and double angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=4$, $CA=5$ and $AB=6$. (a) Use the cosine rule to show that $\cos A=\dfrac34$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\cos C$. [2] (c) Show that $\cos C=2\cos^2A-1$, and hence explain why angle $C$ is twice angle $A$. [3] (d) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos A=\dfrac{5^2+6^2-4^2}{2(5)(6)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{45}{60}=\dfrac34$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos C=\dfrac{4^2+5^2-6^2}{2(4)(5)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5}{40}=\dfrac18$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2\cos^2A-1=2\left(\dfrac{9}{16}\right)-1=\dfrac18=\cos C$ [AG] [M1] Since $\cos C=\cos2A$ [A1] and since $\cos A>0$ means $0<2A<\pi$, while $0<C<\pi$, and cosine is one-to-one on $(0,\pi)$, $C=2A$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $\sin A=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{9}{16}}=\dfrac{\sqrt7}{4}$ [M1] Area $=\tfrac12(5)(6)\dfrac{\sqrt7}{4}=\dfrac{15\sqrt7}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Label the triangle carefully so that each angle is opposite the matching side in the cosine rule. Use $\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1$ to get an exact sine without a calculator.

subtopic: Ambiguous case: peg positions for a rope
statement: A straight wall starts at a point $A$. A post $B$ is $18$ m from $A$, and the line $AB$ makes an angle of $38^\circ$ with the wall. A rope of length $13$ m is fixed at $B$, and its other end $C$ is pegged to the wall. (a) Find the two possible sizes of angle $ACB$. [4] (b) Hence find the two possible distances $AC$. [3] (c) Find the shortest rope length for which it is possible to reach the wall. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin\angle ACB}{18}=\dfrac{\sin38^\circ}{13}$ [M1] $\sin\angle ACB=0.8525$ [A1] $\angle ACB=58.5^\circ$ [A1] or $\angle ACB=180^\circ-58.5^\circ=121.5^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) For $58.5^\circ$: $\angle ABC=180^\circ-38^\circ-58.5^\circ=83.5^\circ$ and $AC=\dfrac{13\sin83.52^\circ}{\sin38^\circ}=21.0$ m [M1] [A1] For $121.5^\circ$: $\angle ABC=20.5^\circ$ and $AC=\dfrac{13\sin20.48^\circ}{\sin38^\circ}=7.39$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) The shortest rope is the perpendicular distance $18\sin38^\circ=11.1$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Test for a second solution whenever you use the sine rule to find an angle: the obtuse supplement is valid if the angle sum is still below $180^\circ$. Keep full calculator precision to avoid drift in the second length.

subtopic: Pythagoras with an unknown side and a double angle
statement: A right-angled triangular flower bed has perpendicular sides of length $x$ m and $(x+7)$ m, and a hypotenuse of length $(x+8)$ m. (a) Show that $x^2-2x-15=0$. [3] (b) Hence find $x$. [1] (c) Let $\theta$ be the smallest angle of the triangle. Find the exact value of $\cos2\theta$. [2]
tips: Expand each bracket carefully before collecting terms. The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side.

subtopic: Exact value of sin 75 degrees and the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=60^\circ$, angle $B=45^\circ$ and $BC=\sqrt6$. (a) Show that $\sin75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$. [3] (b) Find the exact length of $AC$. [2] (c) Find the exact length of $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin75^\circ=\sin(45^\circ+30^\circ)=\sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ+\cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac12$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{AC}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{\sin60^\circ}$ [M1] $AC=\dfrac{\sqrt6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=\sqrt6\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Angle $C=75^\circ$ and $\dfrac{AB}{\sin75^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{\sin60^\circ}$ [M1] $AB=\dfrac{\sqrt6(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{6+2\sqrt3}{2\sqrt3}$ [A1] $=\sqrt3+1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split $75^\circ$ as $45^\circ+30^\circ$ and use a compound angle formula. Rationalize denominators at each step to keep the surds under control.

subtopic: Melting a sphere into cones
statement: A solid metal sphere of radius $6$ cm is melted and recast into identical solid cones, each with base radius $3$ cm and perpendicular height $8$ cm. No metal is lost. (a) Find the volume of the sphere. [2] (b) Find the volume of one cone. [2] (c) Find the number of cones that can be made. [1] (d) Find the total curved surface area of all the cones as a percentage of the surface area of the sphere. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\tfrac43\pi(6^3)=288\pi=905\text{ cm}^3$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\tfrac13\pi(3^2)(8)=24\pi=75.4\text{ cm}^3$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{288\pi}{24\pi}=12$ cones [A1] [1 mark] (d) Slant height $=\sqrt{3^2+8^2}=\sqrt{73}$, so one cone has curved area $\pi(3)\sqrt{73}$ [M1] Total $=12\times3\pi\sqrt{73}=966\text{ cm}^2$ and sphere surface $=4\pi(36)=452\text{ cm}^2$ [M1] Percentage $=\dfrac{966.3}{452.4}\times100=214\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Volume is conserved when a solid is recast, so divide the volumes. Use the slant height, not the vertical height, in the curved surface area formula.

subtopic: Overlapping circles: common region
statement: Two circles each have radius $2$. Their centers $A$ and $B$ are $2$ units apart. The circles intersect at points $P$ and $Q$. (a) Show that angle $PAQ=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. [2] (b) Find the length of the minor arc $PQ$ of the circle with center $A$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the segment cut off from that circle by the chord $PQ$. [3] (d) Hence find the exact area of the region common to both circles. [2] (e) Find the perimeter of the region common to both circles. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AP=AB=BP=2$, so triangle $ABP$ is equilateral and $\angle PAB=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] By symmetry $\angle PAQ=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) Arc $=r\theta=2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sector area $=\tfrac12(4)\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [M1] Triangle $APQ=\tfrac12(4)\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ [M1] Segment $=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The common region is two identical segments [M1] Area $=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}-2\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Perimeter $=2\times\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Spot the equilateral triangle formed by the two centers and an intersection point. The common region of two equal circles is made of two identical segments.

subtopic: Kite string and angle of elevation
statement: A kite is flown on a straight string of length $80$ m, held $1.4$ m above level ground. Assume the string is taut and straight. (a) The string makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the height of the kite above the ground. [2] (b) The wind changes and the kite rises to a height of $60$ m above the ground, with the same string length. Find the new angle the string makes with the horizontal. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height above hand $=80\sin35^\circ=45.89$ [M1] Height above ground $=45.89+1.4=47.3$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) Height above hand $=60-1.4=58.6$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{58.6}{80}$ [M1] $\theta=47.1^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Remember to add (or subtract) the height of the hand when moving between the height above the hand and the height above the ground. Draw a right-angled triangle with the string as hypotenuse.

subtopic: Finding n and a from consecutive coefficients
statement: In the expansion of $(1+ax)^n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and $a>0$, the coefficient of $x$ is $12$ and the coefficient of $x^2$ is $60$. (a) Find the value of $n$ and the value of $a$. [5] (b) Hence find the coefficient of $x^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $na=12$ [A1] $\dbinom n2a^2=60$, so $n(n-1)a^2=120$ [A1] Dividing by $(na)^2=144$: $\dfrac{n-1}{n}=\dfrac{120}{144}=\dfrac56$ [M1] $6n-6=5n$, so $n=6$ [A1] $a=2$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) Coefficient $=\dbinom63(2)^3$ [M1] $=20\times8=160$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Dividing one equation by the square of the other eliminates $a$ and leaves an equation in $n$ alone. Check your values against both given coefficients.

subtopic: Product of binomial expansions and estimation
statement: (a) Find the first four terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the expansion of $(2-x)(1+3x)^6$. [5] (b) By substituting a suitable value of $x$, use your answer to (a) to estimate $1.99\times1.03^6$, giving your answer as a decimal. [2]
tips: When multiplying two expansions, collect each power of $x$ from every pair of terms that gives that power. Choose $x$ so that both brackets match the numbers in the estimate.

subtopic: Sum of coefficients to find n, then a coefficient
statement: The sum of the coefficients in the expansion of $(1+2x)^n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, is $6561$. (a) Find the value of $n$. [2] (b) Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion. [3]
markscheme: (a) Setting $x=1$: $3^n=6561$ [M1] $n=8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) General term $\binom{8}{r}(2x)^r$ [M1] For $x^3$: $\binom{8}{3}\times2^3$ [M1] $=56\times8=448$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The sum of coefficients always comes from substituting $x=1$. Recognize $6561$ as a power of $3$.

subtopic: Coefficient of a negative-power term in (x + c/x^2)^n
statement: Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $\left(x+\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)^9$. [4]
markscheme: General term $\binom{9}{r}x^{9-r}\left(\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)^r=\binom{9}{r}3^r x^{9-3r}$ [M1] $9-3r=3\Rightarrow r=2$ [A1] Coefficient $=\binom{9}{2}\times3^2=36\times9$ [M1] $=324$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Combine the powers of $x$ into a single exponent in $r$ and solve for $r$ before evaluating anything.

subtopic: Term independent of x with an unknown constant
statement: The term independent of $x$ in the expansion of $\left(x^2+\dfrac{k}{x}\right)^6$, where $k>0$, is $240$. Find the value of $k$. [5]
markscheme: General term $\binom{6}{r}(x^2)^{6-r}\left(\dfrac{k}{x}\right)^r=\binom{6}{r}k^r x^{12-3r}$ [M1] Independent of $x$ when $12-3r=0$, so $r=4$ [A1] $\binom{6}{4}k^4=240\Rightarrow15k^4=240$ [M1] $k^4=16$ [A1] $k=2$ since $k>0$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Form an equation in $k$ only after you have identified the correct value of $r$. Use the condition $k>0$ to discard the negative root.

subtopic: Middle term of a two-variable binomial expansion
statement: Find the middle term in the expansion of $(3x-2y)^6$. [4]
markscheme: The expansion has $7$ terms, so the middle term is the fourth, with $r=3$ [M1][A1] Term $=\binom{6}{3}(3x)^3(-2y)^3$ [M1] $=20\times27\times(-8)\,x^3y^3=-4320x^3y^3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: With $n=6$ there are seven terms, so the middle one has $r=3$. Include both variables in your final answer.

subtopic: Ratio of consecutive coefficients to find n
statement: In the expansion of $(1+2x)^n$, where $n\geq3$, the coefficient of $x^3$ is four times the coefficient of $x^2$. (a) Write down, in terms of $n$, the coefficient of $x^2$ and the coefficient of $x^3$. [2] (b) Hence find the value of $n$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Coefficient of $x^2$ is $\binom{n}{2}\times4=2n(n-1)$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^3$ is $\binom{n}{3}\times8=\dfrac{4n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{4n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}=4\times2n(n-1)$ [M1] Dividing by $4n(n-1)\neq0$: $\dfrac{n-2}{3}=2$ [M1] $n=8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Cancel the common factor $n(n-1)$ explicitly and say why it is non-zero. Do not expand the products unnecessarily.

subtopic: Product of a linear factor and a binomial expansion
statement: (a) Find the first four terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the expansion of $(2-x)^6$. [3] (b) Hence find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(1+2x)(2-x)^6$. [3]
tips: List the pairs of terms that multiply to give $x^3$ rather than expanding the whole product. Check that you include the factor $2$ from $2x$.

subtopic: Finding n and a from the first terms of an expansion
statement: The expansion of $(1+ax)^n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$, begins $1-12x+60x^2+\dots$. Find the value of $n$ and the value of $a$. [7]
tips: Two unknowns need two equations, one from each coefficient. Notice that $n^2a^2=(na)^2$ is already known, which avoids solving a quadratic.

subtopic: Pascal identity for binomial coefficients: algebraic proof
statement: (a) Show that, for integers $0\leq r<n$, $\dbinom{n}{r}+\dbinom{n}{r+1}=\dbinom{n+1}{r+1}$. [3] (b) Hence, or otherwise, find all possible values of $k$ such that $\dbinom{15}{6}+\dbinom{15}{7}=\dbinom{16}{k}$. [2]
tips: In the proof, write both fractions over the common denominator $(r+1)!(n-r)!$. In part (b), remember the symmetry $\binom{n}{r}=\binom{n}{n-r}$ gives a second value.

subtopic: Proof that the sum of binomial coefficients is 2^n
statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer. (a) By considering the expansion of $(1+x)^n$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}=2^n$. [2] (b) Show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-1)^r\binom{n}{r}=0$. [2] (c) Hence show that the sum of the binomial coefficients $\dbinom{n}{r}$ over all even values of $r$ is $2^{n-1}$. [2] (d) Hence evaluate $\dbinom{10}{0}+\dbinom{10}{2}+\dbinom{10}{4}+\dbinom{10}{6}+\dbinom{10}{8}+\dbinom{10}{10}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $(1+x)^n=\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}x^r$ [M1] Letting $x=1$: $2^n=\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Letting $x=-1$ in the same expansion [M1] $(1-1)^n=0=\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-1)^r\binom{n}{r}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) Adding the results of (a) and (b): the odd-$r$ terms cancel and the even-$r$ terms double [M1] so $2\displaystyle\sum_{r\text{ even}}\binom{n}{r}=2^n$, giving $2^{n-1}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (d) $2^{9}=512$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Substituting $x=1$ and $x=-1$ into the general expansion is the key idea. In part (c), explain why the odd terms cancel instead of just stating the result.

subtopic: Identity r*C(n,r) = n*C(n-1,r-1) and the sum of r*C(n,r)
statement: (a) Show that, for $1\leq r\leq n$, $r\dbinom{n}{r}=n\dbinom{n-1}{r-1}$. [2] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\binom{n}{r}=n\,2^{n-1}$. [3] (c) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{10}r\binom{10}{r}$. [1] (d) Hence find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{10}r\binom{10}{r}\left(\dfrac12\right)^{10}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r\dbinom{n}{r}=r\cdot\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}=\dfrac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}$ [M1] $=n\cdot\dfrac{(n-1)!}{(r-1)!\,((n-1)-(r-1))!}=n\dbinom{n-1}{r-1}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\binom{n}{r}=n\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{r-1}$ [M1] Letting $s=r-1$: $n\displaystyle\sum_{s=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{s}$ [M1] $=n\,2^{n-1}$ using the sum of binomial coefficients [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) $10\times2^9=5120$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) The term for $r=0$ is zero, so the sum is $\dfrac{5120}{2^{10}}$ [M1] $=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite $r\binom{n}{r}$ with factorials and cancel the factor $r$. In part (d), note that the $r=0$ term contributes nothing, so part (c) applies directly.

subtopic: Expansion with a negative integer power and validity
statement: (a) Expand $(1+2x)^{-3}$ in ascending powers of $x$ as far as the term in $x^3$. [4] (b) State the values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [1] (c) Hence find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(1-x)(1+2x)^{-3}$. [2]
tips: For a negative or fractional power, the expansion is only valid when $|bx|<1$ for $(1+bx)^n$. Remember the factor $2^k$ from $(2x)^k$.

subtopic: Matching coefficients in two binomial expansions with different parameters
statement: The expansions of $(1+ax)^5$ and $(1+bx)^4$, where $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $b>0$, have equal coefficients of $x$. The coefficient of $x^2$ in the expansion of $(1+ax)^5$ is $10$ more than the coefficient of $x^2$ in the expansion of $(1+bx)^4$. Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [6]
markscheme: Coefficients of $x$: $5a$ and $4b$ [M1] $5a=4b$, so $a=\dfrac{4b}{5}$ [A1] Coefficients of $x^2$: $\binom52a^2=10a^2$ and $\binom42b^2=6b^2$ [M1] $10a^2-6b^2=10$ [A1] Substituting: $10\times\dfrac{16b^2}{25}-6b^2=10\Rightarrow0.4b^2=10$ [M1] $b^2=25$, so $b=5$ (as $b>0$) and $a=4$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Translate each sentence of the question into one equation. Expressing $a$ in terms of $b$ from the first equation keeps the second equation simple.

subtopic: Greatest coefficient in a binomial expansion
statement: Let $T_r$ denote the coefficient of $x^r$ in the expansion of $(3+2x)^9$, for $0\leq r\leq9$. (a) Write down an expression for $T_r$. [1] (b) Show that $\dfrac{T_{r+1}}{T_r}=\dfrac{2(9-r)}{3(r+1)}$. [3] (c) Hence determine the values of $r$ for which $T_r$ is greatest. [3] (d) Find the greatest coefficient. [1]
markscheme: (a) $T_r=\dbinom9r3^{9-r}2^r$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{T_{r+1}}{T_r}=\dfrac{\binom{9}{r+1}3^{8-r}2^{r+1}}{\binom9r3^{9-r}2^r}$ [M1] $\dfrac{\binom{9}{r+1}}{\binom9r}=\dfrac{9-r}{r+1}$ [A1] so ratio $=\dfrac{9-r}{r+1}\times\dfrac23=\dfrac{2(9-r)}{3(r+1)}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) $T_{r+1}>T_r\iff2(9-r)>3(r+1)\iff r<3$ [M1] The ratio equals $1$ when $r=3$, so $T_4=T_3$, and for $r>3$ the ratio is less than $1$ [A1] So $T_0<T_1<T_2<T_3=T_4>T_5>\dots$ and $T_r$ is greatest for $r=3$ and $r=4$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $T_3=\dbinom93\times3^6\times2^3=84\times729\times8=489888$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Compare successive terms using their ratio rather than testing every value. Check the boundary case where the ratio equals $1$, since it produces two equal greatest coefficients.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities as terms of an expansion
statement: A biased coin shows heads with probability $0.3$. The coin is tossed $10$ times and $X$ is the number of heads. The probabilities $P(X=r)$ are the terms in the expansion of $(0.7+0.3)^{10}$. (a) Write down an expression for $P(X=r)$ and hence find $P(X=4)$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [3] (b) Show that $\dfrac{P(X=r+1)}{P(X=r)}=\dfrac{3(10-r)}{7(r+1)}$ for $0\leq r\leq9$. [3] (c) Hence find the most likely number of heads, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=r)=\dbinom{10}{r}(0.3)^r(0.7)^{10-r}$ [A1] $P(X=4)=\dbinom{10}{4}(0.3)^4(0.7)^6$ [M1] $=0.200$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{P(X=r+1)}{P(X=r)}=\dfrac{\binom{10}{r+1}}{\binom{10}{r}}\times\dfrac{0.3}{0.7}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{10-r}{r+1}\times\dfrac37$ [A1] $=\dfrac{3(10-r)}{7(r+1)}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) The ratio exceeds $1$ when $30-3r>7r+7$, that is $r<2.3$ [M1] So the probabilities increase up to $r=3$ and decrease afterwards; the most likely number of heads is $3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Consecutive probabilities differ by a ratio that depends on $r$ only. The mode is where that ratio first drops below $1$, so find the largest $r$ with ratio greater than $1$ and add one.

subtopic: Unknown n from the second term, then constant term in (x + c/x^2)^n
statement: The coefficient of the second term, in descending powers of $x$, in the expansion of $\left(x+\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)^n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, is $24$. (a) Find the value of $n$. [2] (b) Hence find the constant term in the expansion. [4]
markscheme: (a) Second term: $\dbinom n1x^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)=2n\,x^{n-3}$ [M1] $2n=24\Rightarrow n=12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) General term $\dbinom{12}{r}x^{12-r}\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)^r=\dbinom{12}{r}2^rx^{12-3r}$ [M1] Constant term when $12-3r=0$, so $r=4$ [A1] $\dbinom{12}{4}\times2^4=495\times16$ [M1] $=7920$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The second term in descending powers has $r=1$. A constant term exists only when the exponent $n-3r$ can equal zero, which holds here since $n=12$.

subtopic: Constant term in the product (a + x^2)(x - c/x)^n
statement: Find the constant term in the expansion of $(3+x^2)\left(x-\dfrac2x\right)^6$. [6]
markscheme: General term of $\left(x-\dfrac2x\right)^6$ is $\dbinom6r x^{6-r}\left(-\dfrac2x\right)^r=\dbinom6r(-2)^rx^{6-2r}$ [M1][A1] Constant term arises from $3\times(\text{term in }x^0)$ and $x^2\times(\text{term in }x^{-2})$ [M1] $x^0$: $r=3$, giving $\dbinom63(-2)^3=-160$ [A1] $x^{-2}$: $r=4$, giving $\dbinom64(-2)^4=240$ [A1] Constant term $=3(-160)+240=-240$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: In a product, find every pair of terms whose powers add to zero. Here the factor $x^2$ needs the $x^{-2}$ term of the second expansion.

subtopic: Smallest n for a coefficient to exceed a value
statement: The coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(1+2x)^n$, where $n\geq3$, is denoted by $c_n$. (a) Show that $c_n=\dfrac{4n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}$. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $c_n>10000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $c_n=\dbinom n3\times2^3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}\times8=\dfrac{4n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Solve $\dfrac{4n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}>10000$ using a table of values or graph [M1] $c_{20}=9120<10000$ [A1] $c_{21}=10640>10000$, so the smallest value is $n=21$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the table feature on your calculator and show the two consecutive values either side of $10000$ as evidence. Give $n$ as an integer.

subtopic: Finding n and a from the coefficients of a fractional-power expansion
statement: The expansion of $(1+ax)^n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$, is $1+3x+\dfrac{27}{2}x^2+\dots$ (a) Find the value of $n$ and the value of $a$. [5] (b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [1] (c) Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion. [2]
markscheme: (a) Coefficient of $x$: $na=3$ [M1] Coefficient of $x^2$: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}a^2=\dfrac{27}{2}$ [M1] $n^2a^2-na^2=27$, and $n^2a^2=9$, so $na^2=-18$ [M1] $a=\dfrac{-18}{3}=-6$ [A1] $n=\dfrac{3}{-6}=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $|{-6x}|<1$, so $|x|<\dfrac16$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Coefficient of $x^3$ is $\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)}{3!}(-6)^3$ [M1] $=\left(-\dfrac{5}{16}\right)(-216)=\dfrac{135}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Since $n$ need not be an integer, do not assume $n$ is positive. Eliminate $n$ by using $(na)^2$ already known from the first coefficient.

subtopic: Proof that the sum of squares of binomial coefficients equals C(2n,n)
statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer. (a) Write down the coefficient of $x^n$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^{2n}$. [1] (b) By writing $(1+x)^{2n}=(1+x)^n(1+x)^n$ and expanding each factor, show that the coefficient of $x^n$ is also equal to $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nr\binom n{n-r}$. [3] (c) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\left(\binom nr\right)^2=\binom{2n}{n}$. [2] (d) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{5}\left(\binom5r\right)^2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dbinom{2n}{n}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(1+x)^n=\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nrx^r$ [M1] An $x^n$ term in the product arises from $x^r$ in the first factor and $x^{n-r}$ in the second [M1] so the coefficient is $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nr\binom n{n-r}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\dbinom n{n-r}=\dbinom nr$ [M1] Equating the two expressions for the coefficient: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}\left(\binom nr\right)^2=\binom{2n}{n}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (d) $\dbinom{10}{5}=252$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Match the powers: choosing $x^r$ from one bracket forces $x^{n-r}$ from the other. The symmetry $\binom{n}{n-r}=\binom{n}{r}$ turns the product into a square.

subtopic: Inverse of a rational function and solving f(x) = f^-1(x)
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq3$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (b) Write down the domain of $f^{-1}$. [1] (c) Solve the equation $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. Give your answers in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) Let $y=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$, so $y(x-3)=2x+1$ [M1] $x(y-2)=3y+1$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}=\dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}$ [M1] $(2x+1)(x-2)=(3x+1)(x-3)$ giving $2x^2-3x-2=3x^2-8x-3$ [M1] $x^2-5x-1=0$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{29}}{2}$ (neither equals $2$ or $3$, so both are valid) [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Collect all terms containing the new variable on one side before factoring. The domain of $f^{-1}$ equals the range of $f$, which excludes the horizontal asymptote value.

subtopic: Composite function: largest domain and range
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq2$, and $g(x)=\sqrt{x+5}$, for $x\geq-5$. (a) Find an expression for $(g\circ f)(x)$ and determine the largest possible domain of $g\circ f$. [4] (b) Find the range of $g\circ f$. [3]
markscheme:
(a) $(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x-2}+5}$ [A1] Need $\dfrac{1}{x-2}+5\geq0$ [M1] $\dfrac{5x-9}{x-2}\geq0$ [M1] $x\leq\dfrac95$ or $x>2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Since $f(x)
eq0$, the expression inside the root is $\dfrac{1}{x-2}+5
eq5$ [M1] On the domain, $\dfrac{1}{x-2}+5$ takes every value in $[0,\infty)$ except $5$ [A1] Range is $y\geq0$, $y
eq\sqrt5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The domain of a composite needs the inner function defined and its output inside the domain of the outer function. For the range, track which output values the inner function can never take.

subtopic: Domain, restricted range and inverse of a logarithmic function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\ln\left(x^2-2x-8\right)$. (a) Find the largest possible domain of $f$. [3] The domain of $f$ is now restricted to $x>4$. (b) Write down the range of $f$. [2] (c) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain. [3] (d) Find $f^{-1}(2.5)$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Need $x^2-2x-8>0$ [M1] $(x-4)(x+2)>0$ [A1] $x<-2$ or $x>4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $x>4$, $x^2-2x-8$ takes every positive value [M1] so the range is $f(x)\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=\ln\left(x^2-2x-8\right)\Rightarrow e^y=(x-1)^2-9$ [M1] $x-1=\sqrt{e^y+9}$, taking the positive root since $x>4$ [A1] $f^{-1}(x)=1+\sqrt{e^x+9}$, domain $x\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $f^{-1}(2.5)=1+\sqrt{e^{2.5}+9}$ [M1] $=5.60$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complete the square to invert a quadratic inside a logarithm, and use the restricted domain to choose the correct root. The domain of the inverse equals the range of $f$.

subtopic: Evaluating composite functions
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x^2-1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(3)$. [2] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [2]
tips: In $(f\circ g)(x)$ the function $g$ is applied first. Work from the inside out and substitute the whole inner expression.

subtopic: Inverse of a rational function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq 3$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (b) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (c) Find $f^{-1}(0)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Let $y=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$, so $y(x-3)=2x+1$ [M1] $x(y-2)=3y+1$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The range of $f$ is $f(x)\in\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)\neq 2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $f^{-1}(0)=\dfrac{1}{-2}=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Collect all the $x$ terms on one side and factorize before dividing. The range of $f$ equals the domain of $f^{-1}$, which gives a quick check on part (b).

subtopic: Self-inverse function with an unknown parameter
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{ax+3}{x-2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq 2$, where $a$ is a constant. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ in terms of $a$. [3] (b) Given that $f$ is a self-inverse function, find the value of $a$. [2] (c) For this value of $a$, find $f(f(5))$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y(x-2)=ax+3$ [M1] $x(y-a)=2y+3$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{2x+3}{x-a}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Self-inverse means $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ for all $x$, so $(ax+3)(x-a)=(2x+3)(x-2)$ [M1] Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$ gives $a=2$ (and the $x$ and constant terms $-1$ and $-6$ also agree) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(5)=\dfrac{13}{3}$ [A1] $f\left(\dfrac{13}{3}\right)=\dfrac{26/3+3}{13/3-2}=\dfrac{35/3}{7/3}=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A self-inverse function satisfies $f(f(x))=x$. Equating $f$ with $f^{-1}$ and comparing coefficients is usually quicker than composing twice.

subtopic: Largest domain and range of standard functions
statement: (a) Find the largest possible domain of $f(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{x-1}$. [3] (b) Find the largest possible domain of $g(x)=\ln(x^2-x-2)$. [3] (c) Write down the range of $h(x)=3-2\cos x$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Require $9-x^2\ge 0$ [M1] so $-3\le x\le 3$ [A1] and $x\neq 1$ since the denominator is zero there [A1] [3 marks] (b) Require $x^2-x-2>0$ [M1] $(x-2)(x+1)>0$ [A1] so $x<-1$ or $x>2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-1\le\cos x\le 1$, so the range is $1\le h(x)\le 5$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: List each restriction separately (square root, denominator, logarithm) and then combine them. For a logarithm the argument must be strictly positive.

subtopic: Restricted domain and solving f(x) = f inverse (x)
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^2-4x+5$, for $x\ge 2$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (b) Given that $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)=y$, explain why $y=x$. [2] (c) Hence solve the equation $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$, giving your answer in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-2)^2+1$ [M1] $y=(x-2)^2+1$ gives $x=2+\sqrt{y-1}$ (positive root since $x\ge 2$) [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x-1}$, with domain $x\ge 1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)=y$ implies $f(y)=x$ [R1] $f$ is increasing for $x\ge 2$, so if $y>x$ then $f(y)>f(x)$, i.e. $x>y$, a contradiction; similarly $y<x$ is impossible, so $y=x$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)=x$ gives $x^2-5x+5=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] The value $\dfrac{5-\sqrt5}{2}\approx 1.38$ is less than 2, so it is rejected [R1] $x=\dfrac{5+\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solutions of $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ for an increasing function lie on the line $y=x$, but always check each root against the restricted domain.

subtopic: Even and odd functions
statement: (a) Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ is an odd function. [2] (b) Show that $g(x)=2^x+2^{-x}$ is an even function. [2] The function $p$ is odd with $p(2)=5$, and the function $q$ is even with $q(2)=3$. (c) Find (i) $r(-2)$, where $r(x)=p(x)q(x)$; (ii) $s(-2)$, where $s(x)=p(x)+q(x)$. [3]
tips: To test symmetry, always simplify $f(-x)$ and compare it with both $f(x)$ and $-f(x)$. Even means $f(-x)=f(x)$; odd means $f(-x)=-f(x)$.

subtopic: Periodic function defined on one period
statement: The function $f$ has period 5 and is defined by $f(x)=x^2$ for $0\le x<5$. (a) Find $f(13)$. [2] (b) Find $f(-1)$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)=4$ for $0\le x\le 12$. [3]
tips: Shift the input by multiples of the period until it lies in the interval where the rule is given. For solving equations, add multiples of the period to each base solution.

subtopic: One-to-one test and restricting the domain using calculus
statement: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=x^4-8x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $g(2)$ and $g(-2)$, and hence explain why $g$ is not one-to-one. [2] (b) Find $g'(x)$ and the stationary points of $g$ for which $x\ge 0$. [3] The domain of $g$ is now restricted to $x\ge k$. (c) Find the smallest value of $k$ for which $g$ is one-to-one, giving a reason for your answer. [2] (d) For this value of $k$, write down the range of $g$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $g(2)=16-32=-16$ and $g(-2)=-16$ [M1] Two different inputs give the same output, so a horizontal line $y=-16$ meets the graph more than once and $g$ is many-to-one [R1] [2 marks] (b) $g'(x)=4x^3-16x$ [M1] $4x(x^2-4)=0$ [M1] $x=0$ or $x=2$ (with $x\ge0$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $g'(x)<0$ for $0<x<2$ and $g'(x)>0$ for $x>2$, so $g$ decreases and then increases, and for any $k<2$ some horizontal line meets the graph twice [R1] The smallest value is $k=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $g(2)=-16$ and $g$ is increasing for $x\ge 2$, so the range is $g(x)\ge -16$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A horizontal line test is a statement about outputs: if one output can come from two inputs, the function is not one-to-one. Use the derivative to find where the direction of the graph changes.

subtopic: Asymptotes and axis crossings of a rational function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{4x^2+1}{x^2-x-6}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ with $x\neq 3$ and $x\neq -2$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the point at which the graph of $f$ crosses its horizontal asymptote. [3] (c) Find the $y$-intercept of the graph of $f$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$ [M1] Vertical asymptotes $x=3$ and $x=-2$ [A1] As $x\to\pm\infty$, $f(x)\to 4$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Set $\dfrac{4x^2+1}{x^2-x-6}=4$ [M1] $4x^2+1=4x^2-4x-24$ [M1] $x=-\dfrac{25}{4}$, so the point is $\left(-\dfrac{25}{4},\,4\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(0)=\dfrac{1}{-6}$, so the $y$-intercept is $\left(0,-\dfrac16\right)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A graph can cross a horizontal asymptote (it only needs to approach it as $x$ becomes large), so solve $f(x)=y_0$ to test for crossings. Vertical asymptotes come from zeros of the denominator that do not cancel.

subtopic: Solving f(x) = g(x) and inequalities with a GDC
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=e^{0.5x}$ and $g(x)=4-x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Solve the equation $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (b) Hence solve the inequality $f(x)>g(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Using a GDC to find the intersections of $y=e^{0.5x}$ and $y=4-x^2$ [M1] $x=-1.90$ [A1] $x=1.41$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) At $x=0$, $f(0)=1<g(0)=4$, so $f$ is below $g$ between the intersections [M1] $f(x)>g(x)$ for $x<-1.90$ or $x>1.41$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch both graphs on your GDC and read off all intersections in the stated domain. For inequalities, test one point to decide which graph is higher between the intersections.

subtopic: Exponential cooling model and its inverse
statement: The temperature $T$ degrees Celsius of a cup of tea, $t$ minutes after it is poured, is modeled by $T(t)=20+75e^{-0.04t}$, for $t\ge 0$. (a) Write down the initial temperature of the tea. [1] (b) Find the time taken for the temperature to fall to $50^\circ$C. [3] (c) Write down the range of $T$. [2] (d) Find an expression for $T^{-1}(x)$. [3] (e) State the domain of $T^{-1}$ and interpret the value $T^{-1}(x)$ in this context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T(0)=20+75=95^\circ$C [A1] [1 mark] (b) $20+75e^{-0.04t}=50$ so $75e^{-0.04t}=30$ [M1] $e^{-0.04t}=0.4$ and $-0.04t=\ln 0.4$ [M1] $t=22.9$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20<T\le 95$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{x-20}{75}=e^{-0.04t}$ [M1] $-0.04t=\ln\left(\dfrac{x-20}{75}\right)$ [M1] $T^{-1}(x)=-25\ln\left(\dfrac{x-20}{75}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Domain is $20<x\le 95$ [A1] $T^{-1}(x)$ is the time, in minutes, taken for the tea to cool to $x^\circ$C [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The domain of an inverse is the range of the original function, so find the range first. In context questions, say what the inverse represents in words, including units.

subtopic: Piecewise tariff and comparing two pricing plans
statement: An electricity company charges \$$C(x)$ for $x$ kWh of electricity used in a month, where $C(x)=0.12x$ for $0\le x\le 300$, and $C(x)=36+0.18(x-300)$ for $x>300$. (a) Find the cost of using (i) 250 kWh; (ii) 420 kWh. [3] (b) A customer's bill is \$70. Find the number of kWh used, to the nearest kWh. [2] A second company charges a flat rate of \$0.15 per kWh. (c) Determine the values of $x$ for which the second company is cheaper than the first. [4]
markscheme: (a) (i) $C(250)=0.12\times250=\$30$ [A1] (ii) uses the second rule since $420>300$: $36+0.18(120)$ [M1] $=\$57.60$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $C(300)=36<70$, so use $36+0.18(x-300)=70$ [M1] $x=488.9\ldots\approx 489$ kWh [A1] [2 marks] (c) For $0\le x\le300$: $0.12x\le0.15x$, so the second company is never cheaper on this range [M1] For $x>300$: $0.15x<36+0.18x-54$ [M1] $18<0.03x$, so $x>600$ [A1] The second company is cheaper only when $x>600$ kWh [R1] [4 marks]
tips: With a piecewise function, check which interval your input lies in before choosing a rule. When comparing plans, solve the inequality separately on each interval.

subtopic: Finding parameters from fg = gf
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=ax+2$ and $g(x)=3x+b$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. It is given that $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$ for all $x$. (a) Show that $b(a-1)=4$. [3] (b) Given also that $(f\circ g)(1)=17$, find the possible pairs of values of $a$ and $b$. [5]
tips: If $f\circ g=g\circ f$ for all $x$, compare the two expanded expressions. Then use a second condition to form a pair of equations and substitute.

subtopic: Domain and range of composite functions
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x-1$ for $0\le x\le 3$, and $g(x)=(x-2)^2$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (b) Find the range of $g\circ f$. [3] (c) Find the largest possible domain of $f\circ g$, and the range of $f\circ g$ on that domain. [4]
markscheme: (a) Range of $f$ is $-1\le f(x)\le 5$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(g\circ f)(x)=(2x-3)^2$ for $0\le x\le3$ [M1] Minimum value $0$ at $x=\dfrac32$ [A1] Values at the endpoints are $9$ and $9$, so the range is $0\le y\le 9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $g(x)$ must lie in the domain of $f$: $0\le (x-2)^2\le 3$ [M1] $2-\sqrt3\le x\le 2+\sqrt3$ [A1] $(f\circ g)(x)=2(x-2)^2-1$ [M1] Since $(x-2)^2$ takes every value in $[0,3]$ on this domain, the range is $-1\le y\le 5$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For $f\circ g$ the output of $g$ must lie inside the domain of $f$. Check turning points as well as endpoints when finding a range.

subtopic: Increasing and decreasing intervals of a product function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=xe^{-2x}$, for $x\ge 0$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and hence find the values of $x$ for which $f$ is decreasing. [3] (b) Find the range of $f$. [3] (c) Write down the largest value of $k$ such that $f$ is one-to-one for $0\le x\le k$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=e^{-2x}-2xe^{-2x}$ [M1] $=e^{-2x}(1-2x)$ [A1] $f'(x)<0$ when $x>\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f$ increases on $\left[0,\tfrac12\right]$ and decreases afterwards, so the maximum is at $x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $f\left(\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac{1}{2e}$ [A1] $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$, so the range is $0\le f(x)\le\dfrac{1}{2e}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $k=\dfrac12$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The sign of $f'(x)$ tells you where $f$ is increasing or decreasing; the exponential factor is always positive so only the bracket matters. A turning point limits both the range and where the function is one-to-one.

subtopic: Composite and inverse values from a table
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined on the domain $\{1,2,3,4\}$ by the table below. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline f(x) & 3 & 1 & 4 & 2 \\ \hline g(x) & 2 & 4 & 1 & 3 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find $(f\circ g)(2)$. [2] (b) Find $f^{-1}(4)$. [1] (c) Solve $(g\circ f)(x)=1$. [2] (d) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=4$. [2]
tips: For an equation such as $(g\circ f)(x)=1$, work backwards from the outside: first find what $f(x)$ must equal, then find $x$. Reading a table from the right-hand column to the left gives inverse values.

subtopic: Sign chart for a polynomial with a repeated root
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=(x+3)(x-1)^2(2-x)$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the zeros of $f$. [1] (b) State, with a reason, whether $f(x)$ changes sign at $x=1$. [2] (c) Solve the inequality $f(x)>0$. [3] (d) Hence solve $f(x)\le 0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=-3,\ 1,\ 2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(x-1)^2\ge0$ for all $x$, so this factor never changes sign [R1] Hence $f(x)$ does not change sign at $x=1$ (the graph touches the $x$-axis) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Testing intervals: for $x<-3$, $f<0$; for $-3<x<1$, $f>0$; for $1<x<2$, $f>0$; for $x>2$, $f<0$ [M1] $f(x)>0$ for $-3<x<2$ [A1] with $x\neq1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $x\le -3$ [A1] or $x=1$ or $x\ge 2$ [A1] [2 marks]
